summary: Open rolls toasted with refried beans and melted cheese, topped with fresh pico de gallo.

items.raw: 2 x 400g tins pinto beans, drained, 60ml liquid kept
4 bread rolls (bolillo or crusty white), split in half

steps.text: Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cumin for 1 minute, then the beans, kept liquid and salt. Cook for 5 minutes, mashing with a potato masher, until thick and mostly smooth.
Mix the pico de gallo ingredients and set aside.
Heat the oven grill to high. Pull out a little of the soft crumb from each roll half, spread the cut sides thinly with butter and toast under the grill for 2 minutes until golden at the edges.
Spread each half thickly with beans and top with cheese. Grill for 3 to 4 minutes, until the cheese is melted and bubbling.
Spoon pico de gallo over the top and serve straight away.

notes: Bolillo rolls are traditional; any crusty white roll works.
Good with a fried egg on top, or a spoonful of salsa verde.

title: Sopa de Fideo
summary: Toasted thin noodles simmered in a tomato and chicken broth, finished with avocado and lime.

steps.text: Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic with 250ml of the stock until smooth.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the broken pasta and fry, stirring constantly, for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden brown. Watch it closely; it turns quickly.
Pour in the tomato mixture carefully, as it will spit, and cook for 3 minutes, stirring, until it darkens slightly.
Add the rest of the stock, the oregano and salt. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, until the pasta is soft. Taste for salt.
Ladle into bowls and top with avocado, coriander, jalapeño if using and a squeeze of lime.

notes: Mexican fideo noodles are sold in some supermarkets' international aisles; broken spaghettini is the same idea.
Use vegetable stock to make it vegetarian.

title: Birria Tacos
summary: Chilli-braised beef in crisp, cheesy tortillas fried in the stew's red fat, with the broth for dipping.

image.credit: Photo: Sarah Stierch / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

items.raw: 4 dried guajillo chillies, stems and seeds removed
3 dried ancho chillies, stems and seeds removed
1.5kg beef chuck, cut into 4 large pieces

steps.text: Toast the dried chillies in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 30 seconds a side, until they smell fragrant but haven't blackened. Put them in a bowl, cover with boiling water and soak for 20 minutes.
Season the beef with the salt. Heat the oil in a large flameproof casserole over medium-high heat and brown the beef well on all sides, in batches, about 8 minutes. Set aside.

Heat the oven to 160°C (140°C fan-forced). Drain the chillies and blend them with the onion, garlic, chipotles, tomatoes, vinegar, cumin, oregano, cinnamon, cloves and 250ml of the stock until very smooth.

Pour the sauce into the casserole and fry, stirring, for 5 minutes until it darkens. Add the rest of the stock, the bay leaves and the beef. Bring to a simmer, cover and braise in the oven for 3 to 3 1/2 hours, until the beef falls apart.
Lift out the beef and shred it with two forks. Skim the red fat from the top of the broth into a small bowl. Taste the broth (the consommé) for salt and keep it hot.

Heat a large frying pan over medium heat. Dip a tortilla in the reserved fat, lay it in the pan, scatter with a little cheese and some beef, and fold it over. Cook for 2 minutes a side, until crisp and the cheese has melted. Repeat with the rest.
Serve the tacos with cups of hot consommé for dipping, and onion, coriander and lime on the side.

notes: The birria keeps for 3 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer, and tastes even better the next day.
Guajillo and ancho chillies are sold at Mexican grocers and some supermarkets. Check the tortilla label if you need these gluten-free.
Food safety:

title: Pão de Queijo
summary: Brazil's chewy little cheese breads, crisp outside and stretchy inside, made with tapioca starch.

image.credit: Photo: Murilo manzini / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan-forced) and line a tray with baking paper.

Bring the milk, oil and salt to a simmer in a small saucepan. Put the tapioca starch in a bowl, pour over the hot milk and stir hard with a wooden spoon until it forms a sticky, lumpy dough. Leave for 10 minutes to cool a little.
Beat in the egg until smooth and glossy, then the parmesan. The dough will be soft and sticky.
With oiled hands, roll the dough into 24 balls the size of a walnut and space them out on the tray.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until puffed and lightly golden. Eat warm.

notes: Brazilians use sour cassava starch (polvilho azedo), sold at Latin grocers; it gives a lighter puff. Supermarket tapioca starch works well.
Freeze the unbaked balls on a tray, then bag them. Bake from frozen, allowing 5 minutes more.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Gallo Pinto
summary: Costa Rica's breakfast of rice and black beans fried with onion and capsicum, with eggs and avocado.

image.credit: Photo: Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 400g tin black beans, drained, with 60ml of the liquid kept
items.prep: drained, with 60ml of the liquid kept

items.raw: 600g cooked white rice, cold from the fridge

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and capsicum for 6 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cumin and cook for 1 minute.
Add the beans and their liquid and simmer for 2 minutes, lightly crushing a few beans with the spoon.
Add the rice, soy sauce, vinegar and salt. Turn and fold for 5 to 6 minutes, until the rice is piping hot and coloured by the beans. Stir through the coriander.
Meanwhile, fry the eggs in the oil in a second pan until the whites are set.
Serve the gallo pinto with a fried egg, avocado, a spoonful of sour cream and hot sauce.

notes: In Costa Rica it's seasoned with Salsa Lizano, a tangy vegetable sauce. If you find a bottle, use 2 tbsp instead of the soy sauce and vinegar.
Use rice cooked the day before and kept in the fridge. Cooked rice shouldn't sit out at room temperature.
Runny yolks aren't recommended for pregnant people, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Fry the eggs until the yolks are firm.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Ropa Vieja
summary: Cuba's shredded beef, braised slowly with capsicum, tomato and cumin, finished with green olives.

items.raw: 1.2kg flank steak (or beef skirt), cut into 4 pieces

steps.text: Season the beef with the salt. Heat the oil in a large heavy saucepan or casserole over medium-high heat and brown the beef well on both sides, about 8 minutes. Set aside.
Turn the heat to medium. Add the onion and both capsicums and cook for 8 minutes until soft. Stir in the garlic, cumin, oregano and paprika for 1 minute, then the tomato paste for 1 minute more.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up the browned bits. Add the tomatoes, stock and bay leaves, and return the beef and any juices.
Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on low heat for 2 to 2 1/2 hours, turning the beef now and then, until it pulls apart easily.
Lift the beef onto a board and shred it along the grain with two forks. Return it to the pot with the olives and simmer uncovered for 10 minutes, until the sauce clings. Taste for salt.
Serve over rice, scattered with parsley.

notes: Black beans and fried ripe plantain are the classic sides.
It keeps for 3 days in the fridge and freezes well.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Moqueca
summary: A Brazilian fish and prawn stew, simmered gently in coconut milk with capsicum, tomato and lime.

image.credit: Photo: Bhasker Thodla / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

items.raw: 600g firm white fish fillets, skinless, cut into 5cm pieces
1 brown onion, sliced into thin rings

steps.text: Toss the fish and prawns with the lime juice, garlic and salt. Cover and refrigerate for 15 to 20 minutes, no longer, or the lime starts to firm the fish.
Heat the oil in a wide, deep frying pan or casserole over medium heat. Cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft, then add the capsicums and cook for 5 minutes more. Stir in the paprika and chilli.
Lay the tomato slices over the vegetables, pour in the coconut milk and bring to a gentle simmer for 5 minutes.

Nestle the fish into the sauce with its marinade, cover and simmer gently for 6 minutes. Add the prawns and cook for 3 to 4 minutes more, until the prawns are pink and the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Taste for salt, scatter with coriander and serve with rice and lime wedges.

notes: In Bahia it's finished with a spoonful of red palm oil (dendê), sold at African and Latin grocers.
Keep the simmer gentle once the fish goes in, so the pieces stay whole.
Food safety:

title: Eggs Benedict
summary: Poached eggs and ham on toasted English muffins, under a lemony, buttery hollandaise.

image.credit: Photo: Jon Mountjoy / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

steps.text: For the hollandaise, bring a small saucepan of water to a bare simmer. In a heatproof bowl that sits snugly over the pan without touching the water, whisk the egg yolks, lemon juice and 1 tbsp water for 2 to 3 minutes, until pale, thick and leaving a trail.

Take the bowl off the heat and whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream, until thick and glossy. Season with the salt and cayenne. If it gets too thick, whisk in a teaspoon of warm water. Keep it warm over the pan, off the heat.

Bring a wide saucepan of water to a gentle simmer and add the vinegar. Crack each egg into a cup. Stir the water into a slow whirlpool, slip in two eggs and poach for 3 minutes, until the whites are set. Lift out onto paper towel and repeat.
Meanwhile, toast the muffins until golden and crisp at the edges, and butter them. Warm the ham briefly in a dry frying pan until it is hot and just starting to sizzle.
Top each muffin half with ham and a poached egg, spoon over the hollandaise and scatter with chives. Serve straight away.

notes: Soft-yolked eggs and hollandaise made with lightly cooked yolks aren't recommended for pregnant people, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. For them, poach the eggs for 5 minutes until the yolks are firm and leave off the hollandaise.
If the hollandaise splits, whisk a fresh yolk in a clean bowl over the water and slowly whisk the split sauce into it.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: French Toast
summary: Thick slices of day-old bread soaked in cinnamon custard and fried in butter until golden.

items.raw: 8 slices day-old white bread, about 2cm thick

steps.text: Heat the oven to 120°C (100°C fan-forced) to keep the first batch warm.
Whisk the eggs, milk, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon and salt in a wide, shallow dish.
Melt a quarter of the butter in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Soak two slices of bread in the custard for 20 to 30 seconds a side, until soaked through but not falling apart.
Fry for 3 minutes a side, until deep golden and the middle feels set when pressed. Keep warm in the oven while you cook the rest, adding butter to the pan each time.
Serve with maple syrup and berries, dusted with icing sugar.

notes: Day-old bread soaks up the custard without going soggy. Fresh bread works if you dry the slices in a low oven for 10 minutes first.
Thick slices of brioche make a richer version.

title: Blackened Fish
summary: White fish crusted in a smoky Cajun spice mix and seared hard in butter, with a crunchy slaw.

image.credit: Photo: Edsel Little / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

items.raw: 4 firm white fish fillets, skinless, about 180g each

steps.text: Mix the slaw ingredients in a bowl and set aside.
Mix the spices, salt and pepper on a plate. Pat the fish dry, brush both sides with half the melted butter and press into the spice mix to coat.
Open a window and turn on the range hood: this gets smoky. Heat a heavy frying pan (cast iron is best) over high heat for 3 minutes, then add the oil.
Cook the fish for 2 to 3 minutes a side, depending on thickness, until the crust is very dark and the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Drizzle the rest of the butter over in the last minute.
Serve with the slaw, rice and lemon wedges.

notes: Use firm fillets about 2cm thick, such as ling, barramundi or snapper. Thin fillets overcook before the crust forms.
Some ready-made Cajun seasonings are very salty. If you use one instead of the mix here, leave out the salt.
Food safety:

title: Pot Roast
summary: Beef chuck braised slowly in red wine and stock with carrots and potatoes until it falls apart.

image.credit: Photo: Mark Miller / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 1.5kg beef chuck roast, in one piece

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C (140°C fan-forced). Pat the beef dry and season all over with the salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a large flameproof casserole with a lid over medium-high heat. Brown the beef well on all sides, about 10 minutes. Set aside.
Turn the heat to medium. Cook the onions for 5 minutes, then stir in the garlic and tomato paste for 1 minute and the flour for 1 minute more.

Pour in the wine and bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up the browned bits. Add the stock, Worcestershire, thyme and bay leaves. Return the beef, bring to a simmer, cover and cook in the oven for 1 1/2 hours.
Turn the beef, then add the carrots, celery and potatoes around it, pushing them into the liquid. Cover and cook for 1 1/2 hours more, until the beef is very tender and the vegetables are soft.
Rest the beef for 10 minutes, then pull it into thick pieces. Skim any fat from the gravy and taste for salt. Serve the beef and vegetables with plenty of gravy, scattered with parsley.

notes: Chuck has the connective tissue that melts into tenderness over a long braise. Leaner cuts like topside go dry.
Leftovers make great sandwiches the next day.
Food safety:

title: Welsh Rarebit
summary: A savoury cheddar, ale and mustard sauce spread thickly on toast and grilled until bubbling.

image.credit: Photo: Jeremy Keith / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

steps.text: Melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir in the flour and cook for 1 minute.
Gradually whisk in the beer until smooth, then the mustard and Worcestershire. Simmer for 2 minutes until thick.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the cheese until melted, then the egg yolk and pepper. Leave to cool for 5 minutes, until it's a thick paste.
Heat the grill to high. Toast the bread on both sides under the grill until golden and crisp.
Spread the cheese mixture thickly over the toast, right to the edges. Grill for 3 to 4 minutes, until bubbling and browned in patches. Serve hot with salad leaves.

notes: Worcestershire sauce contains anchovies, so this isn't vegetarian. Some brands make an anchovy-free version.
The cheese mixture keeps for 3 days in the fridge, ready for quick lunches.

title: Cornish Pasties
summary: Short pastry crimped around raw beef, potato, swede and onion, baked so the filling steams in its own juices.

image.credit: Photo: David Johnson / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

items.raw: 450g beef skirt steak, cut into 1cm pieces

steps.text: For the pastry, mix the flour and salt in a bowl and rub in the butter with your fingertips until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs. Add the water and bring together into a dough without kneading much. Wrap and chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan-forced) and line a large tray with baking paper.
Cut the pastry into four pieces and roll each out on a floured bench to a circle about 22cm across and 4mm thick, using a plate as a guide.
Layer a quarter of the potato, swede, onion and beef across the middle of each circle, seasoning each layer with salt and plenty of pepper. Top with a piece of butter.

Brush the edge with egg, bring the pastry up over the filling and press the edges together along the top until sealed. Crimp the seam by folding it over itself in small pleats. Cut a small steam hole in each side and brush all over with egg until evenly glossy, so the pastry bakes until golden.

Bake for 20 minutes, then turn the oven down to 170°C (150°C fan-forced) and bake for 30 minutes more, until deep golden and a skewer slides easily through the vegetables. Rest for 10 minutes before eating.

notes: Everything goes in raw: the beef and vegetables cook in the steam sealed inside the pastry, so cut them small and thin.
Skirt is the traditional cut. Chuck steak works too, cut finely.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Fish Pie
summary: White fish, salmon, smoked salmon and prawns in a creamy parsley sauce under a buttery mash crust.

items.raw: 400g firm white fish fillets, skinless, cut into 3cm pieces
250g salmon fillet, skinless, cut into 3cm pieces

steps.text: Boil the potatoes in salted water for 18 to 20 minutes until tender. Drain well, mash with the butter, milk and salt, and set aside.
Meanwhile, warm the milk with the bay leaf and onion in a saucepan until steaming. Turn off the heat and leave for 10 minutes, then discard the bay leaf and onion.

Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan-forced). Melt the butter in a clean saucepan over medium heat, stir in the flour and cook for 1 minute. Gradually whisk in the warm milk and simmer for 3 minutes, stirring, until thick. Stir in the mustard, lemon juice and salt, and take off the heat.
Spread the raw fish, salmon, smoked salmon, prawns and peas in a 2.5L baking dish. Stir the parsley through the sauce and pour it over evenly.
Spoon the mash over the top, starting at the edges to seal in the filling, rough it up with a fork and scatter with the cheese.

Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the top is golden and the filling is bubbling at the edges. Check a piece of fish in the middle: it should be opaque and flake easily. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.

notes: Fish pie packs from the supermarket seafood counter make this quicker; use 1kg in total.
Assemble up to a day ahead and keep covered in the fridge. Bake from cold for 45 minutes.

title: Scotch Eggs
summary: Jammy-yolked eggs wrapped in herby sausage meat, crumbed and fried until crisp.

image.credit: Photo: Unhindered by Talent / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

steps.text: Lower the 6 eggs into a saucepan of boiling water and boil for 6 1/2 minutes. Move straight into iced water for 10 minutes, then peel carefully.

Mix the sausage mince with the sage, pepper and nutmeg and divide into six. Flatten each portion into a thin patty on a piece of baking paper, sit an egg in the middle and wrap the meat around it, pinching to seal with no gaps.
Roll each in flour, then the beaten egg, then the panko, pressing it on. Chill for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan-forced). Heat the oil in a deep, heavy saucepan to 160°C, no more than a third full. Fry the eggs two or three at a time for 6 to 7 minutes, turning, until deep golden. Drain on paper towel.

Put them on a tray and bake for 8 to 10 minutes, until the sausage meat is cooked through (75°C when a thermometer is pushed into the meat). Rest for 5 minutes, then halve and serve warm or cold with mustard.

notes: Runny yolks aren't recommended for pregnant people, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Boil the eggs for 9 minutes for firm yolks.
Never leave hot oil unattended. Let it cool completely before you move or strain it.
Sausage mince is sold at the meat counter. Or squeeze good pork sausages out of their skins.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Käsespätzle
summary: Soft homemade egg noodles layered with melting Gruyère and emmental under sweet fried onions.

steps.text: Beat the flour, eggs, milk, salt and nutmeg with a wooden spoon for 3 to 4 minutes, until the batter is thick, smooth and starts to bubble. Rest for 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 20 minutes, stirring often, until deep golden and soft. Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan-forced) and butter a baking dish.

Bring a large saucepan of salted water to the boil. Press a third of the batter through a spätzle maker or a colander with large holes into the water. When the spätzle float, after about 1 minute, lift them out with a slotted spoon.
Layer the hot spätzle in the dish with the cheeses and pepper, finishing with cheese. Repeat with the rest of the batter.
Top with the onions and bake for 10 minutes, until the cheese has melted through. Scatter with chives and serve with a green salad.

notes: If the batter won't drip through the holes, add a splash more milk. If it runs straight through, beat in a little more flour.
The cheeses are made with animal rennet, which some vegetarians avoid.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Kaiserschmarrn
summary: Austria's fluffy torn pancake with rum-soaked raisins, caramelised in the pan and dusted with icing sugar.

steps.text: Soak the raisins in the rum (or warm water) for 10 minutes.
Whisk the egg yolks, sugar and vanilla, then whisk in the milk and flour until smooth. In a clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with the salt to stiff peaks, then fold them gently into the batter.

Melt half the butter in a large non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat. Pour in the batter and scatter over the drained raisins. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until the underside is golden and the top is starting to set.
Cut the pancake into quarters and flip each one. Cook for 3 minutes more, then tear into bite-sized pieces with two forks.
Add the rest of the butter and the extra sugar and toss for 2 minutes, until the edges caramelise and the pieces are cooked through. Dust with icing sugar and serve with apple sauce.

notes: It's meant to look rough: the torn pieces catch the caramel.
Stewed plums are the traditional partner if you have them.

title: Bigos
summary: Poland's hunter's stew of sauerkraut, cabbage, pork, kransky and porcini, slow-cooked until mellow.

image.credit: Photo: Dr. Bernd Gross / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

steps.text: Soak the porcini in the boiling water for 15 minutes. Lift them out, chop them and keep the soaking liquid, leaving any grit behind in the bowl.

In a large heavy saucepan over medium heat, fry the bacon for 5 minutes until the fat runs. Add the pork and brown for 8 minutes. Add the onion and garlic and cook for 5 minutes, then stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute.

Add the sauerkraut, cabbage, apple, porcini and their liquid, wine, stock, bay leaves, allspice, caraway and pepper. Stir well and bring to a simmer until small bubbles break the surface and the cabbage starts to wilt.
Cover and cook on low heat for 1 1/2 hours, stirring now and then and adding a splash of water if it looks dry.
Add the kransky and cook uncovered for 30 minutes more, until the pork is very tender and the stew is thick. Taste for salt; the sauerkraut and bacon may be enough. Serve with rye bread.

notes: Bigos is better the next day and better still the day after. It keeps for 4 days in the fridge and freezes well.
A handful of chopped prunes added with the cabbage is traditional and adds a gentle sweetness.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Lecsó
summary: Hungary's summer stew of yellow capsicum, tomato and onion with sweet paprika, with eggs stirred through.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wide saucepan over medium heat. If using the kransky, fry it for 3 minutes until browned and lift it out.
Cook the onions for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the capsicums and cook for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until softened.

Take the pan off the heat and stir in the paprika (it burns easily), then return to the heat and add the tomatoes, salt and sugar. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, until the tomatoes have collapsed into a thick sauce. Return the kransky, if using.
Pour in the eggs and stir gently over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until just set in soft curds.
Serve straight away with crusty bread.

notes: Long, pale Hungarian wax peppers are traditional. Look for them at greengrocers in late summer.
Without the eggs, lecsó is also a great sauce for sausages or rice.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Pytt i Panna
summary: A Swedish hash of crisp diced potato, ham, kransky and onion, topped with fried eggs and pickled beetroot.

steps.text: Pat the potatoes dry with a tea towel. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the potatoes for 18 to 20 minutes, turning every few minutes, until golden, crisp and tender. Tip into a bowl.
Turn the heat to medium. Add half the butter and fry the onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add the ham and kransky and fry for 5 minutes until browned.
Return the potatoes with the rest of the butter, season with the salt and pepper and toss for 2 minutes until hot through. Stir in the parsley.
Meanwhile, fry the eggs in the rest of the oil in a second pan until the whites are set.
Divide the hash between plates and top each with a fried egg, with pickled beetroot on the side.

notes: It's the Swedish way of using up a roast: swap the ham for leftover roast beef or pork.
Runny yolks aren't recommended for pregnant people, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Fry the eggs until the yolks are firm.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Toast Skagen
summary: Sweden's classic prawn toast: cold prawns in a dill and lemon dressing, piled on butter-fried bread.

items.raw: 400g cooked prawns, peeled and roughly chopped

steps.text: Mix the mayonnaise, crème fraîche, mustard, dill, chives and lemon juice. Fold in the prawns and season with white pepper and salt. Keep in the fridge until needed.
Cut the crusts off the bread and halve each slice diagonally. Melt the butter in a frying pan over medium heat and fry the bread for 1 to 2 minutes a side until golden.
Pile the prawn mixture onto the warm, crisp toast and top each with a dill sprig. Serve straight away with lemon wedges.

notes: Keep the prawns cold until the last minute, and don't leave the finished toasts out for more than 2 hours.
A spoonful of salmon roe on top is the traditional finish.

title: Jansson's Temptation
summary: A Swedish gratin of potato matchsticks, sweet onion and anchovies baked in cream until golden.

image.credit: Photo: Anders Jonsson / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

items.raw: 1kg floury potatoes, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 60g anchovy fillets, drained and chopped, oil kept

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C (180°C fan-forced) and butter a 2L baking dish with a little of the butter.
Melt half the remaining butter in a frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10 minutes until soft and pale gold.
Spread a third of the potatoes in the dish, then half the onions and half the anchovies. Repeat, finishing with a layer of potato. Season with the pepper; the anchovies bring enough salt.
Warm the cream, milk and 1 tbsp of the anchovy oil and pour it over. Scatter with the breadcrumbs and dot with the rest of the butter.
Bake for 50 to 60 minutes, until the top is golden, the cream has thickened and a knife slides easily through the potatoes. Rest for 10 minutes and serve with a green salad.

notes: Swedish 'ansjovis' are sprats in a sweet spiced brine, sold at IKEA food markets. If you find them, use a 125g tin and its brine instead of the anchovies.
It's a Christmas table classic in Sweden, and good alongside roast meats.

title: Aussie Meat Pies
summary: Individual pies of rich beef mince gravy in flaky puff pastry, with tomato sauce on top.

image.credit: Photo: Philip Mallis / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

items.raw: 4 sheets frozen puff pastry, just thawed

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion for 5 minutes, then add the mince and cook for 8 minutes, breaking it up, until browned.

Stir in the flour and tomato paste for 1 minute. Add the tomato sauce, Worcestershire, stock, salt and pepper. Simmer gently, stirring now and then, for 25 minutes, until thick enough to hold its shape. Spread on a tray to cool for 20 minutes, then refrigerate until cold.
Heat the oven to 210°C (190°C fan-forced) with a tray inside. Grease a 6-hole Texas muffin tin (or six 10cm pie tins).
Cut six 14cm circles from the pastry for the bases and six 10cm circles for the lids, re-chilling the pastry if it goes soft. Press the bases into the tin and fill with the cold filling.
Brush the pastry edges with egg, put the lids on and press to seal. Brush the tops with egg and cut a small slit in each.

Set the tin on the hot tray and bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until puffed and deep golden and the filling is piping hot (75°C in the centre). Rest for 5 minutes, then lift out and serve with tomato sauce.

notes: Cold filling stops the pastry going soggy. Make it the day before if you like; cover and refrigerate once cooled.
Cooked pies freeze well. Reheat from frozen at 180°C (160°C fan-forced) for 25 minutes, until piping hot.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Zucchini Slice
summary: The lunchbox classic: grated zucchini, bacon and cheese baked into an easy, sliceable bake.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C (160°C fan-forced). Grease and line a 20 x 30cm slice tin with baking paper.
Squeeze the grated zucchini lightly in your hands to get rid of some of the water.
In a large bowl, mix the zucchini, onion, bacon, cheese and flour.
Whisk the eggs, oil, salt and pepper, pour into the bowl with the parsley and mix well. Spread evenly in the tin.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until golden and firm in the middle when pressed. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes before cutting into squares. Serve warm or cold.

notes: For a vegetarian slice, leave out the bacon and add a grated carrot and a handful of corn kernels.
Keeps for 3 days in the fridge and freezes well in portions.

title: Sang Choy Bow
summary: Quick stir-fried pork mince with water chestnuts and oyster sauce, eaten in cool iceberg lettuce cups.

items.raw: 225g tin water chestnuts, drained and chopped
1 iceberg lettuce, leaves separated into cups

steps.text: Trim the lettuce cups with scissors into neat bowls and keep them in iced water while you cook, then drain well.
Heat the oil in a wok over high heat. Stir-fry the garlic and ginger for 30 seconds, then add the pork and stir-fry for 5 minutes, breaking it up, until browned and cooked through with no pink left.
Add the carrot and water chestnuts and stir-fry for 1 minute. Add the oyster sauce, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine and sesame oil and toss for 1 minute.
Take off the heat and toss through the bean sprouts and most of the spring onion.
Spoon the filling into lettuce cups at the table, topped with fried shallots, chilli, the rest of the spring onion and a little hoisin.

notes: Chicken mince works just as well.
Water chestnuts are what give it the crunch, so don't skip them.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Ricotta Hotcakes
summary: Tall, soft hotcakes made light with ricotta and whipped egg whites, served with maple syrup and berries.

image.credit: Photo: Sarah Stierch / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

steps.text: Mix the ricotta, milk, egg yolks and sugar in a bowl. Sift in the flour and baking powder and stir until just combined.
In a clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with the salt to stiff peaks. Fold them through the batter in two batches, keeping as much air as you can.
Heat a large non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat and brush with a little butter. Drop in 1/4 cup of batter per hotcake, leaving room to spread.

Cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until golden underneath and set around the edges. Flip carefully and cook for 2 minutes more, until golden and springy in the middle. Keep warm in a low oven while you cook the rest.
Serve stacked, with maple syrup and berries, dusted with icing sugar.

notes: Use fresh ricotta from the deli counter if you can. Tub ricotta is wetter; drain it in a sieve for 15 minutes first.
Sliced banana and a slice of honey butter is the cafe way to serve them.

title: Crispy-Skin Barramundi with Greens
summary: Pan-fried barramundi with shatteringly crisp skin, spring greens, baby potatoes and a caper herb dressing.

steps.text: Mix the dressing ingredients and set aside.

Boil the potatoes in salted water for 15 minutes until tender. Add the broccolini, sugar snaps and asparagus for the last 2 minutes, then drain. Toss the greens and potatoes with the olive oil and garlic and keep warm.
Meanwhile, pat the fish skin very dry with paper towel and score it two or three times. Season both sides with the salt.

Heat the neutral oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Lay the fillets in skin side down and press them flat with a spatula for the first 30 seconds so the skin doesn't curl. Cook without moving for 5 to 6 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and the flesh is opaque most of the way up.
Flip, add the butter and cook for 1 minute more, until the fish is just opaque in the middle and flakes easily.
Serve the fish skin side up on the potatoes and greens, with the dressing spooned around (not on the skin, which keeps it crisp).

notes: Dry skin is the whole trick. If you have time, leave the fillets uncovered on a plate in the fridge for an hour first.
Snapper or salmon fillets work the same way.
Food safety:

title: Paneer tikka
summary: Paneer marinated in yoghurt and spices, grilled or pan-fried until golden.

items.raw: 200 g paneer, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Mix yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, ground coriander, ground cumin, garam masala, cayenne, kashmiri chilli powder, lemon juice and salt in a bowl. Add paneer cubes and stir gently to coat. Set aside for at least 10 minutes (or up to 2 hours in the fridge).
Heat oil in a large frying pan or frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

Thread paneer, onion and capsicum onto skewers, alternating pieces (or cook them separate in the pan if you don't have skewers). Working in batches, cook until the paneer is golden on all sides and the vegetables are softened and charred, about 8–10 minutes.
Transfer to a serving plate, scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot with lemon wedges and roti or rice.

notes: Marinade the paneer for at least 10 minutes, but up to 2 hours in the fridge makes it taste even better.
Use a good non-stick pan or oil-brushed stainless steel so the paneer doesn't stick. Don't move the pieces around too much, let them get a nice golden crust.
If you have wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes before threading.

title: Gyeran Mari
summary: Rolled egg omelette with vegetables, a banchan that keeps for three days.

steps.text: Blanch the spinach in salted boiling water for 1 minute, then drain and squeeze dry. Mix with the grated carrot and chopped spring onion in a small bowl.
Crack the eggs into a large bowl, add soy sauce, sesame oil and a pinch of salt, then whisk until well combined. Stir the vegetable mixture into the egg.

Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat. When hot, pour in half the egg mixture and tilt the pan to spread it into a thin, even layer, about 3 mm thick. Cook for 2–3 minutes until the bottom is set but the top is still slightly wet.
Starting from one long edge, roll the omelette tightly towards the opposite edge, using a spatula to help fold as you go. Slide onto a plate and set aside to cool slightly.
Repeat with the remaining 1 tbsp oil and egg mixture to make a second roll.
Once both rolls have cooled to room temperature, wrap them tightly in cling film and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes, this makes them easier to slice.
Unwrap and slice each roll into 1.5 cm thick rounds. Serve chilled or at room temperature.

notes: Keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for 3 days.
Make ahead: prepare and slice the day before; store in an airtight container and eat chilled or bring to room temperature.
For extra fillings, try adding finely chopped mushroom or zucchini, just squeeze out excess moisture first.

title: Beef Mince Tacos with Frozen Veg
summary: Quick weeknight tacos with beef mince and frozen corn and capsicum.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon as it browns, until cooked through (no pink remaining), about 5 minutes. Drain off any excess fat if needed.
Stir in the taco seasoning, frozen corn and frozen capsicum until the seasoning is fragrant. Add the water and bring to a simmer until the sauce has thickened and the vegetables are tender.
Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes or until the vegetables are heated through and the sauce has reduced slightly. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Warm the tortillas in a dry frying pan for 30 seconds each side, or wrap in foil and heat in a 160°C oven for 5 minutes.
Set out the warm tortillas, spiced beef mixture and all the toppings. Let everyone build their own tacos.

notes: Freeze the cooked mince mixture in portions for an even quicker future dinner, just thaw and warm through.
Swap flour tortillas for corn ones, or lettuce leaves if you're out of bread.
Greek yoghurt works just as well as sour cream here.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Roasted Mushroom and Walnut Pie
summary: Earthy mushroom and walnut filling in golden butter pastry with local cream.

items.raw: 700 g mixed mushrooms (swiss brown, button, shiitake), halved or quartered
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it resembles breadcrumbs. Stir in the egg yolk and cold water until the dough just comes together. Shape into a disc, wrap and chill for at least 20 minutes.
While the pastry rests, toast the walnuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, stirring until fragrant. Set aside.
Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the mushrooms to the pan in batches, cooking until golden and any liquid has evaporated, about 15 minutes total. Stir in the toasted walnuts, thyme, cream, salt and pepper. Let cool slightly.
Preheat the oven to 200°C. Roll out two-thirds of the pastry and line a 23 cm pie dish. Spoon in the mushroom filling.
Roll out the remaining pastry to make a lid. Lay it over the filling, press the edges to seal, then trim and crimp. Brush with beaten egg and make a small slit in the centre.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is golden and the filling is bubbling gently at the edges.

notes: Make the pastry up to 2 days ahead and store in the fridge; the filling can also be made a day early and reheated gently before assembling.
If you can't find mixed mushrooms, use whatever is available, button mushrooms alone work just fine, though you'll lose some of that forest-floor flavour.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Tabbouleh
summary: Bulgur salad with parsley, lemon, tomato and olive oil, fresh, simple and foolproof.

items.raw: 200 g fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the bulgur in a large bowl and pour the boiling water over it. Cover with a plate or tea towel and let it sit for 10 minutes until the bulgur is tender and has absorbed the water.
While the bulgur soaks, prepare all your herbs and vegetables: chop the parsley, dice the tomato and onion, and chop the mint.
Once the bulgur is cool enough to handle, fluff it with a fork and add the parsley, tomato, onion and mint.
Pour over the lemon juice and olive oil, then mix everything together gently but thoroughly.
Taste it and season with salt and pepper. Remember: tabbouleh should be bright and tangy, so don't be shy with the lemon.
Let it rest for 10 minutes before serving so the flavours come together. You can eat it at room temperature or chilled.

notes: Make it ahead: tabbouleh keeps in the fridge for up to 2 days in an airtight container. The flavours actually get better the next day.
Swap the fresh mint for dried mint if that's all you have, use about a third of the amount.
Serve with cos lettuce leaves or pita bread for scooping.

title: Lolo Ika
summary: Fish simmered in creamy coconut milk with taro leaves and vegetables.

items.raw: 600 g firm white fish fillets, cut into chunks
1 large dalo (taro), peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook gently until soft and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Add the dalo chunks and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges start to soften.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a simmer until it is gently bubbling. Add the salt and stir well.
Add the fish chunks and taro leaves, folding them gently into the coconut milk. Simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and the dalo is tender.
Taste and adjust the salt and pepper. Serve hot in bowls with the creamy sauce spooned over.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the dalo and taro leaves the day before, stored in separate airtight containers in the fridge.
Swap the white fish for any firm fish, use what's fresh. Trevally, snapper or bream all work beautifully.
Use coconut cream mixed with a little water if you can't find coconut milk, or stir in 2 tbsp grated fresh coconut at the end for deeper flavour.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Canh Chua Rau
summary: Sour tamarind broth with water spinach, tomato and vegetables, a light and tangy vegetarian take on the classic.

items.raw: 200 g water spinach (rau muống), cut into 5 cm lengths
1 medium pumpkin (or squash), peeled and cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: peeled and cut into bite-sized pieces

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Mix the tamarind paste with 2 tbsp warm water until loose, then set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Pour in the vegetable stock and bring to a boil. Add the pumpkin and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until just tender.
Stir in the tamarind liquid and sugar. Taste and adjust the balance of sour and sweet to your liking.
Add the tomato wedges and water spinach, stirring gently. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the spinach wilts and the tomato softens slightly but still holds its shape.
Season with salt and pepper. Pour into bowls and serve with fresh coriander if you wish.

notes: Serve hot for a traditional bowl, or chill it and serve cold on a warm day.
The balance of tamarind and sugar is personal, start with less sugar and add to taste as you simmer.

title: Laksa Ipoh
summary: Creamy tamarind and coconut laksa with fish cakes and tofu.

items.raw: 200 g firm tofu, cut into cubes

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the rice vermicelli until tender, about 3 minutes. Drain and set aside.
In a separate pot, heat the laksa paste in a little neutral oil over medium heat, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the tamarind paste and palm sugar, stirring to combine, then pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce to low heat and cook for 10 minutes to let the flavours settle.
While the laksa broth is simmering, heat a separate small pan over medium-high heat and fry the fish cake slices for 2 minutes on each side until lightly coloured. Remove and set aside.
In the same pan, fry the tofu cubes until golden on a few sides, about 5 minutes total. Set aside.
Taste the broth and adjust the salt as needed. The balance should be creamy, tangy and slightly sweet.
Divide the cooked vermicelli among four deep bowls. Top each with the fried fish cakes, tofu, bean sprouts and spring onions.
Ladle the hot laksa broth over the noodles and vegetables. Garnish with red chilli if using, fresh coriander and a generous scatter of fried shallots. Serve immediately.

notes: The laksa paste is the backbone, a good quality one saves time. If you can't find tamarind paste, soak a ball of tamarind pulp in hot water for 10 minutes, then strain.
Make the broth first and it'll wait for you while you fry the tofu and fish cakes. The noodles should be cooked fresh just before serving.
Some people add prawns to this laksa. If you'd like them, toss in 200 g of cooked prawns if that's how you like it.

title: Sopa de Lentejas
summary: Red lentil soup with dried chillies, cumin, and lime, a Lenten dish that's good all year.

steps.text: Heat a large pot over medium heat. Toast the cumin seeds, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant. Remove and set aside.

In the same pot, warm the neutral oil. Add the guajillo and ancho chillies and toast them, turning gently, until they smell rich and toasted, about 2 minutes. Be careful not to burn them. Remove and set aside.
Add the halved onion and whole garlic cloves to the pot and cook until lightly charred, about 4 minutes. This adds depth to the broth.
Soak the toasted chillies in 250 ml of hot water for 5 minutes until soft, then blend with the soaking water until smooth. Strain through a fine sieve into the pot, pressing the pulp through.

Add the red lentils and vegetable stock to the pot. Crush the toasted cumin seeds and stir them in. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils break down completely and the soup thickens.
Season with salt to taste. The soup should be thick but pourable.
Serve hot with lime wedges on the side. Squeeze lime juice into each bowl and scatter coriander over the top if you like.

notes: Makes a generous batch. Keeps in the fridge for up to 4 days or freezes well for a month.
If you can't find guajillo or ancho chillies, use 3–4 dried red chillies of any kind, the technique is what matters.

title: Phở Gà
summary: Delicate chicken phở with charred ginger and onion, Hanoi-style broth simmered low and slow.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken bones (and pieces such as necks, wings and feet)
items.note: and pieces such as necks, wings and feet

items.raw: 500 g cooked chicken, shredded (or use poached chicken breast)
Fresh herbs: coriander, Thai basil, mint (a big handful altogether)

steps.text: Heat a heavy-based pot or wok over medium-high heat. Place the unpeeled ginger and onion directly on the heat and char them, turning occasionally, until blackened all over, about 8–10 minutes. This gives the broth a subtle, sweet depth. Scrape away the worst of the char if you like, but don't wash it off.

Blanch the chicken bones and pieces: bring a large pot of water to the boil, add the chicken, and simmer for 2 minutes. Drain and rinse the bones under cold water, then scrape away any scum. This keeps your broth clear and clean.

In a clean pot, add 2 litres of water and bring to the boil. Add the blanched chicken bones, charred ginger and onion, star anise, cinnamon stick, garlic, coriander seeds and peppercorns. Bring back to the boil, then reduce the heat to low and simmer, uncovered, for at least 3 hours. The longer you go, the better, Mum simmers hers overnight. Skim off any foam that rises in the first 20 minutes.
About 30 minutes before you want to eat, taste the broth and adjust with fish sauce and salt. Strain the broth through a fine sieve, discarding the solids.
Cook the rice noodles according to packet directions, usually a few minutes in boiling water, until soft and tender but still slightly springy, then drain.

To serve, place a nest of noodles in each bowl. Ladle the hot broth over the noodles, then top with shredded cooked chicken. Scatter with fresh herbs, spring onion and chilli. Serve with lime wedges and extra fish sauce on the side so people can adjust the seasoning.

If you're making this ahead, simmer the broth the night before and refrigerate it. The next day, skim off any fat that has solidified on top, then gently reheat until steaming and bubbling lightly before serving.

notes: Make the broth the night before and chill it; the fat will solidify on top and you can lift it off. This also lets the flavours develop further overnight.
If chicken bones are hard to find, ask the butcher, they'll usually give them to you cheap or free. Chicken feet add real gelatin and depth to the broth.
You can poach a whole chicken breast in the simmering broth for the last 20 minutes, then shred it to serve. Or buy a rotisserie chicken and shred that instead.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

title: Kleicha
summary: Crispy-edged, tender cardamom-date shortbread cookies from Iraq.

items.raw: 250 g dried dates, pitted and chopped

steps.text: Make the filling: heat the 2 tbsp ghee in a pan over medium heat. Add the dates and cardamom, stirring often, until the dates soften into a paste, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and set aside to cool.

Make the dough: in a bowl, cream the softened ghee with the sugar until pale, about 2 minutes. Add the flour, cardamom, cinnamon if using, salt and milk. Mix gently with your hands until the dough comes together, it should be soft but not sticky. If too dry, add a touch more milk.
Roll: working with about 1 tbsp of dough at a time, gently roll each piece into a ball. Flatten between your palms into a disc about 6 cm across and ½ cm thick.
Stuff: place a teaspoon of date filling in the centre of each disc. Fold the edges up and gently seal, then flatten again into a thick oval or disc shape.
Mark: using a fork or the tip of a knife, press a gentle pattern into the top of each cookie, traditional kleicha have a decorative crosshatch or lattice. Do this gently so you don't break through.

Heat the oven to 180°C, then bake: place the cookies on a lined baking tray, leaving a little space between each. Bake for 15–20 minutes, until the edges are golden brown but the centres still feel soft to the touch. They will firm up as they cool.
Cool: let them rest on the tray for 5 minutes, then transfer to a wire rack. They'll crisp up at the edges while staying tender inside.

notes: Store in an airtight container for up to 5 days. They're best eaten the day after baking, when they've set but the date filling is still soft.
If your dates are very dry, soak them in a splash of warm water for 10 minutes before chopping.
You can make these ahead and freeze the unbaked cookies for up to a month; bake from frozen, adding 2–3 minutes to the time.

title: Rendang Daging Sapi Padang
summary: Slow-cooked beef in a rich coconut and spice paste, the signature dish of Padang.

items.raw: 1 kg beef chuck, cut into 4 cm chunks
5 cm piece ginger, peeled and chopped
3 stalks lemongrass, white part only, bruised

steps.text: Blend the garlic, ginger, red chillies, shallots and macadamias with 60 ml of the coconut milk until you have a smooth, thick paste. This is your spice foundation, don't rush it.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the lemongrass and bruise it gently with a wooden spoon to release its oils, about 1 minute.
Add the spice paste and cook, stirring constantly, until it darkens and the raw smell fades, about 8–10 minutes. The paste should start to break apart and release its fragrance.
Add the beef chunks and stir well to coat in the paste. Cook for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is sealed on the outside.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk. Stir well, then bring to a gentle simmer, until small bubbles appear at the edges. Do not boil. Reduce the heat to low.

Simmer, uncovered, for about 60–70 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes or so. The coconut milk will gradually reduce and the sauce will thicken and darken. By the end, the beef should be very tender and the sauce should be thick and cling to the meat, not swim in liquid. This is where patience matters, watch that the heat stays gentle so the coconut doesn't split.
Taste and season with salt. If the rendang feels too sharp, stir in the palm sugar. Remove the lemongrass stalks.
The rendang is ready when the sauce is nearly absorbed, glossy and deep reddish-brown, and the beef is so tender it breaks easily with a spoon. Serve warm.

notes: Rendang improves overnight as the flavours marry. Make it a day ahead and gently reheat, or store in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Use a heavy-bottomed pot so the heat stays even and the sauce doesn't catch at the bottom.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Steamed Perch with Ginger and Soy
summary: Whole perch steamed until just cooked, topped with ginger, spring onion and soy.

items.raw: 1 whole perch (about 500 g), cleaned and scaled
4 cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Remove the perch from the fridge 15 minutes before cooking to bring it to room temperature. This allows the heat to penetrate evenly. Pat dry with paper towel inside and out.

Fill a wok or large pot with water to a depth of about 5 cm and bring to a rolling boil. Set a bamboo steamer rack or metal steaming stand inside, or use a plate on chopsticks to elevate the fish above the water.
Place the perch on a heatproof plate that fits inside your steamer. Season lightly with salt inside the cavity and on the skin.

Carefully transfer the plate to the steamer. Cover with a lid and steam over high heat for 10–12 minutes, until the eye of the fish turns white and cloudy and the flesh is opaque when you gently press it at the thickest part near the backbone.
While the fish steams, warm the neutral oil in a small pan until just smoking, about 2 minutes on medium-high heat.
Remove the fish from the steamer and transfer to a serving plate. Scatter the ginger matchsticks and spring onion lengths over the top.
Pour the light soy sauce over the fish, then immediately pour the hot oil over the ginger and spring onion. The oil will sizzle and release their aromatics. Serve at once.

notes: The key is bringing the fish to room temperature first, it cooks through more evenly. If your perch is larger (750 g), add 2–3 minutes to the steaming time.
If you can't find perch, use any firm white fish whole, about 500 g: bream, snapper, or barramundi work well.
Sashimi-grade fish is not needed here; a regular market-fresh white fish is perfect.

title: Stifado
summary: Beef braised with pearl onions and vinegar until sticky and dark.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck, cut into 5 cm pieces
500 g pearl onions (or baby onions), peeled
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pearl onions, shaking the pot often, until they're coloured on all sides and lightly caramelised, about 8 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the pot. Brown the beef in batches, about 3 minutes per batch, until dark all over. Don't crowd the pan. Set aside.
Return all the beef to the pot. Add the crushed garlic and tomato paste, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the vinegar and red wine, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Add the tinned tomatoes, bay leaves, and cinnamon. Stir well.
Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and braise for 1 hour 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is very tender.

Add the browned pearl onions back to the pot and stir through. Continue to braise, uncovered, for another 30 minutes, until the sauce reduces and becomes sticky and dark, and the onions are completely soft.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh parsley if you like. This is good with crusty bread or over rice to soak up the sauce.

notes: This tastes better the next day, make it ahead and reheat gently.
If pearl onions are hard to find, use small shallots or just brown onion cut into chunks; the cooking time stays the same.
Serve with crusty bread, rice, or soft polenta to soak up the incredible sauce.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Pad Grapow Moo
summary: Stir-fried minced pork with holy basil and chillies served over rice.

items.raw: Handful of fresh holy basil leaves

steps.text: Heat your wok on high heat until it's smoking hot, about 2 minutes.
Add the oil, then immediately add the minced garlic and sliced chillies. Stir constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the pork mince and break it up with the spatula. Stir-fry, without stirring constantly, for 2–3 minutes until cooked through and starting to caramelize. You want colour on it.
Add the fish sauce and palm sugar. Toss well for 30 seconds to combine.
Pull the wok off the heat. Add the fresh holy basil leaves and fold through gently until just wilted and fragrant, don't let them brown.
Transfer the rice to a bowl or plate. Top with the pad grapow moo. Garnish with fried garlic and a fried egg if you want the real street-stall experience.

notes: If you can't find fresh holy basil, Thai basil works fine, use the same amount. Regular basil will change the flavour but won't ruin it.
Prep everything before you start cooking: mince the garlic, slice the chillies, tear the basil, measure the sauce. Once the wok hits temperature, there's no time to stop.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Ahi Poke Bowl
summary: Soy-ginger ahi tuna over rice with crisp vegetables and sesame seeds.

items.raw: 400 g sashimi-grade ahi (yellowfin tuna), cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: In a bowl, whisk together soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger and rice vinegar.
Add the ahi cubes and gently toss to coat. Let sit in the fridge for 5 minutes, until the surface of the fish is lightly coated in the marinade.
Divide the chilled rice between two bowls.
Top each bowl with marinated ahi and its liquid, then layer the cucumber slices and spring onions.
Sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve immediately with lime wedges on the side.

notes: Use only the freshest, sashimi-grade ahi from a reliable fishmonger. Serve immediately after assembly.
Make the rice ahead and chill it completely before building the bowls.
Swap cucumber for daikon radish if you want a bit of crunch and bite.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Bulgogi with Supermarket Steak
summary: Korean marinated beef steak, sliced and seared until caramelised, ready in 25 minutes.

items.raw: 2 spring onions, white and light green, finely chopped
items.prep: white and light green, finely chopped

items.raw: 800 g beef steak (rib eye, sirloin or rump), thinly sliced

steps.text: Combine soy sauce, mirin, sesame oil, garlic, ginger, sugar and spring onion in a bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the sliced beef to the marinade and toss to coat well. Let it sit for 5 minutes while you heat a large pan or wok over high heat.

Heat the oil in the pan until shimmering. Working in two batches so the beef isn't crowded, sear the sliced steak for 2–3 minutes per side, until caramelised at the edges but still tender. Transfer to a plate.
Pour any remaining marinade into the pan and let it bubble for 30 seconds to thicken slightly, then return the beef to the pan and toss to coat.
Transfer to a serving plate, scatter with sesame seeds and coriander if using, and serve straight away with rice and kimchi.

notes: Slice the steak against the grain, it'll be more tender. If it's too thick, pop it in the freezer for 15 minutes first to make it easier to slice.
Any supermarket steak works: the thinner you slice it, the less time it needs. Rib eye stays juicy, sirloin is leaner.
Make the marinade ahead and marinate the beef for up to 2 hours if you want deeper flavour, just let it come to room temperature before cooking.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Espinacas con Garbanzos
summary: Wilted spinach with chickpeas, garlic and olive oil, a simple, generous tapa.

image.credit: Photo: Tubamirum at French Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)

items.raw: 400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring gently, for about 1 minute until fragrant but not coloured.
Add the drained chickpeas and stir to coat with the oil. Cook for 2 minutes, then add the chopped spinach in batches, stirring as it wilts into the pan, this will take about 4–5 minutes in total.
Once all the spinach is wilted and the chickpeas are heated through, season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot or at room temperature with a lemon wedge on the side if you like.

notes: Tastes just as good at room temperature, perfect for setting out on the table while you cook other things.
You can add a pinch of smoked paprika or cumin if you want a little more flavour, but honestly, the simplicity is the point.

title: Kebab İçli Köfte
summary: Hand-rolled spiced meatballs stuffed with lamb and pine nuts, pan-fried until golden.

steps.text: Make the filling: heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 3 minutes. Add the lamb mince, pine nuts, pul biber, cumin and salt. Cook, stirring, until the lamb is no longer pink, about 5 minutes. Tip onto a plate to cool slightly.
Make the meatball mixture: combine the beef mince, chopped onion, flour, pul biber, cumin, salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix gently with your hands until just combined.

Roll and stuff: wet your hands with cold water. Take about 2 tbsp of the beef mixture and press it into a thin oval in your palm. Place about 1 tsp of the lamb filling in the centre, then fold and roll gently to enclose the filling, shaping into an even oval meatball about 8 cm long. Repeat with the remaining beef mixture and filling (you'll make about 16).

Pan-fry the köfte: wipe the pan clean. Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil over medium-high heat until shimmering. Working in two batches, fry the meatballs for 4–5 minutes on each side until deeply golden and cooked through (the filling should be no longer pink inside). Don't crowd the pan.
Serve hot with lemon wedges and fresh parsley, if using.

notes: Make the filling while the onion cooks, so everything comes together quickly.
Keep your hands wet when rolling, it stops the meat from sticking and makes shaping easier.
These freeze well raw; just add a couple of extra minutes to the cooking time straight from the freezer.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Tumpeng
summary: Turmeric rice cone with vegetables, egg and chicken, a ceremonial Balinese centrepiece.

items.raw: 300 g chicken breast, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the lemongrass and turmeric, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the stock and bring to a boil.
Add the rice, stir well, and reduce the heat to low. Cover and simmer for 18 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Season with salt.

While the rice cooks, season the chicken with salt, pepper, garlic, coriander, cumin and turmeric. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large pan over medium-high heat, add the chicken, and cook for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until golden and cooked through.
In the same pan, add the mushrooms and cook for 3 minutes until soft. Transfer to a serving plate.
Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Add the green beans and carrots, and cook for 4 minutes until just tender. Add the cabbage and cook for 1 minute more. Drain and transfer to a serving plate.
In a small pan, heat a little oil over medium heat. Crack the eggs into the pan and cook until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft, about 4 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.

Fluff the rice with a fork. Wet a bowl with water, fill it with rice, and turn it out onto a large serving platter to form a cone. Arrange the cooked vegetables, chicken and fried egg around the base. Garnish with coriander and serve with lime wedges.
To eat, each person breaks apart a piece of the rice cone and takes some of each dish, mixing the flavours together.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Bánh Canh Cua
summary: Thick tapioca noodle soup with crab, slippery and chewy.

items.raw: 400 g crab meat, freshly cooked or from 1 cooked whole crab
items.prep: freshly cooked or from 1 cooked whole crab

items.raw: Spring onion, thinly sliced, to serve

steps.text: Make the noodle dough: Pour 100 ml boiling water over the tapioca starch in a bowl and stir well. Let it cool for 2 minutes. Add the salt, then gradually add cold water while stirring until the mixture is smooth and has the texture of thick pancake batter, it should be glossy and slightly translucent. Let it rest for 10 minutes.

Bring a large pot of water (at least 2 litres) to a rolling boil. Working in batches, push the noodle batter through a large-holed colander or bánh canh press directly into the boiling water. The noodles should be thick and rope-like, about the width of a finger. Stir gently to prevent sticking. Boil for 3-4 minutes until they float and are tender but still chewy. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.
For the broth, heat the chicken stock and water in a large pot over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and simmer for 3 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the fish sauce, sugar and crab meat. Simmer for 5 minutes to warm through and let the crab flavour infuse. Taste and adjust with salt and white pepper.
Divide the cooked noodles among four bowls. Pour the hot crab broth over each serving.
Top each bowl with fresh coriander, spring onion, fried garlic and sliced chilli if using. Serve with a lime wedge on the side.

notes: If you can't find fresh crab, use 400 g tinned crab or frozen crab meat, thawed.
The noodle batter can be made up to 2 hours ahead and refrigerated; let it come to room temperature before using.
A bánh canh press makes thick, even noodles, but a large-holed colander works just as well.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Bún Bò Huế
summary: Spicy beef noodle soup with lemongrass and blood sausage, a Central Vietnamese classic.

items.raw: 600 g beef shin (or chuck), cut into chunks
6 stalks lemongrass, white part only, bruised
200 g pork blood sausage (lạp xưởng), sliced (optional)
300 g fresh rice noodles (or dried rice noodles)
Pickled turnips (cà chua đắng), to serve (optional)

steps.text: Toast the coriander seeds and annatto seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then crush lightly.

Place beef shin, pork knuckle, bruised lemongrass, ginger, onion, and crushed spices in a large pot with 2 litres water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 60 minutes until the beef is tender, skimming foam from the surface occasionally.
Add the whole red chillies and fish sauce, and simmer for another 10 minutes. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
If using pork blood sausage, add to the broth in the last 5 minutes of cooking until warmed through.
Cook the rice noodles according to packet directions. If using fresh noodles, blanch in boiling water for 1 minute.
Divide noodles into serving bowls. Pour the hot broth over the noodles, ensuring each bowl gets beef and a piece of sausage if using.
Serve with lime wedges, fresh coriander, mint, and pickled turnips on the side.

notes: Make the broth a day ahead for deeper flavour; reheat gently and add the sausage and noodles to serve.
The blood sausage is traditional, but if you can't find it, add extra beef shin or pork instead.
Central Vietnamese bún bò is spicier than northern versions, add more chillies to your bowl to taste.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Carnitas Tostadas
summary: Crispy tostadas piled high with slow-cooked pork carnitas, pickled onions and fresh coriander.

items.raw: 1 kg pork shoulder, cut into 5 cm chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat oven to 160°C. Put pork chunks in a heavy-based casserole with onion, garlic, cumin, oregano, bay leaf, salt, pepper and water. Cover and cook in the oven for 2.5 to 3 hours, until the pork is tender and falling apart, stirring halfway through.
While the pork cooks, make the pickled onions. Toss red onion with vinegar and salt in a bowl. Let sit for at least 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Once the pork is done, drain off as much liquid as you can, reserving it. Shred the pork with two forks.

Heat 5 mm of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When hot, lay a tortilla flat and fry for 1 to 2 minutes per side until golden and crisp. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel. Repeat with remaining tortillas.
Divide tostadas among serving plates. Top each with a generous handful of warm carnitas, a spoonful of pickled onions, and a pinch of fresh coriander. Serve with lime wedges.

notes: Make the carnitas up to 2 days ahead; reheat gently in a low oven or on the stove with a splash of water.
The reserved pork cooking liquid is liquid gold, use it to warm the carnitas or sip as a broth.
No corn tortillas? Flour tortillas work fine, but corn is the real deal.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Larb Moo
summary: Spiced minced pork salad with lime, fish sauce and toasted rice powder.

items.raw: 2–3 birds eye chillies, finely chopped (or less if you prefer)

steps.text: Toast the rice in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Tip into a spice grinder or mortar and pound to a fine powder. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the pork mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until cooked through and no longer pink, about 8 minutes.
Remove from the heat and stir through the lime juice and fish sauce. Taste and adjust the balance: it should be hot (spicy), sour and salty in equal measure.
Add the shallots, spring onions, coriander, mint and chillies. Toss to combine. Sprinkle the toasted rice powder over the top and fold through gently.
Transfer to a serving plate. Serve at room temperature with sticky rice and fresh vegetables (lettuce, long beans, cucumber) on the side.

notes: Larb is best served warm or at room temperature. If you can't find toasted rice powder at the markets, toast and grind white rice yourself, it only takes five minutes.
The heat is important: adjust the chillies to your taste, but the dish should have a good kick. Nok doesn't hold back.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Egusi Soup
summary: Melon seed soup with beef and leafy greens, thickened and rich.

items.raw: 2 red chillies, finely chopped (or 1 tsp chilli flakes)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add beef and cook, stirring, until browned on all sides, about 10 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the chopped onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes. Cook for 3 minutes, stirring to combine.
Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the beef stock and bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes until the beef is tender.
In a bowl, mix the ground egusi with 250 ml water to form a smooth paste. Slowly stir this into the soup, breaking up any lumps. Add the chillies and maggi cube.
Simmer gently for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The soup should thicken and become silky.
Add the spinach, stirring well to wilt it into the soup. Cook for 3 minutes. Taste and adjust salt and pepper to your liking.
Serve hot with fufu, rice or cassava bread to soak up the rich broth.

notes: This soup freezes beautifully and tastes even better the next day. Make a double batch on Sunday and freeze in portions for busy weeknights.
If you can't find egusi, you can substitute with equal parts ground almonds and sesame seeds, though the texture won't be quite the same.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Beef Stew with Dumplings
summary: Slow-cooked beef stew with herb dumplings, the meat tender enough to eat with a spoon.

image.credit: Photo: Mothusi Sekhomba / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 1 kg beef chuck, cut into 4 cm chunks
3 celery stalks, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy-based pot or slow cooker insert over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the beef all over, about 3 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion, carrot and celery until softened, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well, and cook for 1 minute.

Return the beef to the pot. Pour in the wine and stock, and add the bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, then either cover and transfer to a slow cooker on low for 6 to 8 hours, or cover and braise in a 160°C oven for 4 to 5 hours.
About 45 minutes before serving, add the potatoes and cook until just tender.

While the stew cooks, make the dumplings. In a bowl, combine flour, baking powder, parsley, thyme leaves and salt. Rub in the butter with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Make a well in the centre, add the egg and enough cold water to form a soft dough. Mix gently until just combined. Divide into 12 pieces and roll each into a ball.
Once the stew is nearly ready and the potatoes are tender, drop the dumplings into the simmering liquid and cook, uncovered, for 15 to 20 minutes until they float and are cooked through.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot.

notes: This stew improves the next day when the flavours have had time to meld. Cool quickly and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
If you don't have wine, use an extra 250 ml beef stock instead.
For camp oven: brown the meat and veg in a big Dutch oven, then pop it straight into the coals for 3 to 4 hours.

Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Gigantes Plaki
summary: Giant butter beans baked in tomato sauce with herbs and olive oil.

items.raw: 800 g tin giant butter beans (gigantes plaki), drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large baking dish or shallow ovenproof pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook gently, stirring, until softened and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes, drained beans, oregano, bay leaves, and chilli flakes. Stir well to combine. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Add 120 ml of water to loosen the sauce slightly, the beans should be mostly submerged in tomato liquid.

Transfer the dish to a 180°C oven (or continue cooking in the pan if it's heatproof). Bake uncovered for 45–50 minutes, until the sauce has thickened and reduced slightly and the flavours have melded. Stir once halfway through.
Taste and adjust seasoning if needed. The beans should be tender and the sauce should coat them richly. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Gigantes plaki is just as good served at room temperature the next day. The flavours deepen as it sits.
If your tin of beans is particularly large (500 g drained), add a little more tomato sauce or water to keep the proportion balanced.

title: Pilau ya Nyama
summary: Fragrant rice with beef and whole spices, a celebration in one pot.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Toast the cumin seeds, coriander seeds, cardamom pods, cinnamon sticks and cloves in a large, heavy pot over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Remove and set aside.
Heat the oil in the same pot over medium-high heat. Add the beef in batches, browning on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set the beef aside.
Add the onions to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and ginger and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the beef to the pot. Add the toasted spices and bay leaves, stir well, and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the rice, stirring to coat in the oil, and cook for 2 minutes. Pour in the beef stock, add the salt and pepper, and stir once.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low, cover tightly, and simmer without stirring for 45 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
