Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork, taste and adjust seasoning. Serve hot with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Pilau tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently with a splash of water.
If beef chuck is hard to find, use beef shin or any tough cut that braises well.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Gaeng Som Pla
summary: Central Thai sour curry with barramundi, tomato and herbs from a homemade paste.

image.credit: Photo: Sumit Surai / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 500 g white fish fillet, cut into chunks (barramundi or snapper)
Thai basil, small handful, roughly chopped

steps.text: Make the curry paste: pound the garlic, shrimp paste and dried chillies together in a mortar until mostly smooth. Add the ground coriander and turmeric and mix well.
Heat the oil in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add the curry paste and fry, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until fragrant.
Pour in the stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the fish sauce, tamarind paste and palm sugar, and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the fish and simmer gently for 8–10 minutes, until cooked through and beginning to flake. Do not stir roughly or the fish will break apart.
Add the tomato and simmer for 2 minutes to warm through.
Remove from the heat and stir in the coriander and Thai basil. Taste and adjust with fish sauce, tamarind or lime juice as needed. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the curry paste up to a day ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Fresh fish is best for this curry, ask your fishmonger what looks good on the day.
Use whatever white fish is fresh and local: snapper, flathead or barramundi all work well.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Karahi Chicken
summary: Tender chicken in a thick tomato and capsicum gravy, cooked in the karahi with whole spices.

items.raw: 800 g chicken thigh, cut into 4 cm pieces
2 red capsicum, cut into thick chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a karahi or heavy-bottomed frying pan over medium heat. Add the cardamom pods, cloves, cinnamon stick and bay leaves. Let them sizzle and colour for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and deep golden, about 8–10 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, stir and cook for 2 minutes until the raw smell goes.

Increase the heat to medium-high. Add the chicken pieces, salt and black pepper, and cook without stirring for 3 minutes to seal, then stir and cook for another 3 minutes until the chicken is no longer pink on the outside.
Add the ground coriander and turmeric, stir well for 30 seconds.

Pour in the tinned tomatoes and their juice, breaking them up with the spoon. Simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 12–15 minutes until the sauce is thick and the oil begins to separate from the tomatoes on the surface.

Add the capsicum chunks and green chilli, stir gently, and cook for 5–8 minutes more until the capsicum is tender but still holding its shape and the chicken is cooked through (75°C at the thickest point).
Taste and adjust the salt if needed. Scatter with fresh coriander and serve hot with naan, roti or steamed rice.

notes: This keeps well in the fridge for 2 days and freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
Ayesha's tip: Don't rush the tomato-breaking-down stage. That's where the flavour sits. If you like more heat, add a pinch of dried chilli flakes with the ground spices or more green chilli.
Food safety:

title: Masala Dosa
summary: Crispy rice and lentil crepe filled with spiced potato curry.

items.raw: 500 g waxy potato, boiled and diced
1 tsp urad dal (white lentils), if you have it

steps.text: Make the potato masala: heat oil in a small pan over medium-high heat. When hot, add mustard seeds and urad dal. Once the seeds crackle (about 30 seconds), add the chopped chilli and curry leaf. Stir for 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced boiled potato, turmeric and cumin. Stir well to coat and warm through, about 2 minutes. Season with salt to taste. Remove from heat and keep warm.
Heat a large non-stick pan or cast-iron griddle (tawa) over medium-high heat for 2 minutes until very hot. Lightly oil the surface.

Pour about 60 ml of dosa batter into the centre of the pan. Using the back of a ladle, spread it in a thin circular motion from the centre outward, working quickly to make a thin crepe about 25 cm across. The thinner the better.
Drizzle a little oil around the edges and under the crepe. Cook until the underside is golden and crispy, about 1–2 minutes. The edges should curl slightly.
Flip the dosa carefully and cook the other side for another 30 seconds until just set. Do not over-cook or it will become chewy instead of crispy.
Slide the dosa onto a plate. Spoon a quarter of the potato masala along one half of the crepe, fold in half, then fold into a triangle if you like.
Repeat with the remaining batter and filling. Serve hot with sambar and coconut chutney for dipping.

notes: Make the dosa batter 1 to 2 days ahead and keep it in the fridge. It ferments and becomes more flavourful. Use it straight from the fridge, don't bring it to room temperature.
If the batter is too thick, thin it with a splash of water. It should pour easily but still coat the pan.
The potato can be boiled and diced an hour ahead.

title: Boil-up
summary: One-pot corned beef, pork bones, potatoes and watercress – kai comfort food.

image.credit: Photo: Matyas Havel / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

steps.text: Place the corned beef, pork bones, onions and salt in a large pot. Cover with 3 litres of water. Bring to the boil, then reduce heat and simmer, partly covered, for 45 minutes.
Add the potatoes to the pot. Simmer, partly covered, for another 30 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the corned beef is cooked through.
Add the watercress and black pepper. Stir gently and cook for 2 minutes until the watercress is just wilted.
Carefully remove the corned beef and pork bones. Slice the corned beef and return to the pot. Serve hot in wide bowls with plenty of the aromatic broth.

notes: Make a bigger batch and cool the broth quickly; it freezes well for up to 3 months.
If you can't find good pork bones, use a ham hock or extra corned beef – the broth won't be quite as rich but it'll still be aroha kai.
Fresh watercress is key. If you can't get it, try silverbeet (spinach) or spring greens – add them the same way, just wilted.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Sugo di Calabria
summary: Deep red Sunday sauce with pork, garden tomatoes, and Calabrian heat.

items.raw: 600 g pork shoulder, cut into 4–5 large chunks

steps.text: Heat a generous glug of olive oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pork chunks on all sides, about 10 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the onion halves to the same pot and cook until caramelised at the edges, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and whole chillies, stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, then add the tinned tomatoes and fresh tomatoes with their juices. Return the pork to the pot and add the oregano. Stir well.

Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover partially and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 hours. The sauce should reduce by half and become deep red and glossy. The pork will fall apart easily when ready.
Remove the pork chunks and shred them with two forks, discarding any large bones or tough bits. Return the shredded pork to the sauce.
Taste and adjust salt and pepper. The sauce should be rich, thick, and warm with heat from the chillies. Serve over pasta with grated parmesan.

notes: Make this the day before and reheat gently, the flavour deepens overnight.
Freeze the sauce in portions for up to three months.
Serve over fresh pasta, pappardelle, or rigatoni, with a scatter of fresh basil and parmesan.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:

title: Hand-Pulled Lanzhou Noodles
summary: Silky stretched wheat noodles in warm beef and spice broth, topped with coriander and chilli oil.

items.raw: 400 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. Add warm water gradually, stirring with your fingers until a shaggy dough forms. Knead on a bench for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
While the dough rests, make the broth: heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add beef pieces in batches and brown on all sides, about 6 minutes total. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add onion, garlic, and ginger. Stir until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Add doubanjiang and stir constantly for 1 minute until it darkens slightly.

Return beef to the pot. Add sichuan pepper, cloves, star anise, bay leaf, and dried chillies. Stir to coat, then pour in stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and cook for 45 minutes until beef is very tender.
Season the broth with soy sauce and salt to taste. Keep warm on a low heat.
Divide the rested dough into two equal pieces. Oil your hands and the bench. Take one piece and stretch it gently into a rough rectangle about 20 cm long.

Fold the rectangle in half, then in half again (folding into quarters), and roll it loosely into a log. Repeat this process two more times, resting 5 minutes between each fold. This builds layers and develops the stretch.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Take your final dough log and, holding each end, gently stretch it by pulling away from your body and up over your arm, then back down, this distributes the gluten evenly. Stretch and fold, stretch and fold, until the noodle is about 50 cm long and very thin.
Pull the stretched noodle away from your arm and, using one fluid motion, lay it down into the boiling water. It will curl and coil, this is perfect. Repeat with the second piece of dough.
The noodles will rise to the surface within 2–3 minutes. Let them cook for another 1–2 minutes until they're just tender, then use a strainer to carefully lift them into serving bowls.
Pour hot broth into each bowl with the noodles. Top generously with coriander, spring onion, a drizzle of chilli oil, and white pepper.

notes: The dough can be made up to 4 hours ahead, wrapped and refrigerated. Let it come to room temperature before stretching.
The broth keeps for 3 days in the fridge and tastes even better the next day.
If you're nervous about pulling noodles, you can roll the final dough thin and cut it into thick strands instead, it won't be quite the same, but it'll still be good.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Mercimek Çorbası
summary: Silky red lentil soup, finished with crispy onion, hot oil and lemon

items.raw: 1 tsp salt, plus more to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and rice to the pot. Stir to coat in the oil, about 1 minute.

Pour in the stock and add the salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, uncovered, until the lentils and rice break down completely and the soup becomes creamy, about 25–30 minutes. Stir occasionally.
Blend the soup until smooth and silky using a blender or stick blender. If it's too thick, add a little water. Season with lemon juice, more salt and black pepper to taste.

For the topping: heat the oil in a small pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring often, until golden and crispy, about 8 minutes. Drain on paper towel. If using butter and Aleppo pepper, warm them together in the same pan.
Ladle the soup into bowls. Top with crispy onion, and drizzle with the hot oil (and butter-pepper mixture if using). Serve with lemon wedges.

notes: If you prefer a thinner soup, add more stock or water before blending.
Make the crispy onion topping ahead and store in an airtight container, it keeps for 3 days and turns any soup into something special.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Ilish Macher Jhol
summary: Hilsa fish in mustard oil and turmeric gravy, Bengal's monsoon dish.

items.raw: 800 g whole hilsa fish, cleaned and cut into steaks (head and tail included)

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat until it just begins to smoke. This is essential: the pungency mellows into warmth.
Add the nigella seeds and let them crackle for a few seconds until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Stir in the turmeric and cook for a few seconds, until fragrant, to release its colour and flavour into the oil.
Carefully arrange the fish pieces in the pan. They will sizzle. Let them sit undisturbed for 2 minutes on each side so the flesh firms gently.
Add the water and green chillies. Bring to a gentle simmer, until small bubbles break the surface. Add salt.

Cover and cook over low heat for about 15 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested, and the broth has begun to amalgamate with the oil and turmeric. Turn the thicker pieces halfway through.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot, with rice. The broth is as important as the fish.

notes: Ilish, hilsa fish, is prized for its soft, buttery flesh and its brief monsoon season. If hilsa is impossible to find, use another oily river fish such as Indian salmon or mackerel, though the dish will be subtly different.
The mustard oil is not negotiable. It is the backbone of this dish. Do not substitute.
Serve with steamed rice to catch every drop of the broth.

title: Kinilaw na Tuna
summary: Raw tuna cured in vinegar and lime, with coconut milk, chilli and ginger.

items.raw: 500 g sashimi-grade tuna, cut into bite-sized cubes
3 spring onions, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Cut the sashimi-grade tuna into bite-sized cubes and place in a glass or ceramic bowl (not metal, as vinegar will react).
Pour the vinegar and lime juice over the tuna and stir gently to combine. Let it sit in the fridge for 5 minutes so the acid begins to denature the fish.
Add the coconut milk, sliced chillies and julienned ginger, and stir gently to coat everything.
Add the spring onions and taste, adjusting salt as needed. The acid should be balanced by the richness of the coconut milk.
Cover and chill until ready to serve. Kinilaw is best eaten the same day, within a few hours of making it, while the texture is firm and the flavours are fresh.

notes: Use the freshest sashimi-grade tuna available. If you're unsure about the source, ask your fishmonger.
Coconut vinegar adds a more authentic Visayan flavour, but white vinegar works well too.
Eat the same day you make it – the acid cures the fish but doesn't preserve it like cooking does.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Borscht
summary: Deep beetroot soup with beef, potatoes and dill, the soup that defines home.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 2 cm pieces
400 g beetroot, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 3 medium waxy potatoes, cut into 1 cm cubes
2 tbsp white vinegar (or apple cider vinegar)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the beef on all sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Set the beef aside.
Add the onions to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Return the beef to the pot and add the beef stock and bay leaf. Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat and simmer, covered, for 30 minutes until the beef is starting to become tender.
Add the beetroot, potatoes, carrots and tomato paste. Stir well and simmer, covered, for 35–40 minutes until the beef is tender and the potatoes are soft.
Stir in the vinegar, then taste and season with salt and pepper. If you prefer a deeper flavour, add a little more vinegar.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot, topped with fresh dill and a spoonful of sour cream if you like.

notes: Borscht keeps well in the fridge for up to 4 days, and the flavour deepens each day. Reheat gently on the stove.
For a vegetarian version, skip the beef and use vegetable stock instead; the soup will need only 45 minutes on the stove after the vegetables go in.
Some cooks add 200 g cooked kidney beans with the potatoes for a heartier soup.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Adobong Manok
summary: Chicken braised in vinegar and soy with garlic and bay leaf, Kapampangan-style.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot or deep pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the chicken pieces all over, about 5 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the crushed garlic and peppercorns. Stir constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the vinegar and soy sauce, stirring well to combine. Return the chicken to the pot and add the bay leaves and water. Bring to a simmer until the liquid is gently bubbling.
Reduce heat to low, cover, and braise gently for 40–45 minutes, turning the chicken halfway through, until the chicken is very tender and cooked through (the juices should run clear when pierced).
Taste and adjust salt as needed. The sauce should be rich and deeply flavoured.
Serve hot with steamed rice, anak.

notes: This adobo tastes even better the next day, anak. Keep it in the fridge and warm it gently before serving.
If you don't have calamansi, use fresh lime juice or good white vinegar, both work beautifully.
Corazon always serves this with plain steamed white rice and a simple green vegetable.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Char Koay Teow
summary: Stir-fried flat rice noodles with prawns, cockles, bean sprouts and egg.

items.raw: 300 g fresh thick rice noodles (kway teow)
100 g cockles (if fresh), or tinned cockles, drained
2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm lengths

steps.text: Set a large wok over high heat until it's very hot, you'll feel the heat rise from it. Add 1 tbsp of the oil and swirl to coat.

Push the noodles into the wok. They'll clump at first, but keep them moving with your spatula, breaking them apart, until they're loosened and just beginning to brown at the edges, about 2 minutes. Push everything to the side of the wok.
Add the remaining oil to the empty side. Crack in the eggs and scramble them quickly with the back of your spatula until just set, then mix them through the noodles.

Push everything to the side again. Add the garlic to the empty spot and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Then add the prawns and cockles, tossing them with the garlic for 1 minute until the prawns turn pink and opaque.
Add the soy sauce, dark soy sauce and oyster sauce, tossing everything together. The noodles will darken and smell wonderful, this takes about 1 minute.
Add the bean sprouts and spring onions, tossing for another 30 seconds. If using fresh chilli, toss that through now.
Taste and add more soy sauce if you need it. Divide between bowls and serve straight away, while it's still hot and the edges are a bit charred.

notes: The noodles need to be fresh and thick (kway teow), sold in the refrigerated section, they're usually stuck together in a slab. If you can only find thin dried rice noodles, use them, but fresh ones give you that lovely charred edge.
The heat and speed are everything here. Once you start cooking, don't stop stirring. A slow char koay teow is a sad char koay teow.
Cockles are traditional, use fresh ones from the fishmonger if you can find them, or tinned ones from the Asian aisle. If you really can't find them, use more prawns instead.
Food safety:

title: Yakitori Momo
summary: Grilled chicken thigh skewers with salt and lemon, cooked in a frying pan.

items.raw: 250 g boneless chicken thigh, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Thread the chicken cubes onto two metal skewers, leaving a small gap between each piece so they cook evenly until cooked through and golden. Pat dry with paper towel.
Heat the neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering, about 1 minute.
Place the skewers in the pan and cook without moving them for 4 minutes, until the bottom is golden and slightly charred.
Turn the skewers and cook for another 4 minutes until golden on the second side.
Turn once more and cook for 2–3 minutes, turning as needed, until the chicken is cooked through (no pink inside). The outside should be blistered and charred in patches.
Transfer to a plate, season generously with salt, and serve immediately with lemon wedges to squeeze over.

notes: Use bone-in chicken thighs if you prefer, they stay juicier. Cut around the bone and into cubes.
Presoaking wooden skewers for 30 minutes prevents burning, but metal skewers work best and cook faster.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Kartoffelpuffer mit Lachs
summary: Crispy potato pancakes topped with smoked salmon and dill crème fraîche.

items.raw: 800 g waxy potato, peeled and coarsely grated
Salt and black pepper, to taste
150 g smoked salmon, sliced or torn

steps.text: Squeeze the grated potato and onion firmly in a clean tea towel to remove as much moisture as possible, this is essential for crispy pancakes.
In a bowl, whisk the eggs, then stir in the drained potato and onion, flour, salt and pepper until combined.

Heat about 5 mm of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the oil is shimmering, carefully spoon the mixture into the pan in loose mounds (about 6 cm across) and flatten them gently with the back of a spatula.

Fry for 4 to 5 minutes until the underside is golden and crisp. Flip and cook the other side for another 3 to 4 minutes until golden. Work in batches and keep cooked pancakes warm on a plate lined with paper towel.
While the pancakes cook, fold the dill into the crème fraîche and season lightly with salt and pepper.
Serve the warm pancakes topped with a spoonful of dill crème fraîche and a few pieces of smoked salmon. Finish with a squeeze of lemon if you like.

notes: Make the potato mixture just before frying, it will start to weep if left to sit. If you must wait, drain and squeeze it again before cooking.
The crème fraîche topping can be made up to a day ahead and kept refrigerated.

title: Quenelles de brochet
summary: Pike dumplings in creamy shellfish sauce, a lighter Lyonnaise bistro classic.

items.raw: 400 g white fish fillet (pike, perch or barramundi)

steps.text: Pulse the fish fillet in a food processor until very finely minced. Add the softened butter and pulse until you have a pale, creamy paste. Work in the eggs one at a time, then fold in the cream by hand. Season with salt, white pepper and nutmeg. Taste a tiny spoonful by poaching it briefly in a small pan of water to check the seasoning. Chill for 10 minutes.

Bring the stock to a gentle simmer in a large, wide pan. Using two warm wet spoons, shape the pike mixture into quenelle shapes (or simply oval dumplings, don't fuss). Gently slide them into the simmering stock. They'll sink, then float to the surface when cooked through, about 4 minutes. Poach in two batches if needed so they're not crowded. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and keep warm on a plate.

For the sauce: melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour to make a smooth roux and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in the stock, then the cream, stirring until smooth. Simmer for 3 minutes. Stir in the cooked prawn and sherry, season with salt, white pepper and a pinch of cayenne. Taste and adjust.
Arrange the quenelles in a warmed shallow dish or on individual plates. Pour the Nantua sauce over and serve at once.

notes: Make the quenelle mixture up to 2 hours ahead and chill. The sauce can be made while the quenelles poach.
If pike isn't available, perch, barramundi or any firm white fish works well, this is a weeknight dinner, not a pilgrimage.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Bacalao a la Vizcaína
summary: Salt cod in dark pepper and tomato sauce, the Vizcaya way.

items.raw: 4 dried choricero peppers (or 3 large dried red peppers)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Soak the salt cod in cold water for 24 hours, changing the water every 6–8 hours. This draws out the salt. After soaking, drain and place in a large pot with 1 litre of fresh cold water. Bring slowly to a gentle simmer, do not boil. Simmer for 8–10 minutes until the flesh is tender and flakes easily. Remove from heat, drain gently, and set aside on a warm plate. Keep the cooking broth.

While the cod simmers, prepare the sauce. Toast the dried choricero peppers briefly in a dry pan over medium heat, about 30 seconds each side, until fragrant. Soak them in 200 ml of warm water for 10 minutes to soften, then drain. Scrape the flesh from the skin with a spoon and discard the skins and seeds. You should have a dark red paste.

Heat the olive oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook gently, stirring occasionally, for about 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the sliced garlic and cook for 1 minute more until fragrant.

Stir in the paprika and cook for 30 seconds. Add the pepper paste you made, the tinned tomatoes, and 2 tablespoons of water. Stir well to combine. Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce darkens and thickens slightly. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.

Carefully place the warm salt cod fillets into the sauce. Pour about 100 ml of the reserved cooking broth around (not over) the cod. Simmer very gently for 5 minutes, the cod will break apart if you're rough with it. The sauce should be rich, dark, and coat the fish.
Serve in deep earthenware bowls with the sauce spooned around the fish. Eat with good bread and a glass of txakoli or dry white wine.

notes: Salt cod must be soaked for 24 hours before cooking. Start the night before.
Choricero peppers are essential, they give the sauce its deep colour and flavour. Find them in Spanish delis or good supermarkets; regular dried peppers work but won't taste the same.
This dish is best made in a heavy earthenware cazuela, but any heavy-bottomed pan works fine.

title: Lamb and Apricot Bredie
summary: Spiced lamb and apricot stew, slow-cooked with turmeric and cinnamon.

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onions over medium heat, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Add the turmeric, cinnamon, coriander and black pepper. Stir through the onions, cooking gently for 1 minute until fragrant.

Return the lamb to the pot. Pour in the stock and add the bay leaves. Stir in the golden syrup and apricots. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook gently for 1 hour, or until the lamb is very tender.
Stir in the lemon juice, taste, and adjust the salt and spices if needed. The stew should be balanced, warm spice, a touch of sweetness from the apricots, and a hint of brightness from the lemon.
Serve hot, spooned over plain boiled rice.

notes: Bredie improves overnight as the spices deepen. Make it the day before and gently reheat it.
If you can't find dried apricots, use dried peaches or a combination of apricots and raisins.
Traditionally made with mutton; lamb shoulder works beautifully and cooks a little faster.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Frikadeller med rødbeder og kartofler
summary: Tender Danish meatballs with caramelised onions, pickled beetroot and buttered potatoes

items.raw: 400 g beetroot, peeled and thinly sliced

steps.text: Start the pickled beetroot: layer the beetroot in a bowl. In a small saucepan, heat the vinegar, water, sugar, salt, pepper and bay leaf over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Pour over the beetroot and let it cool while you cook the rest.

For the caramelised onions, melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced onions and salt, stirring often. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, until very soft and golden; set aside.
Meanwhile, start the potatoes: cut them into even-sized pieces and place in a pot of cold salted water. Bring to a boil and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until tender.

While the potatoes cook, make the meatballs. Mix the pork, beef, grated onion, milk, breadcrumbs, egg, salt and pepper gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork. Shape into 12 to 16 balls about the size of a golf ball.
Heat butter or oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Working in batches if needed, cook the meatballs, turning gently, for 8 to 10 minutes total, until golden and cooked through.
Drain the potatoes and return them to the pot. Add the butter and a pinch of salt, and toss gently to coat.
Divide the potatoes among serving plates. Top with the meatballs and caramelised onions, then serve with the pickled beetroot on the side. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: The pickled beetroot can be made a day ahead and keeps in the fridge for up to a week.
If you can't find waxy potatoes, use any small firm potatoes and cut them in half.
Frikadeller freeze well uncooked; shape and refrigerate on a tray for 30 minutes, then freeze in a bag for up to three months.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Nasu Dengaku
summary: Grilled eggplant with warm miso glaze, charred outside and silky within.

image.credit: Photo: Ewan Munro from London, UK / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

steps.text: Score the flesh of each eggplant half with shallow cuts in a crosshatch pattern, being careful not to pierce the skin.
Brush the eggplant flesh generously with oil. Season lightly with salt.
Heat a grill pan or barbecue to medium-high. Grill the eggplants flesh-side down for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and charred. Turn skin-side down and grill for another 1 to 2 minutes.
While the eggplants cook, whisk together the miso, sugar, mirin, and dashi powder in a small bowl until smooth.
Transfer the grilled eggplants to a serving plate, flesh-side up. Spread the miso glaze generously over the hot flesh, it will warm and soften.
Scatter sesame seeds over the top and serve at once.

notes: The eggplants can be grilled up to 30 minutes ahead; reheat gently in the oven at 180°C for 5 minutes, then glaze and serve.
Red miso gives a deeper colour; white miso is sweeter and milder. Use what you have.
If you don't have a grill pan, use a regular frying pan over medium-high heat, or grill over charcoal if you can.

title: Kol Börek
summary: Crispy fried yufka rolls filled with spiced meat and cheese.

items.raw: 150 g white cheese (feta or beyaz peynir), crumbled

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until softened and golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, stirring to break it up, until browned through, about 6 minutes. Drain off any excess fat.
Stir in the cumin, black pepper, salt and parsley. Remove from heat and let cool for 5 minutes.
Fold in the crumbled cheese and stir to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning. Let the filling cool completely.
Lay one sheet of yufka on a clean work surface. Place 3 tbsp of filling along one long edge, leaving a 2 cm border.

Fold the sides in by about 2 cm on each end, then roll tightly away from you, keeping it as firm as you can. The roll should be about 10 cm long and shaped like a tight cylinder. Repeat with remaining yufka and filling.
Heat neutral oil in a large, deep frying pan to 180°C (or until a small piece of yufka sizzles immediately when dropped in).
Carefully place 2 or 3 börek at a time into the hot oil, don't crowd the pan. Fry until deep golden brown all over, about 3 minutes, turning once halfway through.
Transfer to a paper towel to drain. Serve hot.

notes: Make the filling up to 2 hours ahead and chill. Roll the börek just before frying.
If yufka dries out, cover unused sheets with a damp tea towel.
Leftover börek can be reheated in a 180°C oven for 5 minutes to crisp up again.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

title: Kimchi-jjim
summary: Braised pork belly with aged kimchi and ginger, stewed until tender.

image.credit: Photo: I. H Cho / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

items.raw: 800 g pork belly, skin removed, cut into 5 cm cubes
items.prep: skin removed, cut into 5 cm cubes

items.raw: 500 g aged kimchi (napa cabbage), roughly chopped
3 tbsp kimchi juice (reserved from the jar)
2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Place pork belly cubes in a heavy-bottomed pot or braising pan. Add the water and bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Simmer for 8 minutes, skimming any scum that rises to the surface, until the pork is partially cooked.

Add the aged kimchi, kimchi juice, garlic, ginger, gochugaru, soy sauce, and sugar. Stir well, then return to a simmer. Cover and braise over medium heat for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pork is very tender and falling apart at the edges.
Taste and adjust the salt if needed. Add the spring onions and stir gently, cooking for 1 minute until just wilted.
Transfer to a serving bowl and scatter with toasted sesame seeds. Serve hot with steamed white rice.

notes: Use well-aged kimchi for the deepest flavour; old kimchi that's been fermenting for months is better than fresh.
Don't skip the skimming step, it keeps the braise clean and clear.
Leftover kimchi-jjim reheats gently on the stove with a splash of water.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Pantry Chicken and Lentil Soup
summary: Hearty weeknight soup with chicken, lentils and tomato from your pantry cupboard.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft and starting to colour, about 5 minutes.
Add garlic, carrot and celery. Stir and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add crushed tomatoes, lentils and stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium-low. Cook for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until lentils are very soft.
Stir in the shredded chicken and cook for 5 minutes to warm through. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Divide among bowls and serve hot.

notes: Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if it's thickened too much.
Use rotisserie chicken, or shredded leftover roast chicken. If you don't have cooked chicken, add 300 g raw chicken breast to the pot with the stock and cook for 12 minutes before adding lentils.
Swap red lentils for brown lentils if you prefer a firmer texture; they'll need the full 25 minutes to cook.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Roti with Curried Chickpeas
summary: Soft roti wrapped around spiced chickpea curry, comfort food the Fiji way.

items.raw: 1 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for cooking
1 red chilli, finely chopped (or ½ tsp chilli powder, optional)
400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed

steps.text: Make the roti dough first so it can rest while the curry cooks. Combine plain flour and salt in a bowl. Add 1 tbsp oil and rub it through the flour with your fingers until it looks like breadcrumbs. Slowly add warm water, stirring with one hand, until you have a soft dough. Knead gently for 2–3 minutes until smooth. Cover with a damp cloth and set aside.
Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the cumin, coriander, turmeric and chilli. Stir for 1 minute, then add the drained chickpeas and crushed tomatoes. Pour in 1 cup water and add salt. Bring to a simmer and cook, uncovered, for 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the curry is thick and the flavours have come together. Taste and adjust salt if needed.

While the curry simmers, divide the rested dough into 8 balls. On a lightly oiled surface or oiled palms, flatten each ball into a thin circle, about 20 cm across, working gently so the dough doesn't tear.

Heat a large non-stick frypan or tava over medium-high heat with a small amount of oil. Cook each roti one at a time for about 1 minute on each side until light golden and a little puffy. Stack them on a clean tea towel to keep warm and soft.
Serve the warm roti with the curried chickpeas spooned into the middle. Fold and wrap as you eat, with fresh coriander if you like.

title: Meen Curry
summary: Kerala fish curry with roasted spices, coconut milk and curry leaves.

image.credit: Photo: Kalakki at Malayalam Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.5)

items.raw: 600 g white fish fillets (snapper, barramundi or bream), cut into large chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the cumin and coriander seeds and toast, stirring constantly, until they release their fragrance and darken slightly, about 2 minutes. Watch them closely so they don't burn.
Add the curry leaves, then the onion. Cook, stirring often, until the onion is soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chilli. Cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they break down and the raw edge is gone, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir well. Bring to a gentle simmer, then carefully place the fish pieces into the curry. Season with salt and cook until the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Simmer gently, uncovered, for 8–10 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily. Do not stir aggressively or the fish will break apart; you can gently turn the pieces once if needed.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like, alongside steamed rice.

notes: This curry tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove or in the microwave until warm through.
Use any firm white fish you like, snapper, barramundi, bream or cod all work well. Avoid delicate fish that will fall apart.
Serve with steamed rice, appam, or flatbread to soak up the coconut broth.
Food safety:

title: Tagine d'Agneau aux Pruneaux
summary: Slow-cooked lamb with prunes and warm spices, a classic Moroccan tagine.

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot or tagine over medium-high heat. Season the lamb pieces with salt and pepper, then brown them in batches, 3–4 minutes per side. Set aside.
In the same pot, cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the chopped fresh garlic and fresh ginger, and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the ground ginger, cinnamon, and cumin, stirring constantly for 30 seconds until fragrant, to toast the spices.
Return the lamb to the pot and stir well to coat. Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Cover and cook gently on low heat for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the saffron threads and prunes, and stir. Simmer, covered, for another 20–30 minutes until the lamb is very tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper. Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make it the day before and reheat gently, the flavours deepen. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Serve with couscous or warm flatbread to soak up the sauce.
If you can't find saffron, add a pinch of turmeric instead for warmth and colour.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Katsudon
summary: Crispy panfried pork cutlet over rice with egg and onions, the weeknight donburi that beats takeout.

items.raw: 2 pork loin cutlets, about 150 g each, pounded thin to 5 mm
items.prep: about 150 g each, pounded thin to 5 mm

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 brown onion, halved and thinly sliced
2 cups cooked short-grain white rice, warm

steps.text: Set up your crumbing station: put the flour in one shallow bowl, beaten egg in another, and panko in a third. Season the pork with salt and pepper, then coat in flour, shaking off excess. Dip in beaten egg, then press into panko until fully coated.

Heat 3 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When it's hot and shimmering, carefully lay the pork cutlets in and cook until golden and crisp, 3 to 4 minutes on each side. The pork is done when it reaches 63°C in the thickest part. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium and add the sliced onion. Cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the mirin, soy sauce and water, and bring to a simmer.
Slice each pork cutlet into strips. Return the pork to the pan, nestled among the onions, and simmer for 2 minutes to warm through and coat with sauce.

Push the pork and onions to the sides of the pan. Pour the beaten eggs into the sauce, and without stirring, let them cook for 1 to 2 minutes until just set but still slightly glossy on top, you want the eggs to stay soft.
Divide the warm rice between two bowls. Carefully slide the pork, onions and egg over the rice, spoon the sauce over top, and scatter spring onions and nori strips if using. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the sauce while the pork cooks: mix mirin, soy sauce and water in a small bowl and you're ready to go.
No fresh pork cutlets? Thin chicken breast works just as well, pound it to 5 mm and it'll cook in the same time.
Leftover rice from lunch? This dish is your friend. Just make sure it's still warm when you serve.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Braised Pork Rice
summary: Tender braised pork belly over steamed rice with a jammy egg.

items.raw: 500 g pork belly, cut into 3 cm cubes

steps.text: Blanch the pork belly cubes in boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water until the water runs clear. This removes impurities and keeps the braise clean.
Heat the neutral oil in a medium pot over medium-high heat. Add the blanched pork and cook, stirring occasionally, until the surfaces are lightly golden, about 5 minutes.

Add the garlic, ginger, brown onion, dried shiitake, star anise, rock sugar, soy sauce and dark soy sauce. Stir well, then add the water. Bring to a simmer, then lower the heat to low, cover, and braise for 60–70 minutes until the pork is very tender and the sauce is rich and glossy. Stir every 20 minutes.
While the pork is braising, soft-boil the eggs: bring a small pot of water to the boil, gently add the eggs, and cook for 6–7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Transfer to cold water, then carefully peel.

Divide the cooked rice between two bowls. Top each with the braised pork and sauce, and halve a soft-boiled egg over the top. Scatter with spring onion and drizzle with extra soy sauce or chilli oil if you like.

notes: Make the braised pork up to 2 days ahead. It keeps in the fridge in its sauce and tastes even better reheated.
The eggs are best cooked just before serving, but you can boil them ahead and reheat gently in hot water.

Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Brik aux Oeufs
summary: Crispy fried pastry envelope with egg, tuna and harissa.

items.raw: 4 sheets filo pastry (or malsouka if you can get it)
items.note: or malsouka if you can get it

steps.text: Set up a work station with one sheet of filo pastry in front of you, and have a small bowl of water nearby for sealing. In a small bowl, mix the drained tuna with the harissa, coriander and capers. Taste it and adjust the harissa and salt to your liking.
Take the first filo sheet and brush it lightly with oil on both sides. Fold it in half to create a rough square.

Spoon about 1 tbsp of the tuna mixture into the centre of the folded pastry, leaving a margin around the edges. Make a small well in the tuna mixture, then crack an egg directly into it. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.

Fold the pastry over the filling to create a triangle or envelope, sealing the edges by pressing firmly or brushing them with a little water. The egg should be mostly contained but might leak slightly during cooking, this is normal.
Heat about 3 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C (or until a small piece of bread browns in about 30 seconds). Carefully place the first brik into the hot oil, seam-side down.

Fry for 2–3 minutes, turning once halfway, until the pastry is golden and crispy on both sides. The egg inside should still have a soft yolk. Use a slotted spoon to remove it and drain on paper towels.
Repeat with the remaining briks, making sure the oil returns to temperature between batches.
Serve hot, on their own or with a squeeze of lemon and extra harissa on the side!

notes: The yolk should be soft when you bite in, if you prefer it cooked through, fry for an extra minute, but you'll lose some of the magic!
If the pastry is splitting, brush the edges with a paste of flour and water to seal them better.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Chicken and Mushroom Pie
summary: Creamy chicken and mushroom filling in golden shortcrust pastry, proper comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the butter into the flour and salt until it looks like breadcrumbs. Mix the egg yolk with cold water, pour it in, and bring it together into a dough with your hands. Wrap in cling film and chill while you make the filling.
Melt the butter in a large heavy-bottomed pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it in batches, about 3 minutes each side, don't crowd the pan. Set aside.
In the same pan, add the onion and cook until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and mushrooms, stir, and cook until the mushrooms release their liquid and it evaporates, about 8 minutes.

Sprinkle the flour over the veg, stir well, and cook for 1 minute. Pour in the stock and cream, add the mustard, and stir to combine. Return the chicken to the pan, bring to a simmer, and cook gently for 10 minutes. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Let it cool completely, this is important or the pastry will be soggy.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Pour the cooled filling into a 1.5 litre pie dish. Roll out the pastry on a floured bench to about 5 mm thick and about 2 cm larger than the dish. Lay it over the filling, press the edges down, and trim with a knife. Brush with beaten egg.
Bake for 25–30 minutes until the pastry is golden brown and the filling bubbles at the edges. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.

notes: The filling must cool completely before adding the pastry, or it'll go soggy. Make it the day before if you like.
You can freeze the uncooked pie for up to a month. Bake straight from frozen, adding 10–15 minutes to the cooking time.
Swaps: button mushrooms work fine if you can't get swiss browns, or use a mix. Crème fraîche instead of cream if that's what you've got.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Nkatenkwan (Groundnut Soup)
summary: Ghanaian chicken and groundnut soup with tomatoes and peppers

items.raw: 800 g chicken thigh, bone-in skin-on, cut into chunks
4 medium tomatoes, roughly chopped (or 400 g tin crushed tomatoes)
100 g smooth peanut butter (or 3 tbsp groundnut paste)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, fry the onion for 2 to 3 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and tomato paste, stir well and cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes and cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until they break down slightly.
Pour in the stock and return the chicken to the pot. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer gently for 15 minutes, skimming off any foam.
Add the red and green capsicum, stir and simmer for another 8 to 10 minutes until the peppers are tender but still bright.

Stir the peanut butter into a small cup with a splash of the hot broth until smooth, then stir this mixture back into the pot. Simmer for a final 5 minutes, stirring gently, until the soup is smooth and the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside). Taste and adjust seasoning.
Serve hot in bowls, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Light soup keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and freezes well for a month. Just reheat gently on the stove.
If you can't find groundnut paste, smooth peanut butter works just fine.
Food safety:

title: Dhokla
summary: Steamed fermented chickpea cake, tangy and light with mustard seeds and curry leaves.

items.raw: 200 g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight in cold water
2 cm piece fresh ginger, roughly chopped
½ tsp citric acid (or lemon juice)

steps.text: Drain the soaked chickpeas well and grind them with the ginger and green chillies in a food processor until smooth, adding a little water if needed. The batter should be fine and creamy.

Transfer to a bowl and stir in the salt and citric acid. Cover loosely with a kitchen towel or cling film and leave to ferment at room temperature for 8 to 12 hours, or overnight. The batter will become slightly fluffy and airy.

Set up a steamer: fill a large pot with water and bring to a simmer. Oil a round cake tin or two loaf tins, or a microwave-safe dish if you prefer. Place them in a steamer basket or on a trivet inside the pot so they sit above the water.
Add the bicarbonate of soda to the fermented batter and stir gently but thoroughly, this will make it light and spongy. Do this just before steaming, as it loses its effect if left to sit.
Carefully pour the batter into the prepared tin(s). Cover with foil or a lid and steam for 15 to 20 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean and the top feels springy.

While the dhokla steams, make the tadka: heat the oil in a small pan over medium heat until hot. Add the mustard seeds and let them crackle and pop for 30 seconds, then add the curry leaves and asafoetida. Stir for another 10 seconds until fragrant.

Remove the dhokla from the steamer and carefully run a knife around the edges to loosen it. Turn it out onto a serving plate or board. Immediately pour the hot tadka over the top, letting the oil and seeds soak in.
Leave to cool for a few minutes, then cut into squares or wedges and serve warm with chutney if you like. Leftover dhokla can be wrapped and kept in the fridge for 3 to 4 days.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the batter the night before and ferment it. In the morning, add bicarbonate of soda and steam. The whole dish takes about 40 minutes from start to finish the next day.
No fermenting time? Use ½ tsp of instant yeast mixed into the batter with a little warm water, and let it rise for 2 to 3 hours instead.
Serve with sweet chutney, green chutney or a spicy tomato achaar for dipping.

title: Curry Goat
summary: Fall-apart goat meat in a rich, aromatic curry with potatoes and spring onions.

image.credit: Photo: Leon Brocard from London, UK / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

items.raw: 1.5 kg goat shoulder, cut into 5 cm chunks
4 spring onions, chopped (white and green parts separated)

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the goat meat on all sides, about 3–4 minutes per batch. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the onions and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Stir in the curry powder, cumin and turmeric, and cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the spices are dark and fragrant.

Return the goat to the pot. Add the water and crushed tomatoes, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom. Stir in the salt, pepper and thyme. Bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is bubbling lightly.
Cover with a lid and simmer gently for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the meat is beginning to soften.
Add the potato chunks and the white parts of the spring onions. Simmer, covered, for a further 30–35 minutes until the meat is fall-apart tender and the potatoes are soft. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Stir in the green parts of the spring onions just before serving. Serve hot in a deep bowl with the broth.

notes: Make it a day ahead: the flavours deepen as it sits. Reheat gently on the stove top.
Serve with rice and peas, or plain white rice to soak up the curry.
Can't find goat? Lamb shoulder works, though it cooks faster, check it at 60 minutes.

title: Scotch Broth
summary: A warming barley broth with ham bone, root vegetables and lentils, proper Scottish comfort in a bowl.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a large pot. Add the ham bone or hock and bay leaf. Skim off any foam from the surface, then reduce the heat and simmer gently for 30 minutes.
Add the pearl barley and brown lentils. Simmer for another 15 minutes.
Add the carrots, parsnips, swede and leek. Stir well and simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the potato and simmer for a further 15 minutes, until all the vegetables are tender and the barley is soft.
Remove the ham bone. If there's any meat clinging to it, shred it and return it to the pot; discard the bone. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with fresh parsley if you like. Serve hot with good bread.

notes: This freezes beautifully, make a double batch and freeze half. Thaw overnight and reheat gently.
Any root vegetables work here: turnip instead of swede, celeriac, or even a bit of cabbage. Swap parsnip for more carrot if that's what you've got.
If you can't find a ham bone, a ham hock works just as well, or use chicken stock and add a splash of ham or bacon for flavour.

title: Tagliatelle al Ragù
summary: Tagliatelle with Bolognese ragù: slow-cooked ground meat, tomato and milk.

image.credit: Photo: Ivan Vighetto / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the pancetta and cook, stirring, until the fat renders, about 4 minutes.
Add the onion, carrot and celery. Cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. This is your soffritto, don't rush it.

Increase the heat to medium-high. Add the beef and pork mince, breaking it up with a wooden spoon. Cook, stirring often, until the meat is no longer pink, about 10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Pour in the white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot to lift the browned bits. Let the wine reduce until nearly evaporated, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute. Add the crushed tomatoes and stir well.
Reduce the heat to low. The ragù should barely simmer, just occasional lazy bubbles. Cook uncovered for 2 hours, stirring every 15 minutes or so. The sauce will thicken and darken.
Pour in the milk and stir well. Continue to simmer on low heat for another 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The sauce will be rich, thick and deep brown. Taste and adjust the salt and pepper.
About 30 minutes before serving, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the tagliatelle for 2 to 3 minutes, or until tender. Fresh pasta cooks fast.
Drain the pasta, reserving a cup of pasta water. Toss the tagliatelle with the ragù in the pot, adding a splash of pasta water if needed to loosen it. Serve with freshly grated Parmesan.

notes: The ragù freezes beautifully for up to three months. Make a double batch when you have time.
Fresh tagliatelle is essential here. If you can't find it, use dried pappardelle, cook it to packet instructions instead.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Galette de blé noir aux moules
summary: Buckwheat crêpes topped with mussels, shallots, white wine and cream.

steps.text: Make the galette batter: whisk together buckwheat flour and salt. In another bowl, beat the egg with milk and water until combined. Pour the wet ingredients into the flour, whisking until you have a smooth batter with no lumps. Let it rest for 15 minutes.

Heat a non-stick crêpe pan or 25 cm frying pan over medium-high heat and lightly butter it. Pour in 80 ml batter, tilting the pan so it spreads thinly and evenly. Cook for about 2 minutes until the bottom is lightly golden, then flip and cook the other side for 30 seconds. Transfer to a plate. Repeat with remaining batter to make 2 galettes.
While the batter rests, prepare the topping: melt butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Add shallots and cook gently for 3 minutes until soft and sweet.
Pour in white wine and bring to a simmer. Add the mussels, cover, and cook for 4–5 minutes, shaking the pan once halfway through, until they open. Discard any that don't.
Pour in the cream and stir gently to combine. Warm through for 1 minute, then taste and season lightly with salt if needed.
Place a galette on each plate, top generously with mussels, shallots and cream sauce, scatter with fresh parsley if you like, and serve at once.

notes: The galette batter can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept covered in the fridge. Bring to room temperature for 10 minutes before cooking.
Clean mussels well under cold running water, pulling away any beard. Discard any that are open and won't close when tapped.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Sapasui
summary: Samoan chop suey with corned beef, cabbage and onion, the weeknight family favourite.

items.raw: 340 g tin corned beef, broken into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wok over medium-high heat.
Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the cabbage and garlic, and cook, stirring often, until the cabbage is tender but still has a bit of crunch, about 6 minutes.
Add the corned beef and stir to break it up and mix through the veg, about 1 minute.
Add the soy sauce and oyster sauce, and stir to coat everything. Cook for 2 minutes until heated through.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper as needed. Serve hot.

notes: Swap the corned beef for tinned tuna or cooked chicken if that's what you've got.
Serve over rice or with fresh bread to soak up the sauce.
Any leftover veg works here, carrots, green beans, capsicum, whatever's in the crisper.

title: Pasta ca' le Sardine
summary: Fresh pasta with sardines, wild fennel, saffron and pine nuts, a Sicilian classic.

items.raw: 400 g fresh sardines, scaled and gutted
150 g wild fennel (fronda di finocchietto), fresh or frozen, chopped

steps.text: Make the pasta: pile the flour on a clean bench, make a well in the centre and crack the eggs into it. With a fork, beat the eggs lightly, then gradually incorporate the flour, mixing with your fingers until a shaggy dough forms. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap in plastic wrap and rest for 30 minutes.
While the dough rests, steep the saffron in the warm water until the colour is deep gold, about 5 minutes.
In a small frying pan over medium heat, lightly toast the pine nuts, shaking often, until fragrant, about 3 minutes. Set aside.

Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook gently, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the chopped garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.

Add the fresh sardines (or break them into large pieces if very large) to the pan and cook gently, stirring carefully, until the flesh is opaque and beginning to flake, about 5 minutes. Pour in the saffron water and add the chopped wild fennel. Stir gently and simmer for 5 minutes. Season with salt and black pepper. Turn off the heat.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil until it is at a rolling, bubbling boil.

Roll out the pasta dough thinly (about 2 mm) on a floured bench. If you have a pasta machine, use it. Cut into long, irregular ribbons or shapes, traditional pasta ca' le sardine is not uniform; think rustic and handmade.
Cook the pasta in the boiling water, stirring gently, until al dente, about 4–5 minutes for fresh pasta. (Test a piece; it should have a slight bite.)
Reserve 200 ml of the pasta cooking water, then drain the pasta.

Gently reheat the sardine sauce over medium-low heat. Add the cooked pasta to the sauce and toss carefully, adding pasta water a little at a time to loosen the sauce and help it coat the pasta. The pasta should look silky, not dry or soupy.
Divide among bowls, scatter the toasted pine nuts over the top, and serve at once.

notes: Wild fennel (fronda di finocchietto) is the leafy fronds, not the seeds. In Australia, you may find it frozen in the Asian or Italian section; if not, a small amount of fresh dill mixed with a pinch of ground fennel seed is an acceptable substitute, though the taste won't be quite the same.
The pasta can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept covered on the bench. You can also freeze it on a tray, then bag it; cook from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the cooking time.
If fresh sardines are hard to find, use tinned sardines in oil (drain well and add them to the sauce at the end, just to warm through, so they don't fall apart).
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Soy and Ginger Chicken Thighs with Bok Choy
summary: Chicken thighs braised in soy, ginger and star anise with quick bok choy on the side.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper, then place skin-side down in the hot pan. Cook until the skin is golden and crisp, about 6 minutes. Flip and cook for another 2 minutes.
Add the ginger slices and star anise to the pan, stirring for about 1 minute until fragrant. Pour in the soy sauce and chicken stock, then add the caster sugar. Bring to a simmer.
Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and braise for 12–15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (75°C in the thickest part of the thigh). The skin may soften slightly; that's fine.
While the chicken braises, bring a small pot of salted water to the boil. Add the bok choy and cook for 2 minutes until tender-crisp. Drain well.
Transfer the bok choy to serving plates. Remove the chicken from the pan and place on the plates, then spoon the braising liquid (with the ginger and star anise) over the top.

notes: Food safety:

title: Yassa au Poulet
summary: Chicken braised in mustard, lemon and onions, a Senegalese weeknight staple.

items.raw: 800 g chicken pieces (thighs and drumsticks), skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium-high heat. Season the chicken with salt and pepper, then brown it skin-side down for 4 to 5 minutes until golden. Turn and brown the other side for another 3 minutes. Remove to a plate.

Add the sliced onions to the pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and starting to caramelise, about 8 minutes. Stir in the mustard and turmeric, then add the lemon juice, scraping up any sticky bits from the bottom.

Pour in the stock and return the chicken to the pot, nestling it among the onions. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and braise for 25 to 30 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside) and the onions are very soft.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve warm over rice, spooning the sauce generously over each portion.

notes: Yassa is even better the next day. Cool quickly, cover and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat gently on the stove.
Use thighs and drumsticks rather than breast, they stay moist and the skin crisps beautifully in the pan.
Food safety:

title: Tempe Goreng Sambal Matah
summary: Crispy fried tempeh with raw sambal of shallots, chilli and lime.

items.raw: 250 g tempeh, sliced into 1 cm rectangles

steps.text: Make the sambal matah first: combine the shallots, chillies and garlic in a bowl. Add the lime juice and neutral oil, then taste and add salt. Set aside while you fry the tempeh.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Test with a piece of tempeh, it should sizzle immediately.
Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, fry the tempeh slices until golden and crispy on both sides, about 3–4 minutes total. Drain on paper towel and sprinkle with salt while still hot.
Arrange the hot fried tempeh on a plate and spoon the sambal matah over the top. Eat straight away, the contrast between the crispy, hot tempeh and the cool, bright sambal is the whole point.

notes: Make a big batch of sambal matah and keep it in the fridge for up to three days, it's brilliant on rice, eggs, or any leftover protein.
If you can't find fresh lime, use lemon or bottled lime juice, but fresh is so much better.
Tempeh keeps in the fridge for ages; fry it whenever you need a quick, protein-packed lunch.

title: Esqueixada
summary: Shredded salt cod salad with tomatoes, onions and olives, the Empordà way.

image.credit: Photo: Birding In Spain / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 400 g salt cod fillet, soaked overnight (or 24 hours)
100 g mixed olives (green and black), pitted
1 can (400 g) tinned tomatoes (optional, if fresh tomatoes lack flavour)
items.note: 400 g; optional, if fresh tomatoes lack flavour

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Drain the soaked salt cod and check for any remaining small bones. Flake the cod roughly into bite-sized pieces by hand, don't cut it; the irregular shreds are essential to esqueixada.
In a large bowl, combine the flaked salt cod, fresh tomatoes, red onion and olives. If using tinned tomatoes, drain well and add them too.
Dress with the olive oil and red wine vinegar, tossing gently to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt (go easy, the cod is already salty) and a good grind of black pepper.
Let the salad rest at room temperature for 15 minutes, until the tomato juices have mingled with the dressing and the flavours meld, then scatter with parsley if you like and serve.

notes: The salt cod must be soaked overnight or up to 24 hours, changing the water 2–3 times. This is not a shortcut dish.
Esqueixada is best served at room temperature, never chilled. The oil and vinegar need warmth to carry the flavours.
In summer, use the ripest tomatoes you can find. If they're bland, the tinned tomatoes (well-drained) give the dish needed acidity and body.

title: Żurek
summary: Sour rye soup with kielbasa and potatoes, a Polish Sunday supper from Kraków.

items.raw: 3 good-quality kielbasa sausages (about 400 g), sliced into thick rounds
1 kg waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into chunks
150 ml żur (Polish sour rye starter, fermented rye flour)
items.note: Polish sour rye starter, fermented rye flour

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the kielbasa slices until the edges are crispy, about 5 minutes. Set them aside on a plate.
In the same pot, sauté the onions until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat with oil. Pour in the stock and bring to a simmer. Add the bay leaves and cloves, then cook until the potatoes are tender, about 20 minutes.

Pour the żur into a small bowl and stir it with a little warm stock to loosen it, then pour this mixture back into the pot. Stir well and simmer for 5 minutes, letting the sour flavour meld into the soup.
Return the kielbasa to the pot and simmer for another 5 minutes to warm through and let the flavours combine.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Ladle into bowls, top each with a spoonful of sour cream and a scatter of fresh dill. Serve with good rye bread.

notes: Żur (sour rye starter) can be found in Polish or Eastern European grocery shops, or made at home by fermenting rye flour in water for 24 hours. It keeps in the fridge for weeks.
Make this a day ahead if you can, the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of water if needed.
Good kielbasa makes this soup. Don't skip it or use thin sausages; you need that smoky, meaty backbone.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

title: Lemon Myrtle Chicken
summary: Roasted chicken with lemon myrtle leaves, a native Australian citrus with peppery notes.

items.raw: 2 tbsp lemon myrtle leaves, roughly chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat your oven to 200°C.
Pat the chicken dry with paper towels. Season the cavity generously with salt and pepper, then stuff with the lemon myrtle leaves and onion halves.
Brush the outside of the chicken all over with neutral oil, then season the skin with salt and pepper.

Place the chicken breast-side up on a roasting tray. Roast for 60 to 75 minutes, or until the thickest part of the thigh reaches 75°C when tested with a meat thermometer. The skin should be golden and crispy.
Remove from the oven and rest for 10 minutes before carving. Serve with a wedge of lemon or lime on the side if you like.

notes: If you can't find fresh lemon myrtle leaves, dried lemon myrtle powder works well, use about 1 tsp mixed with a little salt and pepper to season the cavity and skin.
The pan juices make a simple sauce: deglaze the hot tray with a splash of water or stock, scraping up the browned bits, and drizzle over the carved chicken.
Food safety:

title: Lamb Souvla
summary: Marinated lamb skewers charred over coals with lemon, oregano and garlic.

items.raw: 2 tbsp fresh oregano, chopped (or 2 tsp dried oregano)
800 g lamb shoulder, cut into 3 cm cubes
2 red onions, cut into 3 cm chunks
2 red capsicums, cut into 3 cm chunks

steps.text: Combine olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper in a bowl. Add lamb and stir until coated. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Thread lamb onto skewers, alternating with onion and capsicum pieces. If using wooden skewers, soak them in water first.
Heat your grill or chargrill to high until very hot, or get your coals hot and glowing, covered in a light grey ash.
Lay skewers on the grill and cook for 20–25 minutes, turning every 2–3 minutes to char evenly on all sides. The lamb is ready when it's charred outside and pink inside.
Rest for 2 minutes, then serve with lemon wedges and extra oregano.

notes: Marinate overnight if you have the time, it'll be even more tender.
Cook over charcoal if you can. It makes all the difference, mate.
Pink lamb is the way. It's not overcooked until it's grey.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Gravad lax med senapssås
summary: Cured salmon with mustard sauce, a Swedish classic to make when you have time.

items.raw: 800 g sashimi-grade salmon fillet, skin on

steps.text: Mix the salt, sugar, and crushed peppercorn together in a small bowl. Pat the salmon dry with paper towel. Spread half the salt mixture over the flesh side of the salmon, then scatter half the dill on top.

Place the salmon skin-side down on a large piece of plastic wrap or in a shallow dish. Spread the remaining salt mixture and dill over the flesh. If you have a second salmon fillet, lay it flesh-side down on top to make a sandwich (this helps the curing), but a single fillet works fine.
Wrap tightly in plastic wrap or cover with a plate. Place on a tray to catch any liquid, then put in the fridge for 3 days. Turn the package over every day so the cure spreads evenly.
On day 3, unwrap the salmon and rinse off the cure under cold running water. Pat dry and slice thinly at an angle, leaving the skin behind. You should get 8 to 12 slices.
Make the mustard sauce: whisk both mustards, sugar and vinegar together in a bowl. Slowly drizzle in the oil while whisking until emulsified. Stir in the fresh dill. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Arrange the gravad lax on a board with sliced rye bread and the mustard sauce alongside. Serve with lemon wedges if you like.

notes: The salmon can be cured up to 5 days ahead; keep it wrapped in the fridge. Slice only what you need and use the rest within a day or two.
The mustard sauce keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days.
Use the best salmon you can find, it's almost raw, so freshness matters.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.

Food safety: The seafood here is served raw or cured, so buy sashimi-grade, keep it cold and eat it the day it is made; for anyone who should avoid raw fish, cook it until opaque. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Ful Medames
summary: Slow-cooked broad beans with garlic, lemon and olive oil, a Lebanese vegan breakfast staple.

image.credit: Photo: Zachbe at en.wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

items.raw: 800 g tin broad beans, drained and rinsed
60 ml olive oil, plus extra to serve
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant and just starting to turn golden, about 1 minute. Don't let it brown.
Add the drained broad beans and stir to coat with the oil and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5 minutes.

Add 250 ml water and the ground cumin. Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cook, uncovered, stirring often and mashing some of the beans against the side of the pot as they soften, for 35–40 minutes. The beans should break down into a creamy, chunky sauce.
Add the lemon juice and taste. Season with salt and pepper to your liking. If the mixture is too thick, stir in a splash more water.
Transfer to a serving bowl and make a well in the centre. Drizzle generously with extra olive oil. Serve warm with pita, and top with parsley and halved hard-boiled egg if you like.

notes: Ful keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen it back up.
If using dried broad beans instead, soak overnight, then simmer for about 90 minutes until completely tender before following the rest of the method.

title: Sambal Ikan Bilis
summary: Crispy anchovies coated in a fierce, garlicky sambal that'll make you sweat.

steps.text: Remove the heads and innards from the ikan bilis. Rinse gently under cold water and pat dry well with paper towels.

Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in batches if needed, fry the ikan bilis until they are golden and crispy, about 5–6 minutes, stirring frequently. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towels.
While the ikan bilis fry, pound the bird's eye chillies and garlic together in a mortar until you have a coarse paste. Mix the tamarind paste with 2 tbsp water.
Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil in a clean pan over medium heat. Add the chilli-garlic paste and fry, stirring often, until fragrant and the oil is starting to darken around the edges, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the tamarind mixture and stir well. Cook for 1 minute until it comes together into a thick sambal. Taste and add salt as needed.
Add the crispy ikan bilis to the hot sambal and toss quickly to coat evenly. Serve immediately while still warm.

notes: Make the sambal ahead and reheat it just before frying the ikan bilis, the anchovies need to go in hot to stay crispy.
If the ikan bilis are very small, you don't need to clean them; just rinse and fry whole.
For less heat, remove some of the chilli seeds before pounding.

title: Burrata, Freekeh and Charred Greens
summary: Creamy burrata, chewy roasted freekeh and bitter charred silverbeet with lemon dressing.

items.raw: 200 g silverbeet, leaves and stems separated
2 tbsp olive oil, plus extra for drizzling
1 ball fresh burrata, at room temperature
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a boil in a medium saucepan. Add the freekeh, reduce to a simmer, and cook until tender and the liquid is absorbed, about 20–22 minutes. Season with salt and pepper, then set aside.
While the freekeh cooks, separate the silverbeet stems from the leaves. Roughly chop both stems and leaves.

Heat 1 tbsp olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the silverbeet stems and cook for 3 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they soften. Add the silverbeet leaves and cavolo nero, and cook for another 4–5 minutes, stirring often, until the greens are tender and the leaves have some charred edges.
Squeeze the juice from one lemon half over the greens and toss. Season with salt and pepper. Transfer to a plate.

Divide the warm freekeh between two bowls. Top each with the charred greens. Place half the burrata in each bowl, then drizzle everything with a good glug of olive oil and a squeeze from the remaining lemon half.
Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and black pepper, and serve.
