notes: The freekeh can be made up to 2 days ahead and reheated gently. The greens are best charred fresh, but leftovers keep in the fridge for a day.
Burrata is best at room temperature. Pull it out of the fridge 10 minutes before serving.

title: Künefe
summary: Crispy shredded pastry with melted white cheese, hot honey syrup and walnuts.

items.raw: 200 g white cheese (feta or halloumi), crumbled or sliced

steps.text: Make the honey syrup first so it's ready to pour hot. In a small saucepan, combine the honey, water, lemon juice and cinnamon stick. Bring to a simmer over medium heat until the syrup is bubbling and slightly thickened, then remove from the heat and let it cool slightly while you prepare the pastry.
Preheat the oven to 190°C. Gently separate the kataifi pastry strands, they'll come apart easily if you loosen them with your fingers.
Pour a thin layer of melted butter into a round baking dish about 20 cm across. Spread half the kataifi strands evenly over the base, pressing gently to form a layer. Drizzle with more butter.
Scatter the crumbled cheese and walnuts over the pastry, leaving a small border around the edges.
Layer the remaining kataifi strands on top, press down gently, and pour the rest of the melted butter evenly over everything. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and crispy.

Remove from the oven and immediately pour the hot honey syrup all over the künefe. It will sizzle and soak into the pastry. Scatter the pistachios on top if using, and serve right away with plenty of napkins.

notes: Make the honey syrup up to 2 hours ahead and reheat gently before serving.
Use a good white cheese, feta works, but halloumi won't melt as much. Some people use a mix.
Künefe is best eaten warm and straight away, when the pastry is still crispy.

title: Empanadas de Carne
summary: Crispy baked beef empanadas with hard-boiled egg and olives.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the dough: rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until it resembles breadcrumbs. Make a well, add the egg yolk and 80 ml of the warm water, mix gently with your fingertips until it comes together, adding more water if needed. Knead briefly until smooth, then wrap and rest for 20 minutes.

While the dough rests, cook the filling: heat the oil in a pan over medium heat, add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 6 minutes. Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until cooked through and no pink remains, about 8 minutes. Stir in the cumin and paprika, cook for 1 minute, then remove from heat. Let cool slightly, then fold in the hard-boiled egg and olives. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Preheat the oven to 200°C.
Divide the dough into 12 equal pieces and roll each into a ball. On a floured surface, roll each ball into a circle about 15 cm across and 3 mm thick.
Place 2 tbsp of filling on one half of each circle, leaving a 1 cm border. Fold the dough over to form a half-moon, press the edges to seal, then crimp with a fork.
Place the empanadas on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Brush each with beaten egg.
Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden and crisp. Serve warm.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the filling and dough the day before, keep both covered in the fridge. Assemble and bake fresh when you're ready.
Freeze: uncooked empanadas freeze well for up to a month. Bake straight from frozen, adding 5–7 minutes to the cooking time.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Negima
summary: Chicken and spring onions skewers brushed with soy-mirin glaze, grilled in a frying pan.

items.raw: 200 g chicken breast, cut into 2 cm pieces
2 spring onion, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Mix soy sauce, mirin, sugar and garlic in a small bowl.
Heat a frying pan over medium-high heat. Add oil and let it smoke lightly.
Working quickly, add chicken pieces to the pan and cook, stirring occasionally, for 4 minutes until lightly browned on the edges.
Add spring onion pieces and toss to combine. Cook for 1 minute.
Pour the tare over everything and stir constantly for 2–3 minutes until the liquid is sticky and coats the chicken and onion. Check that the chicken is cooked through.
Taste and add salt if needed. Serve hot.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Shanghainese Soup Dumplings
summary: Delicate wheat dumplings with a pork and gelatin filling, steamed and served in their own rich broth.

items.raw: 50 g gelatine, finely chopped (or 4 leaves gelatine, finely chopped)

steps.text: Make the dough: mix the hot water into the flour and salt with chopsticks or a fork until a shaggy dough forms. Once cool enough to handle, knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should feel soft and slightly sticky, this high hydration gives you that tender wrapper. Cover and rest for at least 30 minutes.

Make the filling: mix the pork, gelatine, spring onion, soy sauce, sesame oil, shaoxing wine, ginger and sugar in a bowl. Stir until just combined, don't overwork it or it will become dense. Taste and adjust seasoning if needed.

Divide the dough into 16 equal pieces. Roll each into a ball, then use a small rolling pin or your fingers to flatten into a thin disc about 10 cm across, slightly thicker at the edges than the centre.

Place about 1 tbsp of filling in the centre of each wrapper. Bring the edges up and gather at the top, pleating as you go, then twist gently to seal. The dumpling should look like a little purse. Place seam-side up on a small square of baking paper (this stops it sticking to the steamer).
Set up a steamer: bring water to a boil in a wok or large pot, and place a bamboo steamer basket or metal steamer rack above it, making sure the water doesn't touch the base of the basket.

Working in batches, carefully place 4–6 dumplings seam-side up in the steamer, still on their paper squares. Steam over simmering water for 10–12 minutes, until the wrappers are translucent and cooked through. You'll see a slight sheen on them when they're ready.

Transfer the cooked dumplings to a serving platter. Warm the chicken stock gently with the ginger slices and spring onion if using, then ladle into small bowls or a shallow serving dish. Serve the dumplings alongside, with black vinegar and extra stock for dipping.

notes: The dough can be made up to 8 hours ahead and kept covered at room temperature. If it dries out, spritz lightly with water.
The filling can be made several hours ahead and refrigerated. Assemble the dumplings no more than 1 hour before steaming.
If you don't have a bamboo steamer, use a metal steamer rack or even a heatproof plate set on chopsticks above the simmering water, the key is gentle, steady steam.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Pasta alla Nduja
summary: Spaghetti with spicy Calabrian nduja, tomato, garlic and a touch of cream.

items.raw: 150 g nduja, chopped into small pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the spaghetti until just al dente, about 9–10 minutes. Reserve 200 ml of pasta water, then drain.

While the pasta cooks, place the nduja and garlic in a large frying pan over medium-low heat. Stir gently for 2–3 minutes until the nduja starts to break down and release its oils, don't let it brown.
Add the crushed tomatoes to the pan and stir well to combine with the nduja and garlic. Simmer for 4–5 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly.
Pour in the cream and stir through. Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Add a splash of pasta water if the sauce is too thick, it should coat the pasta loosely.
Add the cooked spaghetti to the pan and toss gently to coat every strand. Add a little more pasta water if needed to loosen the sauce.
Divide among four bowls and finish with a generous handful of grated parmesan and a basil leaf, if you like.

notes: Nduja keeps well in the fridge for weeks once opened. Wrap it tightly or keep it in an airtight container.
If you can't find nduja at your local deli, check the Italian section at a good supermarket or order it online, it's worth the hunt.

title: Doubles
summary: Spiced chickpea curry tucked into fried bread, Trinidad's essential street snack.

items.raw: 1 tbsp neutral oil, plus more for frying

steps.text: Make the bread dough: mix flour, baking powder and salt in a bowl. Add oil and stir, then add warm water a little at a time, mixing until you have a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 2 minutes until smooth, then set aside to rest for 15 minutes.
Make the chickpea curry: heat oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until soft, about 4 minutes. Add garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add turmeric, cumin and asafoetida, stirring constantly for 1 minute to bloom the spices. Add green chillies and salt, then the drained chickpeas and water.

Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the curry has thickened slightly and the flavours have come together. The chickpeas should be soft and well coated. Taste and adjust salt and spices. Keep warm.

Divide the dough into 8 equal pieces and roll each into a ball. On a lightly oiled surface, use your hands or a rolling pin to stretch each ball into a thin, roughly rectangular shape about 3 mm thick.

Heat oil in a large, deep pan to 170°C (a piece of dough will sizzle gently when it touches the oil). Working in batches, fry each piece of dough for about 1 minute each side until golden and puffed. Drain on paper towels.

To serve, split a fried bread open or lay two pieces on a plate. Spoon a generous amount of warm chickpea curry into or over the bread. Top with pepper sauce and tamarind chutney if using, scatter with fresh coriander, and eat while it's hot.

notes: The chickpea curry can be made ahead and reheated gently; make the bread fresh just before serving for the best texture.
If your kitchen scales aren't handy, the bread dough works with about 2 cups flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1 tbsp oil, and ¾ cup warm water.
Doubles are best eaten fresh and hot, the contrast between the warm spiced chickpea and crispy-soft bread is half the magic.

title: Tahdig
summary: Crispy golden rice crust with butter and yoghurt, the whole point of the pot.

image.credit: Photo: Stephen Howard / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

steps.text: Rinse the basmati rice under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. This removes excess starch. Soak in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain.

Bring a large pot of salted water (like the sea) to a boil. Add the drained rice and cook uncovered for about 8 minutes, until the grains are just starting to soften on the outside but still firm in the centre. The rice should be only half-cooked.
Drain the rice well through a fine sieve, shaking gently to remove excess water.
Melt the butter in the same pot over medium heat. Add the drained rice, stirring gently to coat with butter. Spread it in an even layer. Make a well in the centre with the back of a spoon.

Wrap the lid tightly in a clean kitchen towel so the steam stays trapped, then place it firmly on the pot. Reduce the heat to medium-low and cook for 30 minutes. You want to hear a gentle crackling sound after about 15 minutes, that's the tahdig forming.

Remove from heat. Let it rest for 5 minutes with the lid still on. Carefully run a thin knife around the edges of the pot, then place a large serving platter upside-down over the pot and flip everything out in one confident motion. The rice will mound on the platter with the golden tahdig crust on top.
Serve the tahdig hot with cold Greek yoghurt on the side. Break off pieces of the crispy rice and eat it together with a spoonful of yoghurt. This is the prize.

notes: The key is steam. Wrap that lid in a towel, no shortcuts. If your kitchen is very cold, you may need another 5 minutes.
Listen for the gentle crackling around 15 minutes in. That's how you know it's working.
If the tahdig is too dark or burns, it happens. Serve it anyway, bitter tahdig with yoghurt is still tahdig.

title: Shrimp and Grits
summary: Creamy stone-ground grits with sautéed shrimp, crispy bacon, and spring onions.

image.credit: Photo: Jason Riedy / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

items.raw: 800 g raw shrimp (prawns), peeled and deveined
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a boil in a saucepan. Slowly whisk in the grits, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Once combined, reduce the heat to low and cook, stirring often, for 25 to 30 minutes until the grits are creamy and tender and pull away from the sides of the pan.
While the grits cook, fry the bacon in a large cast-iron frying pan over medium heat until crispy, about 8 minutes. Remove to a plate, leaving about 1 tbsp of bacon fat in the pan.
Add the butter to the frying pan with the bacon fat. Once foaming, add the garlic and cook, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant.

Season the shrimp well with salt and pepper. Add half to the frying pan in a single layer and cook without stirring for 2 minutes until the underside is pink. Stir and cook for a further 2 to 3 minutes until fully opaque throughout with no translucency. Transfer to a plate and repeat with the remaining shrimp.
Once the grits are creamy, stir in the cream, lemon zest, and cooked bacon. Season to taste with salt, pepper, and lemon juice.

Return all the shrimp to the frying pan and warm through over medium heat for about 1 minute. Top with spring onions and a drizzle of hot sauce if you like. Serve the shrimp alongside the creamy grits.

notes: Cook the shrimp in batches to avoid crowding the pan, this ensures even cooking and a proper sear.
Stone-ground grits take longer than instant grits and have better flavour. Don't skip the low-and-slow cooking.
Food safety:

title: Sheet Pan Chicken Thighs with Root Vegetables
summary: One-pan roasted chicken thighs with potatoes, carrots and onions.

items.raw: 8 bone-in chicken thighs, skin on (about 1.5 kg)
500 g waxy potato, halved or quartered
400 g carrot, cut into 5 cm pieces
1 large brown onion, cut into wedges
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oven to 220°C. Pat chicken thighs dry with paper towels and place them skin-side up on a large sheet pan.
Toss potatoes, carrots and onion with olive oil, thyme, oregano, salt and pepper. Scatter around the chicken.

Roast for 35–40 minutes, until the chicken skin is golden and crispy and the internal temperature at the thickest part of the thigh reaches 75°C. The vegetables should be tender and caramelised at the edges.
Let rest for 5 minutes, then serve. A squeeze of lemon over everything is nice if you have it.

notes: Make it ahead: prep the vegetables and pat the chicken dry the night before, then assemble and roast when you get home.
Swap in whatever root veg you have, parsnips, sweet potato or beets all work. Keep the total weight around 900 g.
Leftovers reheat brilliantly at 180°C for 15 minutes, or shred the chicken and toss with the vegetables for a next-day grain bowl.
Food safety:

title: Gudeg Nangka Muda
summary: Young jackfruit stewed in coconut milk and spices until tender, a Yogyakarta specialty.

image.credit: Photo: Aqilla Rahmi / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

items.raw: 1 kg young green jackfruit, peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat a large, heavy-based pot or dutch oven over medium heat. Add the sliced shallots, garlic, and ginger, stirring constantly until they release their fragrance and soften, about 3 minutes.
Stir in the ground turmeric and coriander, stirring for 1 minute more until the spices coat the aromatics.
Add the jackfruit chunks, stirring well to combine with the spice paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and water. Add the bay leaves, makrut lime leaves, and red chillies. Bring to a simmer until gently bubbling and fragrant.

Reduce the heat to low and simmer gently, uncovered, for 75–90 minutes, stirring occasionally. The jackfruit will soften, fray at the edges, and turn golden as it absorbs the coconut and spices. The sauce will thicken and deepen in colour.
Taste and adjust the salt. The gudeg is ready when the jackfruit is very tender and almost dissolving, and the sauce is rich and silky.

notes: Gudeg keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Reheat gently on the stove.
Serve with steamed rice and a simple fried chicken or hard-boiled eggs on the side, Yogyakarta style.

title: Penang Assam Laksa
summary: Sour and spicy rice noodle soup with mackerel, tamarind and shrimp paste.

items.raw: 2 cm piece fresh ginger, roughly chopped
2 whole mackerel (about 400 g), cleaned and halved

steps.text: Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 10 minutes until soft. Drain and roughly chop.
Pound the softened chillies, garlic, galangal, ginger, shrimp paste and 2 tbsp tamarind paste together in a mortar until you have a rough paste (or blend in a food processor).
Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the laksa paste and fry, stirring, for about 3 minutes until fragrant and darker in colour.
Pour in the fish stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Add the halved mackerel and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the fish is cooked through, the flesh should flake easily.

Stir in the coconut milk and the extra 2 tbsp tamarind paste. Taste and season with salt and palm sugar if you like a bit of sweetness. Simmer for another 2 minutes. The broth should be spicy, sour and rich.
While the soup cooks, blanch the fresh rice noodles in a large pot of boiling water for 1 to 2 minutes until just tender. Divide among serving bowls.
Carefully remove the mackerel pieces from the soup and divide among the bowls. Ladle the hot broth over the noodles.
Top each bowl with cucumber, pineapple, a hard-boiled egg half, fresh herbs and fried shallots. Serve hot.

notes: The laksa paste can be made the day before and kept in an airtight container in the fridge.
Use the freshest mackerel you can find, the quality makes all the difference. If fresh mackerel is hard to find, try Spanish mackerel or another firm white fish.
The broth can be made ahead and reheated gently; cook the noodles fresh just before serving.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Cơm Chiên Hải Sản
summary: Saigon seafood fried rice with squid and prawns, crispy edges and fish sauce

items.raw: 3 cups cooked white rice, cold (about 600 g)
200 g squid tube, cleaned and sliced into thin rings
items.prep: cleaned and sliced into thin rings

items.raw: 2 spring onion, sliced (white and green parts separated)

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a large wok or heavy-based frying pan over high heat until smoking hot. Add the squid and prawns, stirring constantly until cooked through, about 2–3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the wok. Add the garlic and white parts of the spring onion, stirring for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the cold rice, breaking up any clumps with the back of a spatula. Stir-fry for 4–5 minutes, letting some rice stick to the bottom of the wok and char slightly.
Return the squid and prawns to the wok. Add the fish sauce and sugar, tossing everything together. Cook for 1 minute more, letting more rice crisp against the hot pan.
Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Stir through the green parts of the spring onion.
Serve hot from the wok, scraping up those golden, crispy bits from the bottom. Top with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Cold, leftover rice works best, warm rice gets mushy. Spread it on a tray and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.
The key to those crispy golden bits (cơm cháy) is letting the rice sit untouched on the hot pan for 30 seconds at a time before stirring.
For extra flavour, add a splash of soy sauce or a drizzle of chilli oil after cooking.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Koeksister
summary: Crispy plaited pastry strips fried and drenched in hot ginger-cinnamon syrup.

steps.text: Make the syrup first so it's ready when you need it. In a small saucepan, combine the sugar, water, ground ginger and cinnamon stick. Bring to the boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Remove from the heat, stir in the lemon juice, and set aside. The syrup must stay hot.
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt into a bowl. Rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs. Do this gently, you want the dough light, not worked.

In a small jug, whisk the egg and milk together. Make a well in the centre of the dry ingredients and pour in the egg mixture. Mix gently with a fork until a soft dough forms. Do not knead. If it's too dry, add a few drops more milk.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and shape into a ball. Wrap in cling film and rest for 10 minutes.
Roll the dough out thinly, about 3 mm thick. Using a sharp knife, cut into strips about 2 cm wide and 12 cm long.
Take each strip and plait (braid) it gently, pinching the ends to seal. The plaits should be loose and airy.
Heat the oil in a deep frying pan to 180°C (a cube of bread should brown in 30 seconds). Working in batches so you don't crowd the pan, carefully lower the plaited strips into the hot oil.
Fry for about 1 minute on each side until deep golden. They should be crisp and light. Remove with a slotted spoon.
Immediately dip each hot koeksister into the hot syrup, turning to coat all over. The syrup will cling and caramelize on the outside. Place on a rack or paper towel to cool and set.
Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: The syrup can be made an hour ahead and kept warm in a low oven or over a very low heat. It must be hot when you dip the koeksisters.
Make sure your oil is at the right temperature, if it's not hot enough, the koeksisters will be greasy instead of crisp.
Store cooled koeksisters in an airtight container for up to 2 days, though they're best fresh and warm.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Crawfish Étouffée
summary: Crawfish in a thick, spiced brown roux sauce served over rice.

items.raw: 500 g crawfish tail meat, fresh or frozen
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Melt butter in a heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add flour and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, for 12 to 15 minutes until the roux is dark brown and nutty-smelling. This is the foundation, don't rush it or let it burn.
Add the chopped onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir well and cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute.
Stir in the cayenne, paprika, oregano and thyme. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the chicken stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes to let the flavours blend.
Add the crawfish and stir gently. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until the crawfish is heated through. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Serve over steamed rice, garnished with spring onion and fresh parsley.

notes: If fresh crawfish isn't available, frozen works just fine, thaw it first.
The roux is everything: low and slow, stirring often. Once it's dark brown, you've got the soul of the dish.
Make this ahead: the étouffée keeps for 3 days in the fridge and tastes even better reheated.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Bariis iskukaris
summary: Fragrant Somali spiced rice with cardamom, cinnamon and cloves.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the cardamom pods, cinnamon stick and cloves, stirring for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and lightly golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the rice and stir to coat in the oil and spices, cooking for 2 minutes.
Pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Stir once, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook for 18–20 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let sit, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork, season with salt and pepper, and serve.

notes: Make ahead: cook the rice up to 4 hours ahead, then reheat gently with a splash of water in a covered pot over low heat.
This rice holds well in a warm thermos if you're taking it to a family gathering.

title: Carne Asada
summary: Grilled marinated beef with citrus and chilli, charred and juicy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Blend the orange juice, lime juice, minced garlic, cumin, oregano, torn guajillo chillies, salt and pepper in a blender until smooth. Pour in the olive oil and pulse to combine.
Place the skirt steak in a large bowl or a zip-lock bag and pour the marinade over it, making sure all sides are coated. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight for best flavour.
Remove the steak from the fridge 30 minutes before cooking. Preheat your grill to high heat and oil the grates well.
Pat the steak dry with paper towels and season lightly with salt and black pepper on both sides.

Grill the steak for 6–8 minutes on the first side, without moving it, until charred and a crust forms. Flip and grill for 4–6 minutes on the second side for medium-rare (internal temperature of 60°C).
Transfer to a clean board, tent loosely with foil and rest for 5 minutes. This keeps the meat juicy.
Slice against the grain into strips and serve hot with lime wedges, fresh coriander and warm flour tortillas.

notes: The marinade works best overnight. Plan ahead or marinate for at least 4 hours.
Leftover carne asada is great in tacos, quesadillas or over rice the next day.
Food safety:

title: Ceviche de Corvina
summary: Raw white fish cured in lime juice, ají amarillo, and red onion, bright, clean, and classically Peruvian.

image.credit: Photo: Maor X / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 500 g sashimi-grade white fish fillet (corvina or snapper), cut into 2 cm cubes
4 ají amarillo (yellow Peruvian chillies), stems and seeds removed

steps.text: Soak the sliced red onion in salt water (about 1 tsp salt per 250 ml water) while you prepare the fish. This takes the edge off the raw onion and cures it slightly, about 5 minutes.
Blend the ají amarillo with the garlic clove and 2 tbsp of the fresh lime juice until smooth. Pass through a fine sieve if you want a completely silky sauce.

Put the fish cubes in a glass or ceramic bowl. Add the ají amarillo paste, the remaining lime juice, and a pinch of salt. Stir gently to coat all the fish. Let sit for 10–15 minutes, the lime juice will turn the fish opaque and firm. Taste and adjust salt.
Drain the cured red onion and gently fold it into the ceviche just before serving, along with any juice from soaking.

Serve in chilled bowls with fresh coriander and toasted corn kernels scattered over the top. Eat while the ceviche is at its brightest, don't leave it sitting or the acid will keep breaking down the fish.

notes: Use only the freshest sashimi-grade fish. Ask your fishmonger for corvina or snapper that's been kept for raw preparation.
The ceviche is at its best eaten within 30 minutes of mixing, the acid continues to work and the texture gets softer the longer it sits.
Make the ají amarillo paste fresh if you can find the chillies; if using paste from a jar, start with 3 tbsp and adjust to taste.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Arepa con queso
summary: Warm, crusty corn arepa filled with melted white cheese, how Andrés starts every morning

items.raw: 150 g white cheese (queso de mano or mozzarella), cut into strips

steps.text: Mix the corn flour, warm water and salt in a bowl, stirring until you have a soft, moist dough. Let it rest for 2–3 minutes.
Wet your hands. Divide the dough into 2 balls and gently flatten each into a thick disc about 8 cm across and 1 cm thick.
Heat a griddle or heavy frying pan over medium heat. Once hot, place the arepas on the griddle.
Cook for 6–7 minutes until the bottom is golden and crusty, then flip and cook the other side for another 6–7 minutes until both sides are golden and the arepa sounds hollow when tapped.
Using a thin knife, carefully cut a pocket into the side of each warm arepa without splitting it open completely.
Stuff each arepa with the cheese strips while the arepa is still warm, the residual heat will melt the cheese slightly. Serve immediately.

notes: Make ahead: Mix the dough and shape the arepas up to 2 hours before cooking, then refrigerate, bring to room temperature before cooking.
Swap: If you can't find queso de mano, fresh mozzarella or even mild cheddar works, though it won't be quite the same.
You can cook arepas on a griddle, heavy-bottomed frying pan, or a cast-iron frying pan, whatever you have. The sound and smell tell you more than the time does.

title: Mole Negro Oaxaqueño
summary: My mother's black mole from the comal, chocolate, chilhuacles, and thirty years of making it right

items.raw: 60 g sesame seeds (plus extra for serving)

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Toast the cinnamon stick, cloves and coriander seeds until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the deseeded chillies, a few at a time, pressing them gently against the bottom of the pot for a few seconds until they release their aroma. Do not burn them. Remove to a bowl.
In the same pot, add 2 tbsp oil. Cook the garlic and onion over medium heat, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Meanwhile, soak the toasted chillies in 500 ml hot water for 10 minutes until very soft. Strain, reserving all the soaking liquid.
Add the soaked chillies, raisins, almonds, sesame seeds and torn tortilla to the pot with the garlic and onion. Stir to combine and cook for 3 minutes.

Working in batches, transfer the mixture to a blender with 250 ml of the reserved chilli soaking liquid. Blend until completely smooth. Pour through a fine sieve into a clean pot, pressing with the back of a spoon to extract all the mole.

Add the remaining reserved soaking liquid (about 250 ml) to the strained mole and stir to combine. Place over medium-low heat and simmer, stirring often, for 20 minutes. The mole should be thick but pourable.

Warm the chicken stock in a separate pot. Add 250 ml of the warm stock to the mole and stir well. Continue simmering, stirring often, for 15 minutes. Add the remaining stock, a little at a time, until you reach the consistency you want, it should coat the back of a spoon but flow slowly.

Reduce the heat to very low. Add the chocolate and the remaining 2 tbsp oil, stirring constantly until the chocolate is completely melted and incorporated. Taste and add salt as needed. Keep warm until you're ready to serve.
Serve the mole poured over cooked chicken, rice or with warm tortillas. Sprinkle with the extra sesame seeds.

notes: This mole keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days and freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Make it ahead, it tastes better the next day.
Use the mole with poached chicken, or pour it over enchiladas, turkey or meatballs. A little mole goes a long way.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Ugali na Sukuma
summary: Cornmeal mush with sautéed collard greens, Kenya's everyday plate

steps.text: Bring the water to a boil in a pot with a pinch of salt. Slowly pour in the cornmeal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps, until the mixture thickens, about 5 minutes.
Keep stirring as the ugali cooks and pulls away from the sides of the pot, another 5 to 8 minutes. When it's thick and smooth, press it down and let it sit off the heat.
Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 3 minutes.

Add the sukuma wiki and stir to coat with oil. Cook for 2 minutes, then add the tomato and chilli, if using. Stir and cook until the greens are tender and the tomato is soft, about 3 to 4 minutes. Season with salt to taste.
Turn the ugali out onto a platter, shape it into a mound with the back of a spoon, and serve the sukuma wiki on the side or spooned over the top.

title: Kırmızı Mercimekli Köfte
summary: Spiced lentil and bulgur meatballs, pan-fried until crispy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Rinse the lentils and place in a saucepan with 500 ml water. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 12 minutes until just soft but not falling apart. Drain well and let cool slightly.

In a large bowl, combine the warm lentils with the bulgur, diced onion, garlic, tomato paste, cumin, Aleppo pepper, cinnamon and parsley. Mix gently but thoroughly until it just comes together. Season with salt and pepper. Let sit for 10 minutes so the bulgur absorbs moisture.
With damp hands, shape the mixture into oval meatballs about 4 cm long. Place on a plate.
Heat a thin layer of oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once shimmering, carefully add the köfte in batches, don't crowd the pan.
Fry for 3 to 4 minutes on each side until golden and crispy all over. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel.
Serve warm with lemon wedges and yoghurt on the side.

notes: Make ahead: shape the köfte up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate on a tray, covered. Fry when ready to serve.
Serve with yoghurt, lemon wedges, and fresh salad, or tuck into flatbread with tomato and onion.

title: Shiitake Jjim
summary: Braised shiitake mushrooms with soy and sesame, deep and meditative.

image.credit: Photo: Fernanda da Silva Lopes / Pexels

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a large shallow pot or braising pan over medium heat.
Add the shiitake mushrooms, cut side down, and let them sit undisturbed for 2 minutes until they begin to brown.
Turn the mushrooms and cook for another 2 minutes, then pour in the soy sauce, sugar, and water.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then lower the heat and braise, uncovered, for about 15 minutes, until the mushrooms are tender and the liquid has reduced by half.
Taste and adjust the soy sauce or water as needed, the braise should taste rich but not overly salty, with a glossy, slightly thickened sauce and tender mushrooms.
Scatter the spring onions over the top and cook for 1 minute, then transfer to a serving bowl.
Finish with the toasted sesame seeds and a pinch of black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Keeps well in the fridge for up to 5 days; reheat gently or eat cold as part of a banchan spread.
The mushrooms release their own moisture, so don't add more water than called for or the dish will taste thin.

title: Cơm Tấm Chay
summary: Broken rice with marinated tofu, fresh herbs and fried shallots, everyday southern Vietnamese comfort, vegetarian

items.raw: 400 g extra-firm tofu, pressed and cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: pressed and cut into bite-sized pieces

items.raw: 1 cup fresh herbs (mint, coriander, Vietnamese mint), roughly chopped
2 spring onions, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Combine the tofu, soy sauce, 2 tbsp oil, garlic, ground coriander and black pepper in a bowl. Let sit for at least 15 minutes, turning the tofu gently halfway through.

Meanwhile, rinse the broken rice well under cold water until the water runs clear. Cook in 4 cups water in a saucepan over medium-high heat, stirring occasionally, until tender and the liquid is absorbed, about 15 minutes. Fluff with a fork.
Heat a large non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the marinated tofu (discarding excess marinade) and cook, turning gently, until lightly golden on all sides, about 8 minutes.
Divide the warm rice among bowls. Top each with a portion of the tofu, cucumber, tomato, herbs and spring onions. Scatter the fried shallots over and serve with lime wedges.

notes: Cook the rice in advance and cool quickly; reheat gently before serving if you like. You can marinate the tofu overnight.
Fried shallots keep in an airtight container for a week.
The marinade ingredients are flexible, add a pinch of chilli flakes or a splash of rice vinegar if you like.

title: Rugbrød med leverpostej og agurkesalat
summary: Open rye sandwich with liver pâté, cucumber salad and crispy bacon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
100 g pâté, preferably Danish liver pâté (leverpostej)

steps.text: Make the cucumber salad: toss the sliced cucumber with the vinegar, sugar, salt and pepper. Set aside for at least 10 minutes so the cucumbers soften and flavour the brine.
While the cucumber sits, cook the bacon in a frying pan over medium-high heat until crispy, about 5–6 minutes. Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel.
Lightly toast the rye bread until just crisp at the edges if you like it warm, or leave it as is.
Spread each slice generously with pâté.
Top each slice with 2 rashers of bacon, then a spoonful of the cucumber salad (drain off excess liquid first). Sprinkle with fresh dill if you have it, and a pinch of flaky salt.
Serve straight away while the bacon is still warm.

notes: The cucumber salad can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge. Drain before serving.
Use the best-quality pâté and bacon you can find, this sandwich lives or dies by those two things.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).

title: Erbsensuppe
summary: Thick split pea soup with ham hock and leeks, the way Oma made it in winter.

items.raw: 2 leeks, white and light green parts, sliced into 2 cm rounds
items.prep: white and light green parts, sliced into 2 cm rounds

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the split peas, ham hock, bay leaves and water into a large pot. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer, uncovered, for 45 minutes.
Add the carrots and leeks. Stir well and simmer for another 45 minutes, until the peas have nearly dissolved and the soup is thick. Stir occasionally to prevent sticking.
Remove the ham hock. When cool enough to handle, shred any meat and discard the bone and skin. Return the shredded meat to the pot.
Fish out the bay leaves. Season with salt and pepper. If the soup is thicker than you like, add a splash of water. Serve hot.

notes: The soup thickens considerably as it cools. Reheat gently with a little water if needed.
Make it a day ahead, the flavour improves overnight. Store in the fridge for up to 4 days.

title: Khoresh Fenugreek
summary: Kidney beans and beef in a dark, aromatic stew with dried fenugreek leaves and lime.

items.raw: 600 g beef chuck, cut into 3 cm pieces
400 g tin kidney beans, drained and rinsed
2 tbsp dried fenugreek leaves, rubbed through your fingers
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Season beef with salt and pepper. Working in batches, sear the meat until golden on both sides, about 2 minutes per side. Set aside.
Add onions to the pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent, about 8 minutes. Add turmeric and cumin, stirring for 1 minute until fragrant.

Return beef to the pot. Add kidney beans and beef stock. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Add the halved dried limes. Cover and cook for 60 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is tender.

Stir in the dried fenugreek leaves. Simmer, uncovered, for 15 minutes more. The sauce should darken and thicken slightly. Taste and adjust salt and pepper. The stew is ready when the beef is fall-apart tender and the flavour is deep and bitter-herbaceous.

notes: This stew tastes better the next day. Make it ahead and reheat gently on the stove.
Dried limes (omani limes) are available at Middle Eastern grocers; if you can't find them, preserved lemon works but use less, the flavour is more intense.

Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft. If using dried kidney beans, soak them, then boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering, to destroy a natural toxin.

title: Saucisson braisé aux lentilles
summary: Braised sausage with lentils, a Lyonnaise bistro classic.

items.raw: 4 sausages (good-quality pork sausage or saucisson de Lyon), about 400 g
items.note: good-quality pork sausage or saucisson de Lyon

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based pot or braising dish over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped garlic and carrot rounds, and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the lentils, tinned tomatoes, chicken stock, bay leaf and thyme. Bring to a simmer until gently bubbling, then nestle the whole sausages into the lentil mixture.

Cover and braise over a low heat for 35–40 minutes, until the lentils are tender and the sausages are cooked through. The sausages should be opaque and firm inside (check by piercing with a knife; juices should run clear).
Remove the bay leaf and thyme sprig. Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Serve the sausages on a bed of lentils, spooning the braising liquid over the top.

notes: Leftovers keep, covered, in the fridge for three days and taste even better reheated gently on the stove.
If you can find saucisson de Lyon or a good Lyonnaise sausage, use it; otherwise a quality pork sausage works fine.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Spam Musubi
summary: Grilled spam between seasoned rice and nori, a Hawaiian plate lunch classic in one hand

items.raw: 1 tin (340 g) canned luncheon meat, sliced into 8 pieces

steps.text: While the rice is still warm, mix the rice vinegar, caster sugar and salt together, then fold gently through the rice until well combined. Set aside to cool slightly.

Heat the neutral oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the luncheon meat slices for 2–3 minutes each side until the edges are golden and crispy. Brush with kecap manis while still in the pan.
Place a sheet of nori shiny side down on a clean work surface. Wet your fingers and spread about 1 cup of seasoned rice firmly across the nori, leaving a 1 cm border at the top.
Place a slice of fried luncheon meat across the centre of the rice.
Starting from the bottom, roll the nori tightly, using the border at the top to seal. Slice in half crosswise with a sharp, wet knife.
Repeat with the remaining nori sheets, rice and meat. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the musubi the morning before and keep wrapped in the fridge. Bring to room temperature before eating, or warm gently in the microwave.
Swap the sweet soy sauce for tamari or regular soy sauce if that's what you've got, the musubi will taste less sweet but still good.
Any leftover seasoned rice can be used to make onigiri or fried rice.
Food safety: Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Sigara Börek
summary: Crispy fried pastry tubes filled with feta and herbs, a Turkish snack that's dangerously easy to eat.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the filling: combine feta, parsley, dill, spring onion, half the beaten egg, salt and pepper in a bowl. Mix gently, you want the cheese to hold together, not become mushy. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Set up your workspace: lay one sheet of yufka on a clean bench, long edge closest to you. If the yufka is very large, cut it in half lengthwise to make two strips.

Spoon about 2 tbsp filling along the bottom edge, leaving 2 cm on each side. Fold the sides in over the filling, then roll tightly away from you until you have a long, thin, cigarette-shaped roll. Press gently to seal. The seam should be on the bottom.
Brush the outside lightly with remaining beaten egg to help it seal and get golden. Repeat with remaining yufka and filling.
Heat the oil in a deep heavy-bottomed pan or Dutch oven to 170–180°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test with a small piece of pastry, it should sizzle immediately and brown in about 30 seconds.
Working in batches of 3 or 4, fry the börek seam-side down first until they're golden and crispy, about 2 minutes. Turn carefully and fry the other side until evenly golden, another 1–2 minutes.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel. Keep warm while you fry the rest.
Serve hot, while they're still crispy, with lemon wedges and yoghurt for dipping if you like (though purists like Nonna would serve them plain).

notes: Make the börek up to 4 hours ahead and fry them just before serving. Cooked börek can be reheated in a 180°C oven for about 5 minutes, but they're best fresh.
No yufka? Filo pastry works, but use 2 sheets together and brush between them with melted butter. Not quite the same, but it'll do.
The oil temperature matters. Too cool and they'll be greasy; too hot and they'll burn before the inside heats through.

title: Arrós a Banda
summary: Rice cooked in seafood stock with grilled fish, a weeknight Catalan take on the Valencia classic.

image.credit: Photo: Javier Lastras / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

items.raw: 750 ml seafood stock (or fish stock), warm
4 white fish fillets, 150 g each (sea bream, sea bass or barramundi)
items.note: sea bream, sea bass or barramundi

items.raw: Sea salt and black pepper, to season

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a wide, shallow pan (a paella pan if you have one) over a medium heat. Add the finely chopped onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. This is the sofregit, don't rush it, as the sweetness is the soul of the dish.
Add the grated tomato to the sofregit and cook, stirring, until the mixture is thick and darkened, about 5 minutes more. The tomato should lose its rawness and merge into the oil and onion.
Stir in the rice until well coated in the sofregit, about 1 minute. Pour in the warm seafood stock all at once, add the salt and saffron if using, and bring to a simmer.

Simmer, without stirring, for about 18 to 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and has absorbed almost all the stock. The top should look dry, with perhaps a few grains still glistening. Do not stir once the stock is added.

While the rice cooks, prepare the fish. Heat the olive oil in a large frying pan or on a grill plate over a medium-high heat until smoking slightly. Season the fish fillets with salt and pepper, then lay them skin-side down in the pan. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the skin is golden and crisp, then flip and cook for another 1 to 2 minutes until just cooked through.
Divide the rice among four shallow bowls or plates. Top each with a grilled fish fillet and a generous dollop of aioli. Serve immediately.

notes: Make your own aioli (garlic, mayonnaise, salt) or buy it, the rice and fish are the stars.
Ask the fishmonger for fillets that are thick and skin-on; the crispy skin is essential. Any firm white fish works.
The sofregit can be made ahead and refrigerated; reheat it gently before adding the rice.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Undhiyu
summary: Mixed vegetable and chickpea medley baked in banana leaves, sweet-spicy-tangy and deeply flavoured.

items.raw: 200 g potato, cut into 2 cm chunks
200 g sweet potato, cut into 2 cm chunks
150 g eggplant, cut into 2 cm chunks
150 g unripe plantain, peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks

items.raw: 100 g pumpkin, cut into 2 cm chunks
150 g green beans, cut into 5 cm lengths
400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed

steps.text: Prep all vegetables: potatoes, sweet potato, eggplant, plantain, pumpkin and green beans. Thinly slice the onion. Have the chickpeas and peanuts ready.
Heat 3 tbsp oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them crackle, about 1 minute. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring, until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add asafoetida, ground coriander, turmeric and cayenne. Stir constantly for 1 minute until fragrant, being careful not to burn the spices.
Add all the prepared vegetables (potato, sweet potato, eggplant, plantain, pumpkin and green beans) and stir to coat with the spiced oil, about 2 minutes.
Add the drained chickpeas and roasted peanuts. Stir through.
Dissolve the jaggery in 60 ml warm water. Mix in the tamarind paste. Pour this over the vegetables and stir well to combine. Taste and add salt as needed.

Line a large baking dish or Dutch oven with banana leaves. Spoon the vegetable mixture into the centre. Fold the banana leaves over to cover, or add more leaves if needed to create a parcel. The leaves will char slightly but won't burn, and the vegetables should be tender when pierced with a knife.
Cover the baking dish tightly with foil. Bake at 180°C for 1 hour 15 minutes, until the vegetables are very tender and the flavours have melded into a rich, sweet-spicy-tangy mixture.
Unfold the banana leaves carefully (they will be hot), scatter with fresh coriander if you like, and serve warm with rotli, rice or as part of a thali.

notes: Prep the vegetables the evening before and store in the fridge, makes baking day much easier.
Undhiyu keeps well and tastes even better the next day. Reheat gently in the oven or microwave.
If banana leaves aren't available, bake covered in parchment paper and foil; it won't have the same flavour but will still be delicious.

title: Frijoles Charros
summary: Pinto beans with bacon, chorizo and jalapeños, a norteño staple.

image.credit: Photo: Christa Reyes / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 2 × 400 g tin pinto beans, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Cook the bacon in a large heavy-based pot over medium-high heat until crispy, about 5 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.
Add the chorizo to the pot and cook, breaking it up as it cooks, until it releases its fat and is cooked through, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the onion and cook, stirring, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the jalapeños and garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute.
Pour in the chicken stock and add the pinto beans. Stir well to combine.
Bring to a gentle simmer and cook, uncovered, for 10 minutes to let the flavours meld.
Return the bacon to the pot and stir through. Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Serve hot, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: cook through step 6, cool quickly, and store in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently before serving.
Dried beans: soak 300 g dried pinto beans overnight, then simmer with stock for 1 to 1.5 hours before adding the chorizo and bacon.

title: Oka
summary: Raw fish marinated in coconut cream and lime, a Samoan to'ona'i essential.

items.raw: 600 g sashimi-grade fish (snapper or tuna), cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Put the cubed fish into a large bowl and pour over the lime juice, stirring gently to coat. The lime juice will start to cure the fish immediately.
Leave the fish in the lime juice for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the flesh turns opaque (you're looking for it to look cooked through even though it's raw).
Drain most of the lime juice from the fish, leaving just a thin coating. Pour in the coconut cream and stir gently to combine.
Add the onion, tomatoes, cucumber and spring onions, stirring carefully so you don't break up the fish. Season with salt to taste.
Let it sit for another 5 minutes so the flavours come together, then serve straight away in a large bowl with coriander scattered over if you like.

notes: Use only the freshest sashimi-grade fish, ask your fishmonger if it's safe to eat raw.
Don't skip the draining step after the lime cure, or your oka will be too liquid.
Oka is best served straightaway, but you can make it up to 2 hours ahead and keep it cool.

The fish here is eaten raw or only cured in citrus. Buy sashimi-grade fish from a fishmonger, keep it cold and eat it the same day; skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Frying pan Cornbread
summary: Golden, buttery cornbread baked in a cast-iron frying pan with a crispy edge and subtle sweetness.

items.raw: 60 g butter, melted, plus extra for the pan
items.prep: melted, plus extra for the pan

steps.text: Heat your cast-iron frying pan in the oven at 200°C for 10 minutes until very hot.
Whisk together the cornmeal, plain flour, caster sugar, baking powder and salt in a large bowl.
In another bowl, whisk the buttermilk, eggs and melted butter together until well combined.
Pour the wet mixture into the dry ingredients and stir until just combined, a few lumps are fine.
Carefully remove the hot frying pan from the oven and add a tablespoon of butter, swirling to coat the base and sides.
Pour the batter into the hot frying pan and return to the oven. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden brown and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Let cool in the pan for 5 minutes before turning out or serving straight from the frying pan.

notes: Best served warm with butter and honey or alongside chilli.
Can be made ahead and reheated, wrapped in foil, at 150°C for 10 minutes.

title: Sinigang na Baboy
summary: Tamarind pork rib soup with leafy greens, radish and okra, comfort in a pot.

items.raw: 800 g pork ribs, cut into 5 cm pieces
2 medium waxy potatoes, cut into chunks
200 g leafy greens (spinach or bok choy), chopped

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the pork ribs on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, fry the onion and garlic until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Stir in the tamarind paste until well combined, then return the pork ribs to the pot.
Pour in the water and bring to a boil. Skim off any scum that rises to the surface. Reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 30 minutes until the pork is tender.
Add the potatoes and radishes. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes until starting to soften.
Add the okra and leafy greens. Stir gently and cook for another 5 minutes until the greens are wilted and the okra is tender but still bright.
Season with salt and pepper to taste. Add the green chilli if using. Taste and adjust the tamarind and salt as needed, it should be sour, savoury and warm.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with rice.

notes: Make it ahead: cool the sinigang completely, then store in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove. The flavours get better the next day, anak.
If you can't find tamarind paste, use 3 tbsp fresh lime juice instead, added at the end.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Mì Quang
summary: Turmeric noodles with pork and shrimp, salty and aromatic, the way it's done in central Vietnam.

items.raw: 400 g pork shoulder, cut into 2 cm pieces
200 g raw prawns, peeled and deveined
300 g fresh rice noodles (turmeric mì Quảng noodles if you can find them)
items.note: turmeric mì Quảng noodles if you can find them

steps.text: Toss the pork with 1 tbsp fish sauce and turmeric powder, and set aside for 5 minutes.

Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pot over high heat. Add the pork in a single layer and cook without stirring for 2 minutes until light golden, then break apart and cook for another 3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add remaining oil to the pot. Add chopped garlic and sliced shallots, and fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the pork to the pot and add chicken stock, extra fish sauce, and salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 12 minutes until the pork is tender.
Add the prawns and simmer for 3 minutes until they turn pink and are cooked through.
While the broth simmers, bring a separate large pot of water to a boil. Add the turmeric noodles and cook according to packet instructions until tender. Drain well.
Divide the noodles among four bowls. Ladle the broth, pork, and prawns over the noodles.
Top each bowl with crushed roasted peanuts, fried shallots, sliced spring onion, fresh dill, and chilli if using. Serve immediately.

notes: If you can't find fresh turmeric noodles, dried ones work fine, cook them a minute or two longer. Some shops sell them as bánh mì quang.
The broth is the hero here: don't skip the shallots and garlic, and don't be stingy with the fish sauce.
Prep the pork and prawns ahead of time, but make the dish fresh when you're ready to eat.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Oyakodon
summary: Chicken and egg in a silky dashi broth over rice, on the table in 20 minutes.

items.raw: 200 g boneless chicken thigh, cut into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Bring the dashi, soy sauce and mirin to a gentle simmer in a large frying pan or shallow pan over medium heat, until small bubbles break the surface.
Add the chicken pieces and onion, and simmer for about 5 minutes until the chicken is just cooked through.
While the chicken cooks, lightly beat the eggs in a small bowl.
When the chicken is done, pour the beaten eggs slowly over the simmering broth in a thin stream, moving the pan gently so the eggs create soft curds. This should take about 1 minute.
Let the eggs set for another minute without stirring, they should be creamy and just cooked, not scrambled solid.
Divide the warm rice between two bowls and pour the broth, chicken and eggs over the top. Sprinkle with spring onion if using, and serve right away.

notes: Make ahead: Prep the chicken and onion earlier in the day, and cook the rice. The broth comes together in 10 minutes flat.
Chicken breast works too, but thigh stays juicier and cooks just as fast.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Mum's Nonya Chicken
summary: Chicken in spiced coconut and tamarind sauce, the weeknight way.

items.raw: 600 g chicken thigh fillet, cut into bite-sized pieces
1 brown onion, cut into thick wedges

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the laksa paste and fry, stirring, for about 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the coconut milk and tamarind paste, stirring to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until bubbling lightly and the sauce is smooth.
Add the chicken pieces and stir to coat in the sauce. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through.
Add the onion wedges and simmer for another 5 minutes until the onion is just tender but still holding its shape.
Taste and adjust seasoning with salt. Serve hot with a squeeze of lime and coriander if you like it.

notes: Serve with steamed jasmine rice or on its own with a squeeze of lime.
If you can't find laksa paste, use 2 tbsp of any red curry paste as a swap, it won't be quite the same, but it'll still be good.
Makes good leftovers; reheat gently on the stove.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Devilled Chicken
summary: Quick-fried chicken with onions, chilli and mustard, the spicy stir-fry for night shift.

items.raw: 1 brown onion, halved and thinly sliced
600 g chicken breast, cut into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the mustard seeds and cook, stirring, until they start to pop, about 1 minute.
Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and translucent, about 4 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger and green chillies, and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the cumin and turmeric, cook for another 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the chicken pieces and cook, stirring frequently, until they're cooked through, no pink inside, about 8 to 10 minutes.
Pour in the vinegar and salt, and stir through. Taste and add more salt if needed. The dish should have a sharp, spicy edge.
Serve hot with rice, roti or hoppers, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Makes great lunch packet food, it reheats well and tastes even better the next day.
Beef works just as well: use 600g diced beef steak and cook for 10 to 12 minutes until tender.
Store leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Risotto ai Funghi Porcini
summary: Creamy risotto with porcini mushrooms, Alba-style. Takes patience. Worth it.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Soak the dried porcini in 200 ml of hot water for 10 minutes. Strain through a fine sieve, keeping the soaking liquid. Roughly chop the porcini.
Heat the stock in a separate pot until steaming, and keep it at a gentle simmer throughout cooking.
Heat the olive oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the rice to the onion and stir for 1 minute until lightly toasted. Pour in the white wine and stir until almost completely absorbed.

Add the porcini soaking liquid to the rice and stir until absorbed. Start adding the warm stock one ladle at a time, stirring gently, waiting for each ladle to be absorbed before adding the next. This takes about 18 minutes.
After about 16 minutes, taste the rice. It should be creamy but with a slight firmness at the centre of each grain. Stir in the chopped porcini.

When the rice is almost done and most of the stock is absorbed, remove from heat. Add the butter and parmesan, stirring gently until combined. The risotto should flow slightly on the plate, not stiff, not soup.
Season with salt and pepper. Serve immediately.

notes: The soaking liquid is flavour, don't skip it.
Once you add stock, don't walk away. Risotto demands your attention for those 18 minutes.
Alba cooks would argue about the exact ratio. Make it how you like it.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Slow-Roasted Gemista
summary: Tomatoes and peppers stuffed with rice and herbs, slow-roasted until they collapse into themselves.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Cut the top off each tomato and set aside. Using a spoon, scoop out the insides, leaving about 1 cm of flesh around the walls. Chop the scooped flesh and set aside. Cut the capsicums in half and remove the seeds.
Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for another minute, stirring.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes to toast it lightly. Add the chopped tomato flesh, parsley, mint, oregano, and a pinch of salt and pepper. Stir well and remove from heat. Let cool slightly.

Arrange the tomato shells and capsicum halves in a large baking dish, cut-side up. Divide the rice mixture evenly among them, pressing gently and mounding slightly, they'll settle as they cook until the rice is tender and the tops are lightly golden.
Drizzle the remaining 2 tbsp olive oil over everything. Pour the water into the dish around (not over) the vegetables. Replace the tomato tops. Season with salt and pepper.

Roast, uncovered, at 180°C for about 60 minutes, until the tomatoes and capsicums are very soft and the edges are slightly charred. The rice will have absorbed most of the liquid. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: These are best served warm or at room temperature, not hot, the flavours settle beautifully as they cool.
You can make them a few hours ahead and reheat gently in a 150°C oven for 15 minutes.
If your tomatoes are not very ripe, add a tbsp of tomato paste to the rice mixture for more depth.

title: Winter Melon and Pork Rib Soup
summary: Slow-simmered Cantonese soup with tender pork ribs, pale winter melon, and earthy dried mushrooms.

items.raw: 800 g pork spare ribs, cut into 5 cm pieces
1 kg winter melon (about 1/4 of a melon), peeled and cut into 5 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the pork ribs and blanch for 2 minutes. Drain and rinse the ribs under cold water until the water runs clear, scrubbing gently to remove impurities. This takes about a minute and makes the soup clean and bright.

In a large pot, add 2 litres of fresh water. Bring to a boil, then add the blanched pork ribs, dried shiitake mushrooms, dried scallops, smashed ginger, and half of the spring onion. Return to a boil, then lower the heat until the broth is at a gentle, rolling simmer with small bubbles.
Simmer uncovered for 60 minutes. The pork should be almost tender and the broth fragrant. Skim any foam that rises to the surface in the first 15 minutes.

Add the winter melon chunks. Bring back to a gentle simmer and cook for another 45 to 60 minutes, until the melon is very soft and translucent and the pork is completely tender. The broth should taste deep and savoury from the long cooking.
Taste and season with salt. Discard the ginger and the first batch of spring onion. Serve hot, garnished with the fresh spring onion.

notes: This soup tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days; reheat gently.
If you can't find dried scallops, the soup is still good made with just shiitake mushrooms, use 10 or 12 instead.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Sambar
summary: Tangy Tamil lentil and vegetable stew with curry leaves and asafoetida, served with rice or dosa.

items.raw: 200 g mixed vegetables (carrots, beans and eggplant), cut into 1 cm pieces

steps.text: Toast the cumin seeds, coriander seeds, black pepper and dried chillies in a dry pan over medium heat for 1 minute, shaking the pan, until fragrant. Set aside to cool, then grind to a powder with a mortar and pestle. Stir in the chilli powder.
Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook, stirring, until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the asafoetida and toasted spice powder, and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Add the lentils, vegetables, tamarind paste, water and salt. Stir well, then bring to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils have broken down and the vegetables are very tender.
Stir in the torn curry leaves and cook for another 2 minutes. Taste and adjust the salt and tamarind to your liking, the stew should be tangy and well-seasoned. Serve hot with steamed rice or dosa.

notes: Make ahead: sambar keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the flavours deepen. Reheat gently on the stove.
Vegetable swap: use whatever you have, pumpkin, beans, carrots and drumstick are all traditional. Avoid watery vegetables like tomato.
If you have a pressure cooker, this halves the time: toast the spices, cook the base (steps 2–3), then pressure cook for 5 minutes once steaming.

title: Bún Chả Hà Nội
summary: Grilled pork patties with herbs, vermicelli and dipping sauce, Hanoi street food for weeknight dinner.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Fresh lettuce, such as cos or butter lettuce
items.prep: such as cos or butter lettuce

steps.text: Make the dipping sauce first: whisk together fish sauce, sugar, lime juice, garlic, chilli if using, and warm water in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust the balance of salty, sour and sweet, it should be sharp and punchy. Set aside.

Put the pork mince in a bowl with garlic, fish sauce, sugar, salt and pepper. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the patties will be tough. Divide into 8 portions and shape each into a flat oval patty about 1.5 cm thick.

Heat a grill pan or barbecue hotplate over medium-high heat. Brush with oil, then cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on each side, until cooked through (no pink inside) and charred at the edges. Transfer to a plate.
While the pork cooks, bring a pot of water to the boil and cook the rice vermicelli according to packet instructions until soft and tender. Drain and rinse with cold water to stop it cooking.
Arrange the lettuce, mint, coriander, thai basil if using, cucumber and noodles on a platter. Place the warm pork patties on top and scatter over the crushed peanuts.
Serve with the dipping sauce on the side, each person tears some herbs and lettuce, takes a bite of pork, and dips it all into the sauce.

notes: Make the patties up to 4 hours ahead and keep in the fridge; cook them just before serving.
The dipping sauce keeps in a jar in the fridge for a week, good for leftovers too.
Swap the herbs around depending on what's growing; mint and coriander are the core two, but thai basil and Vietnamese mint both work.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Arroz e Feijão
summary: Perfectly cooked rice and beans, the foundation of every Brazilian meal.

image.credit: Photo: Felipe Spina / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

items.raw: 800 g tin black beans, drained and rinsed

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until softened and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the minced garlic and cook for another minute until fragrant.

Add the drained beans to the pot along with the chicken stock. Stir well and bring to a simmer. Cook, uncovered, for 8 to 10 minutes until the beans have absorbed some flavour and the liquid has reduced slightly. Season with salt to taste. The beans should be creamy and not watery.
While the beans are cooking, heat the oil in a separate large pot over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook until softened and golden, about 4 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Add the rice to the pot and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until the grains are coated in oil and slightly translucent at the edges.
Pour in the water and add the salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover with a lid, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes until the rice is tender and all the liquid is absorbed.
Remove the rice from heat and let it rest, covered, for 3 to 4 minutes. Fluff with a fork. Serve the rice and beans together on plates or in meal prep containers.

notes: Make ahead: cook both the rice and beans in bulk on Sunday. Store in separate airtight containers in the fridge for up to 4 days, or portion into meal prep containers.
The beans should be creamy but not mushy. If your liquid reduces too quickly, add a splash more stock.
Serve with hot sauce, lime wedges, or fresh salsa on the side.

title: Pâté de foies de morue
summary: Creamy cod liver pâté, a traditional Breton spread for toast and crackers.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a small pot of salted water to a gentle simmer. Add the cod livers and poach for 4–5 minutes, until they turn pale and opaque. Skim any foam from the surface. Drain well and let cool slightly.
In a mortar and pestle or small food processor, crush or pulse the warm cod livers with the softened butter until completely smooth and creamy, this should take 2–3 minutes.
Fold in the minced shallot, Dijon mustard and red wine vinegar, stirring until just combined. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Press the pâté through a fine-mesh sieve into a serving bowl or small jar, pushing gently with the back of a spoon to create a silky texture. Alternatively, leave it chunky if you prefer.
Cover and chill for at least 30 minutes before serving. Serve on warm buttered toast or crackers.

notes: The pâté keeps in a sealed jar in the fridge for up to 4 days.
If you can find it, a layer of clarified butter poured over the top helps preserve it and keeps the surface from darkening.
A small glass of cold white wine or a squeeze of fresh lemon on the side is lovely.
Food safety:

title: Pepper Soup
summary: Fiery Nigerian beef or goat soup, spiced and medicinal, served steaming hot.

image.credit: Photo: Nancy Nwachukwu / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 800 g beef shanks (or goat meat), cut into chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the meat and brown on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove and set aside.
In the same pot, add the onion halves, whole chillies, crushed garlic and ginger. Stir for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the tomato paste, cayenne and black pepper. Stir well for 1 minute to coat the meat.
Return the meat to the pot. Add the crushed stock cubes and water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer until the broth is fragrant and the meat is tender.
Cover and cook for 1 to 1.5 hours, until the meat is very tender and the broth is rich and deeply flavoured. Stir occasionally.
Remove the onion halves and whole chillies (or leave them in if you like more heat). Taste and season with salt.
Serve hot in bowls, with a piece of meat and plenty of the spiced broth.

notes: Make a big batch and freeze half. It keeps well and tastes even better reheated.
Goat meat works just as well, some say better. If using goat, cook for a bit longer, maybe 2 hours.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Fiji-Style Fish Curry
summary: White fish in a rich coconut curry with turmeric and fenugreek, the island way.

items.raw: 700 g firm white fish fillet (barramundi or snapper), cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the sliced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, and stir until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add the turmeric, fenugreek seeds and cumin seeds, stirring constantly for 1 minute to bloom the spices.
Pour in the coconut milk and water, and stir well to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer until the sauce is steaming and lightly bubbling at the edges.
Add the fish pieces and salt. Simmer gently, uncovered, for 12–15 minutes until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily with a fork. Don't stir aggressively or the fish will break apart.
Taste and adjust the salt. Add lime juice to brighten the flavour. Serve hot with roti or rice, scattered with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Serve with roti, steamed rice or just with flatbread to soak up the sauce.
This curry is best eaten the day you make it, but keeps in the fridge for 2 days. Reheat gently so the fish doesn't toughen.
Food safety:

title: Crispy Fish with Burnt Butter and Capers
summary: Pan-fried white fish finished with browned butter and capers.

items.raw: 4 × 150 g white fish fillet (barramundi, snapper or flathead), skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the fish dry and season both sides generously with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once shimmering, place the fish skin-side down and cook without moving for 4–5 minutes, until the skin is crispy and golden. Flip gently and cook for a further 2–3 minutes until just cooked through. Transfer to a warm plate.
Return the pan to medium heat and add the butter. Let it melt, then keep cooking, swirling often, until it turns golden and smells nutty, about 2–3 minutes. Watch it, it can burn quickly.
Add the capers to the butter and cook for 30 seconds, until they sizzle, split open and the butter smells nutty and turns golden brown. Remove from heat and stir in the lemon juice.
Pour the burnt butter and capers over the fish. Scatter with parsley if you like, and serve straight away.

notes: Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Injera
summary: Spongy fermented flatbread that serves as both plate and utensil in Ethiopian meals.

image.credit: Photo: Dr. Ondřej Havelka (cestovatel) / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

steps.text: Mix the teff flour with about 375 ml of water and salt in a large bowl, stirring well to combine. The batter should be thick but pourable, similar to pancake batter. Add more water a little at a time if needed.

Cover the bowl loosely with a clean cloth and leave at room temperature for 3 days. Stir the batter once or twice a day. You'll see bubbles form and smell a pleasant sourness develop, this is the fermentation happening.
On the third day, stir the batter well. It should be slightly thinner and bubbly. If it seems too thick, add a little warm water and stir until it reaches the consistency of a thin pancake batter.
Heat a large non-stick frying pan or injera pan (or crepe pan) over medium-high heat. You want it very hot but not smoking. Don't oil the pan.
Once hot, pour about 150 ml of batter into the centre of the pan and immediately tilt and rotate the pan so the batter spreads out evenly to the edges, just like making a large, thin crêpe.

Cook for 2 to 3 minutes. The top will bubble and steam holes will form. You're looking for the bread to be cooked through but still pale, it shouldn't brown. The edges will lift slightly when it's ready.

Slide the injera onto a large plate once the surface is covered in small holes and the edges are just lifting and set. The spongy side (top) will have absorbed the steam and created the holes that make it perfect for scooping. Repeat with the remaining batter.
Stack the finished injera on a plate to keep warm. Serve immediately with your favourite stews and dishes.

notes: Injera keeps for a few days wrapped in a clean cloth at room temperature, or refrigerated for up to a week. Reheat gently in a covered pan.
The fermentation time is essential, don't rush it. The sour flavour and spongy texture both come from the three days of fermentation.
For the best results, use a proper injera pan (a shallow, wide non-stick pan) or a large non-stick crepe pan. A regular frying pan works but the edges can be harder to achieve.

title: Roti Canai
summary: Flaky stretched flatbread with spiced dal curry for dipping, mamak stall breakfast at home.

image.credit: Photo: Qwerty Binary / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
