items.raw: 2 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for folding and cooking
items.prep: plus extra for folding and cooking

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a large bowl. Slowly add warm water while stirring, then add 2 tbsp oil. Mix until shaggy, then knead for 8–10 minutes by hand until smooth and elastic. Cover with damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the dal curry: heat oil in a pan, fry onion until golden, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and ginger, cook for 1 minute. Add turmeric, cumin and chilli powder, cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.

Rinse lentils and add to the pan with coconut milk and 200 ml water. Bring to simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, until lentils break down and curry thickens, about 15–20 minutes. Season with salt to taste.

Divide dough into 4 equal balls. Lightly oil a bench top. Take one ball and press flat, then stretch it out slowly with your hands, working from the edge, until thin enough to almost see through, about 30 cm across. Don't worry if it tears.
Fold the stretched dough into a square or triangle shape, tucking in the edges to create layers. Flatten gently with your palms until it's about 1 cm thick.

Heat a non-stick pan or griddle over medium-high heat with a little oil. Cook each roti for 2–3 minutes on each side, pressing gently with a spatula, until golden and puffed with crispy edges. Transfer to a plate and cover with a clean cloth to keep warm.
Serve roti warm, torn into pieces, alongside the hot dal curry for dipping.

notes: The dough can be made ahead and refrigerated overnight; let it come to room temperature before stretching.
If your roti doesn't stretch thin enough, let it rest for a minute and try again, don't force it or it'll tear.
Dal curry keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheats gently over low heat.

title: Çilbir
summary: Poached eggs in garlicky yoghurt with chilli oil and sumac.

items.raw: ½ tsp pul biber (Turkish chilli flakes)

steps.text: Mix the yoghurt with the chopped garlic and a pinch of salt. Divide between two shallow bowls and set aside.
Fill a saucepan with water, add a splash of white vinegar, and bring to a gentle simmer until tiny bubbles rise from the base, but the water is not at a rolling boil.

Crack an egg into a small cup, then slide it into the simmering water. Repeat with the remaining eggs, spacing them out. Poach for about 3 minutes, until the whites are just set but the yolks are still soft.
Using a slotted spoon, lift each egg out of the water and place on top of the yoghurt in the bowls.
Warm the chilli oil gently in a small pan, just until fragrant, don't let it smoke. Drizzle over the eggs and yoghurt.
Sprinkle the sumac and pul biber over the top. Serve straight away while everything is still warm.

notes: If you don't have chilli oil, melt a knob of butter in a pan with a pinch of pul biber or dried chilli flakes.
The yoghurt can be mixed with garlic up to 30 minutes ahead; keep it at room temperature.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Chiles Rellenos
summary: Poblano peppers stuffed with Oaxaca cheese, fried and topped with tomato sauce.

items.raw: 200 g fresh mozzarella, cut into 4 batons
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the sauce first: put the tinned tomatoes, onion and garlic in a pot. Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes until the tomato has broken down and the onion is soft. Blend until smooth (or blitz with a hand blender). Season with salt. Set aside.

Roast the poblanos directly over a gas flame, turning often with tongs, until the skin is blackened all over, about 5 minutes. If you don't have gas, put them under a hot grill. Place in a plastic bag for 5 minutes to steam, the skin will come off easier.
Peel off the blackened skin under cold running water, gently rubbing with your fingers. Make a slit down one side and carefully remove the seeds and white membrane, keeping the pepper whole.
Insert a baton of mozzarella into each pepper. Be gentle, they tear easily. Lay on a plate and let rest.
Beat the eggs in a bowl until pale. Spread the flour on a plate. Heat about 5 cm of oil in a deep frying pan to 170°C.
Working one at a time, coat each pepper in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in beaten egg to coat completely. Carefully slide into the hot oil.
Fry for 2 to 3 minutes each side until golden brown, turning gently. You want the outside crispy and the cheese melting inside. Drain on paper towel.
Pour the tomato sauce into a serving dish. Place the fried chillies on top, or serve the sauce on the side. Eat while the cheese is still hot.

notes: Make the sauce up to a day ahead and reheat gently.
You can roast and peel the chillies an hour before you fry them; keep them in a covered container at room temperature.
Fresh mozzarella is the closest you'll find to Oaxaca at Coles; if you can get to a Latin American grocer in Marrickville, grab the real thing.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Peperoni Cruschi Ripieni
summary: Dried Calabrian peppers stuffed with breadcrumbs, raisins, pine nuts and anchovies.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Soak the dried cruschi peppers in warm water for 10 minutes until they're soft and pliable. Drain them well and pat dry with a clean cloth. Carefully make a slit down one side of each pepper and gently remove the seeds and white membrane, being careful not to tear the flesh.

While the peppers soak, combine the breadcrumbs, pine nuts, raisins, anchovies, garlic and parsley in a bowl. Season with salt and black pepper. The mixture should be moist but not soggy; if it seems dry, add a splash of water, a teaspoon at a time.
Preheat the oven to 180°C. Stuff each pepper generously with the breadcrumb mixture, pressing it in gently so it holds. Don't overstuff or the peppers will split.
Pour the olive oil into a small baking dish and arrange the stuffed peppers in a single layer, seam-side up. Drizzle any remaining oil over the top.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the peppers are heated through and the breadcrumb filling is golden. They should smell wonderful. Serve at room temperature or slightly warm.

notes: Make the filling ahead and store it in the fridge for up to 2 days. Stuff the peppers just before baking.
These are just as good at room temperature the next day, and they keep for 3 days in an airtight container.

title: Lahori Biryani
summary: Fragrant basmati rice layered with marinated meat and caramelised onions.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck (or lamb shoulder), cut into 4 cm pieces

steps.text: Combine the meat with yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, green chillies, cumin, coriander, turmeric, garam masala, salt and pepper. Mix well, cover and marinate for at least 30 minutes (or up to 4 hours in the fridge).

While the meat marinates, heat 100 ml of the oil in a large, heavy-based pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they are golden brown and crispy, about 20 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels. Set aside, reserving the oil.

Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the basmati rice and the whole spices (black cardamom, cinnamon, green cardamom, bay leaves, cumin and cloves). Cook until the rice is just cooked through but still has a slight firmness, about 8 minutes. Drain well and set aside.

In the same heavy-based pan used for the onions, heat the remaining 50 ml oil over medium-high heat. Add the marinated meat in a single layer and cook, stirring occasionally, until lightly browned on all sides, about 8 minutes. Do not cook through.

In a heavy-based pot with a tight-fitting lid (or use a biryani handi if you have one), layer: half the cooked rice, then all the meat and its juices, then the remaining rice. Scatter the caramelised onions on top, reserving some for garnish.

Cover the pot tightly with foil, then place the lid on top. Cook on high heat for about 2 minutes until steam builds, then reduce heat to low and cook for 45 minutes. Do not open the lid during cooking.

Remove from heat and let rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Open the lid carefully and gently mix the biryani with a fork, being careful not to break the rice grains. Garnish with the remaining fried onions, fresh coriander, fresh mint and fried garlic if using. Serve hot.

notes: Make ahead: marinate the meat for up to 4 hours in the fridge, and caramelise the onions an hour before cooking.
The dum pukht (sealed steaming) is essential, resist the urge to open the lid. This is where the magic happens.
Some cooks add saffron soaked in warm milk to the rice before the final layer. If you have it, scatter 1 tsp saffron threads soaked in 100 ml warm milk over the meat layer.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Varenyky
summary: Soft hand-folded potato and cheese dumplings with caramelised onions and sour cream.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the dough. Mix flour and salt in a bowl, then make a well in the centre. Add the egg and half the warm water, then stir to bring the flour in. Add more water a little at a time until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms. Knead for 2 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

While the dough rests, boil the diced potato in salted water until very tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well, then mash with butter until smooth. Stir in the grated cheese, salt and pepper. Set aside to cool.
Caramelise the onions. Heat oil in a large frying pan over medium heat and cook the sliced onions, stirring often, until deep golden and soft, about 15 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Roll the dough as thin as you can (about 2 mm) on a floured surface. Using a 7 cm glass or cutter, cut out circles. Place 1 tbsp filling just off-centre on each circle.
Fold the dough in half over the filling, then bring the corners together and press to seal into a little purse shape. Place each finished dumpling on a floured tray.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, add the varenyky and cook until they float to the surface, then cook for another 2 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and transfer to a serving dish.
Top the warm varenyky with caramelised onions and serve with a dollop of sour cream. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: Dough can be made ahead and refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Bring to room temperature before rolling.
Cooked varenyky freeze well for up to 1 month. Reheat by boiling briefly in salted water until they float again, or pan-fry with the caramelised onions.
The filling is traditional, but varenyky are also delicious filled with fried cabbage and mushrooms, or with cherries and sugar for dessert.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Kimbap with NZ Veg
summary: Korean seaweed rice rolls packed with local vegetables and dressed with sesame oil.

items.raw: 1 carrot, cut into matchsticks (about 15 cm long)
1 courgette, cut into matchsticks (about 15 cm long)

steps.text: Cook the rice. Rinse the sushi rice under cold water until the water runs clear. Bring 300 ml water to the boil in a small saucepan, add the rice, stir once, then cover and simmer on low heat for 15 minutes until tender. While still hot, transfer to a large bowl and drizzle with rice vinegar, caster sugar and salt; fold gently with a spatula until combined. Set aside to cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes.

Warm the vegetables. Heat 1 tbsp sesame oil in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the carrot and courgette matchsticks and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until just softened but still crisp. Transfer to a plate. In the same pan, add the spinach with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring, for 1–2 minutes until wilted. Transfer to a separate plate.

Cook the egg. Beat the egg lightly in a small bowl. Heat the remaining 1 tbsp sesame oil in the frying pan over a medium heat, then pour in the egg to make a thin omelette. Cook for 1–2 minutes each side until set, then slide onto a board and slice into thin strips.

Toast the nori. Working with one sheet of nori at a time, hold it flat about 15 cm above a gas flame (if using an electric hob, skip this step and use the nori untoasted). Keep your hands well away from the flame and use tongs to rotate the sheet slowly for 5–10 seconds until it turns darker and more fragrant. Transfer to a board. Do not touch the nori directly over the flame.

Assemble the rolls. Lay the toasted nori shiny side down on a bamboo mat or board. Spread a thin layer of cooled rice across three-quarters of the nori, leaving the top quarter bare. Arrange a line of carrot, courgette, spinach and egg down the centre of the rice, not overfilling.

Roll and serve. Using the mat or board to help, roll the nori tightly away from you, sealing the edge where the bare nori meets the rice. Slice the roll in half with a sharp, wet knife, then slice each half into thirds, wiping the knife between cuts. Arrange on a plate and serve with a dab of kewpie mayonnaise on the side if you like.

notes: If you don't have a gas hob, skip the nori toasting, the rolls will still taste great untoasted.
Make ahead: assemble and slice the rolls up to 2 hours before serving; keep wrapped in cling film in the fridge.

title: Mango and Black Rice Buddha Bowl
summary: Nutty black rice, crispy tofu, fresh mango and cucumber with peanut-lime dressing.

items.raw: 150 g black rice (glutinous or jasmine black rice)
200 g firm tofu, pressed and cut into 2 cm cubes
items.prep: pressed and cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Rinse the black rice under cold water. In a saucepan, bring the water to a boil, add the rice and a pinch of salt, stir once, then reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer for 25–30 minutes until the rice is tender and the water is absorbed. Set aside.

While the rice cooks, pan-fry the tofu: heat the oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the tofu cubes in a single layer and fry, turning occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until golden and crispy on all sides. Season with a pinch of salt and set aside.
Make the dressing: in a small bowl, whisk together the peanut butter, lime juice, tamari and ginger. Add a splash of water (about 2 tbsp) to loosen it to a drizzle consistency.

To serve: divide the warm (or cooled) rice between two bowls. Top each with crispy tofu, mango slices and cucumber. Drizzle generously with the peanut-lime dressing and scatter fresh mint over the top.

notes: Cook the rice the night before and store in the fridge; it keeps for 3 days and is great eaten cold.
Press the tofu for 15 minutes before cutting to get it crispy, wrap it in a clean towel with a weight on top.
Swap the mango for peaches or papaya if that's what's at the farmers' market.

title: Couscous aux Sept Légumes
summary: Fluffy couscous with seven seasonal vegetables, chickpeas and spiced broth.

items.raw: 2 medium waxy potatoes, cut into 3 cm chunks
2 medium carrots, cut into 3 cm chunks
1 small pumpkin (about 400 g), cut into 3 cm chunks
2 medium zucchini, cut into 3 cm chunks
1 small turnip, cut into 3 cm chunks
200 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the halved onion and cook until golden, about 4 minutes. Stir in the garlic, harissa, cumin and caraway seeds, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the chicken stock and add salt and pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer. Add the potatoes, carrots and pumpkin, and simmer for 15 minutes until starting to soften.
Add the zucchini, turnip, green beans, chickpeas and bay leaf. Simmer for another 12 minutes until all vegetables are tender but not falling apart.
While the vegetables cook, put the couscous in a bowl with the salt. Pour the 400 ml of boiling broth over it and stir once. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and let sit for 5 minutes.
Fluff the couscous with a fork, breaking up any lumps. Add the butter and stir through gently until each grain is separate and glossy.

Taste the broth and adjust seasoning. Remove the onion halves and bay leaf. Mound the couscous on a large platter or bowl and arrange the vegetables and chickpeas around it. Pour some of the spiced broth over the top and serve the rest on the side.

notes: The vegetables can be prepped the night before and stored in the fridge; keep the broth separate.
Use any seasonal vegetables you like: swap turnip for parsnip, or add cabbage instead of zucchini.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for 3 days; reheat gently in the oven with a splash of broth.

title: Som Tam
summary: Green papaya salad with lime, chilli and fish sauce, crushed fresh at the table.

image.credit: Photo: Sumit Surai / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.raw: 1 medium green papaya, peeled and julienned
3 Thai bird's eye chillies, roughly chopped
30 g long beans, cut into 2 cm lengths

steps.text: Pound the chillies and garlic in a mortar until bruised and fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the long beans and tomatoes, gently bruise them, about 30 seconds, don't crush them to mush.
Add the papaya and gently pound and toss everything together, crushing and mixing, about 2 minutes. The papaya should start to release juice.
Add the lime juice, fish sauce and palm sugar. Toss everything well, tasting as you go.
Transfer to a plate, top with crushed peanuts, and serve right away while it's still crisp.

notes: The salad is best eaten immediately while the papaya is still crisp. Don't make it ahead.
Adjust the chilli to your heat level, start with 1 or 2 birds eyes if you're not used to heat, then add more.
A proper pestle and mortar is key here; don't use a food processor, which will break down the vegetables too much.

title: Camp Oven Brisket
summary: Slow-roasted brisket with bush tomato and native pepper rub, cooked low and long in a camp oven.

items.raw: Sea salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Combine wattleseed, bush tomato, native pepper, salt and black pepper in a small bowl. Rub all over the brisket, working it into the meat, and let sit for 10 minutes.
Heat oil in a heavy camp oven or large, heavy-bottomed oven-safe pot over medium-high heat. Sear the brisket on both sides until well browned, about 4 minutes each side. Remove and set aside.
Add onion and garlic to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft, about 3 minutes. Pour in stock and red wine, scraping up the browned bits from the bottom.
Return the brisket to the pot, fat-side up. Add bay leaves and thyme. Season with salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer until small bubbles break the surface of the liquid steadily.
Cover tightly and transfer to a 140°C oven (or set camp oven on low coals). Cook for 5 to 6 hours, turning the brisket halfway through, until the meat is so tender it falls apart with a fork.
Remove from the oven and let rest for 15 minutes. Skim any excess fat from the liquid. Slice the brisket or pull it apart, and serve with the pan juices.

notes: This feeds a crowd and tastes even better the next day. Cool and refrigerate; reheat gently in a low oven.
No camp oven? Works just as well in a covered Dutch oven in the oven at home.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Ginataang Isda
summary: White fish simmered in coconut milk with turmeric, ginger and spring onion – a quick Visayan comfort dish.

items.raw: 600 g white fish fillets (barramundi, snapper or flathead), cut into bite-sized pieces
3 cm piece ginger, peeled and sliced
3 spring onions, cut into 5 cm lengths (white and green parts separate)

steps.text: Bring the water and coconut milk to a gentle simmer in a large pot or deep pan over medium heat, until small bubbles form around the edge and the liquid is steaming.
Add the ginger slices and turmeric, stirring well. Let it bubble gently for 3 minutes until fragrant.
Add the fish pieces and the white parts of the spring onion. Return to a simmer and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily.
Stir in the fish sauce and taste. Add salt if needed – go easy, as the fish sauce brings plenty of salt already.
Add the green parts of the spring onion and cook for 1 minute more until just wilted.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with steamed white rice to soak up the silky broth.

notes: Serve with steamed white or jasmine rice to soak up the broth.
You can swap the white fish for any firm white fish you have – barramundi is classic, but flathead and snapper work just as well.
Food safety:

title: Falafel
summary: Crispy chickpea fritters with fresh herbs, perfect in bread with tahini sauce

items.raw: 200 g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight and drained
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the drained chickpeas dry with a clean tea towel. This removes excess moisture so they'll bind better and fry crisper.

Add the chickpeas, onion, garlic, parsley, coriander, spring onions, green chilli, cumin, ground coriander and cayenne to a food processor. Pulse until the mixture is combined but still coarse, not smooth like a paste. It should hold together when squeezed but still have some texture.
Transfer to a bowl, stir through the flour, and season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours. Cold mixture holds together better when you fry.

Pour about 8 cm of neutral oil into a deep heavy-based pan and heat to 170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, drop a small piece of bread in, it should sizzle gently and turn golden in about 30 seconds.
Wet your hands lightly to stop the mixture sticking. Shape the mixture into 20 balls about the size of a walnut, then gently flatten each one slightly. Work quickly so they stay cold.

Carefully lower the falafel into the hot oil in small batches, don't crowd the pan or the temperature will drop and they'll absorb oil instead of crisping. Fry for 3–4 minutes until deep golden all over, turning halfway. They should be golden outside and cooked through inside.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm in flatbread with tahini sauce, fresh tomatoes and coriander. Eat them straightaway while they're still crisp.

notes: Make ahead: Shape and refrigerate the falafel for up to 24 hours before frying. You can also freeze shaped falafel for up to 3 months and fry from frozen, adding a minute or two to cooking time.
Oil temperature matters: Too cold and they absorb oil; too hot and they brown outside before cooking through. Stick to 170°C.
Why dried chickpeas: Tinned chickpeas are too soft and will fall apart. Dried chickpeas, once soaked, have the right texture to bind and crisp up.

title: Pad Cha Gung
summary: Stir-fried prawns with dry curry paste, lemongrass and galangal.

items.raw: 3 tbsp dry curry paste (or more to taste)
3 stalks lemongrass, white part only, sliced thin

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wok or large frying pan over high heat until it shimmers, about 1 minute.
Add the curry paste and stir-fry for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the prawns, lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaves. Stir-fry for 2 minutes, tossing often, until the prawns start to change colour.
Add the chilli, fish sauce and palm sugar. Keep tossing until the prawns are cooked through and curled, about 2 more minutes.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with more fish sauce or palm sugar if needed.
Serve in bowls with fresh Thai basil scattered over and a lime wedge on the side.

notes: If you can't find fresh lemongrass or galangal, use 1 tbsp lemongrass paste and ½ tsp ground galangal instead.
This works just as well with any firm white fish cut into chunks, cook for 2–3 minutes until opaque.
Food safety:

title: Tlayudas de Chapulines
summary: Crispy Oaxacan tortilla topped with beans, quesillo cheese, and garlicky fried grasshoppers.

items.raw: 4 large flour tortillas (or corn tortillas if you can find them)
items.note: or corn tortillas if you can find them

items.raw: 200 g quesillo (oaxaca cheese), torn into strings (or fresh mozzarella)
2 tbsp neutral oil, plus more for cooking the tlayudas
items.prep: plus more for cooking the tlayudas

steps.text: Warm a comal or large dry frying pan over medium-high heat. Working with one tortilla at a time, lay it flat on the comal and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until it becomes golden, crispy and starts to char slightly. Press gently so it cooks evenly. Set aside on a plate.

In a small frying pan, heat 2 tbsp oil over medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and cook, stirring, for about 1 minute until fragrant. Add the dried grasshoppers and cook, tossing often, for 3 to 4 minutes until they are heated through and crunchy. Squeeze juice from 1 lime wedge over them and season with salt. Remove from heat.
Spread a thin layer of mashed black beans on each crispy tortilla, leaving a small border.
Top each tlayuda with a generous handful of torn quesillo cheese, distributing it evenly.
Pile the garlicky fried grasshoppers on top of the cheese.
Serve immediately while the tortilla is still warm and crispy, with lime wedges on the side for squeezing over.

notes: If you can't find dried chapulines, fresh ones can be lightly toasted in a hot dry pan first, then fried with garlic.
Make the tortillas ahead and keep them wrapped in cloth; they stay crispy for an hour or two.
This is best eaten right away while the tortilla is still warm and crispy.

title: Suqaar
summary: Somali minced meat stew with tomatoes and spices, served over rice

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
2 cups cooked white rice, to serve

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until cooked through, about 8 minutes. Tip off any excess fat if needed.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes, chilli, cumin and cardamom. Stir well to combine.
Reduce the heat to medium and simmer, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the sauce is thick and the flavours have melded. Season to taste with salt and pepper.
Divide the rice between bowls and spoon the suqaar over the top.

notes: Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Miyeok Guk
summary: Korean seaweed soup with beef stock, sesame oil and soy, eaten after blood donation or childbirth.

items.raw: 200 g beef brisket (or chuck), thinly sliced

steps.text: Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes until soft, then drain well and set aside.
Heat 1 tbsp sesame oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the beef slices and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until just cooked through, breaking the meat into small pieces.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant.
Pour in the beef stock and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat to medium and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the drained wakame and soy sauce, then simmer for a further 8 minutes.
Taste and season with salt and white pepper. Finish with the remaining 1 tbsp sesame oil stirred through just before serving.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with sesame seeds if you like.

notes: The stock is the soul of this soup. If you don't have time to make your own, use a good-quality shop-bought beef stock, but warm it through gently, never let it boil hard.
Some cooks add a small handful of minced beef cooked separately; cooking it in the pot is simpler, and either way works.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Edamame Shio
summary: Salt-boiled soybeans, the obvious beer companion.

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil, until large bubbles break the surface constantly, and add the salt.
Add the edamame and return to a boil, then cook until the pods are bright green and the beans are tender.
Cook for 5 minutes if fresh, 4 minutes if frozen, until bright green and tender.
Drain in a colander and cool slightly.
Transfer to a bowl and serve. Squeeze the beans out of the pods into your mouth as you eat.

title: Timman Z'affaran
summary: Saffron-scented rice with fried onions and black lentils, everyday comfort food.

steps.text: Rinse the lentils and place in a saucepan with the 3 cups water. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer gently until just tender, about 20 minutes. Season with salt.
While the lentils cook, place the saffron threads in a small bowl and pour the ½ cup boiling water over them. Let steep for at least 10 minutes.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until deep golden and crispy, about 10 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside on paper towel, leaving about 2 tablespoons of oil in the pan.

Rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear. Add to the pan with the remaining oil and stir gently for 2 minutes to coat each grain. Pour in the saffron and its steeping water, and ½ cup of fresh water. Stir to combine.

Bring to a simmer, then stir in the cooked lentils with any remaining cooking liquid. Cover with a tight-fitting lid, reduce heat to low, and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until all liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender.
Remove from heat and let rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, then transfer to a serving dish. Scatter the crispy fried onions over the top and serve warm.

notes: Make-ahead: cook the lentils and fry the onions an hour or two ahead. Finish the rice just before serving.
Swap black lentils for brown lentils if black are hard to find; they'll cook in about the same time.

title: Nasi Kucing
summary: Tiny fragrant rice portions with different sambals and sides, Sundanese comfort food that stretches rice and leftovers.

items.raw: 200 g tempeh, sliced and fried until golden

steps.text: Make sambal matah: toss the sliced shallots and chillies with lime juice and salt, then pour over the hot oil and set aside to infuse.
Make sambal terasi: pound the chillies, shrimp paste, garlic and salt into a rough paste in a mortar, then stir through lime juice. (Or blend if you prefer it smoother.)
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium-high heat. Add the minced garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the cooled rice, breaking up any lumps as it fries, about 5 minutes.
Stir through the spring onions, season with salt and white pepper to taste, and remove from heat.
Form the fried rice into small mounds on a large serving platter, each person gets 2 or 3 little portions to build on.

Arrange the tempeh, cucumber and tomato around the rice, and put both sambals in small bowls alongside. Everyone builds their own plate, taking a mound of rice and topping it with sambal, tempeh and veg as they like.

notes: Make it ahead: fry the rice earlier in the day and reheat gently, or serve at room temperature. Both sambals keep 2 days in the fridge.
Stretch it: add more veg sides like pickled papaya, blanched long beans or leftover roasted vegetables. Boiled egg, leftover chicken, or fried tofu work just as well as tempeh.
Food safety: Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Milanesa de Ternera
summary: Thin-pounded veal cutlet, breaded and fried golden, served with lemon and chimichurri.

image.credit: Photo: José Maria Ali Anaya Ccallocunto / Pexels

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
15 g fresh oregano, finely chopped (or 1 tsp dried oregano)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the chimichurri first: whisk together the olive oil and red wine vinegar, then stir in the parsley, oregano, garlic, chilli flakes, salt and pepper. Set aside.
Place each veal escalope between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound with a meat mallet or rolling pin until very thin, about 3 mm. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with flour, one with beaten eggs, and one with breadcrumbs. Coat each escalope in flour, shaking off excess, then dip in egg, then press firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides.
Heat about 1 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Test with a small piece of bread, it should sizzle and brown quickly.
Carefully lay the breaded veal into the hot oil and fry for 2–3 minutes until golden brown. Turn and fry the other side for another 2–3 minutes until crispy and golden. Do not overcrowd the pan.
Transfer to a plate lined with paper towel to drain. Serve hot with lemon wedges and chimichurri on the side, with optional fresh parsley garnish.

notes: Use veal or beef. Veal is more tender, but a thin beef cutlet works just as well.
Don't skip the meat mallet. The escalopes must be thin so they cook through before the breadcrumb coating burns.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Melanzane alla Parmigiana
summary: Baked eggplant layered with tomato sauce and melted cheese, a southern Italian vegetable classic.

items.raw: 800 g eggplant, cut into 5 mm slices

steps.text: Arrange eggplant slices on a clean tea towel or paper towels. Sprinkle both sides generously with salt and let sit for 15 minutes to draw out moisture. Pat dry thoroughly.

While the eggplant rests, heat the tomato sauce: warm 2 tbsp of the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add minced garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with a wooden spoon. Tear in most of the basil leaves (reserve a few for garnish). Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Season with salt and pepper. Set aside.

Heat the remaining oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Once hot, fry eggplant slices in batches for 3–4 minutes per side until golden brown and soft. Transfer to paper towels to drain. Don't crowd the pan; let them cook in a single layer.
Preheat the oven to 180°C.

Spread a thin layer of tomato sauce over the base of a 23 × 33 cm baking dish. Arrange a layer of fried eggplant slices over the sauce, overlapping slightly. Top with a layer of fresh mozzarella, then a sprinkle of grated parmesan. Repeat the layers, sauce, eggplant, mozzarella, parmesan, until everything is used, ending with a good handful of parmesan on top.
Bake uncovered for 30–35 minutes until the top is golden and bubbling at the edges. Let rest for 5 minutes before serving. Tear over the reserved fresh basil.

notes: Make it a day ahead and reheat gently at 160°C for 20 minutes, the flavours marry beautifully overnight.
Short on time? Buy good passata instead of tinned tomatoes and skip the simmering step.
If you can't find fresh mozzarella, use half the quantity of low-moisture mozzarella and mix it with the parmesan.
For a vegetarian version, use a vegetarian hard cheese (made without animal rennet).

title: Pork and Chive Dumplings
summary: Stuffed wheat dough pockets filled with pork and chives, boiled then pan-fried until golden.

items.raw: Neutral oil, for the work surface

steps.text: Make the dough: mix plain flour with salt in a bowl. Pour in boiling water, stirring with chopsticks until it comes together. Once cool enough to handle, knead on an oiled surface for 10 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Make the filling: combine pork mince, garlic chives, soy sauce, sesame oil, ginger and water in a bowl. Mix gently with chopsticks, don't overwork it or the filling gets tough. Chill until ready to use.
Divide the dough into 16 pieces. Roll each into a ball, then flatten with your palm. Using a rolling pin or your fingers, stretch each into a 10 cm circle, keeping the edges thinner than the centre.
Place 1 tbsp filling in the centre of each circle. Fold in half to make a half-moon, pinching the edges to seal. Then bring the two pointed ends together and press to seal, forming a purse shape.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, gently drop dumplings in and stir so they don't stick. Once they float, simmer for 2–3 minutes more. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain well.

Heat 2 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Arrange dumplings flat-side down and fry without moving for 3–4 minutes until golden and crisp. Pour in 120 ml water, cover, and steam for 2 minutes. Uncover, let the water evaporate, and fry for another minute until the base is crispy again.
Serve hot with soy sauce or chilli oil for dipping.

notes: Make the dough and filling the morning before and chill separately. Shape the dumplings while they're cold.
Boiled dumplings can be frozen uncooked on a tray, then transferred to a freezer bag, boil from frozen, adding a couple of minutes to the cooking time.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

title: Quesadillas de Flor de Calabaza
summary: Soft corn tortillas filled with sautéed squash blossoms, onion and cheese.

items.raw: 150 g fresh mozzarella (or quesillo), torn into small pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onion and cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until just softened.

Add the chopped squash blossoms and a pinch of salt. Cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring gently, until the flowers have wilted and released their moisture. The mixture should be tender but not mushy. Taste and adjust salt.
Warm the corn tortillas in a dry frying pan or directly over a gas flame for 15 seconds each, or wrap them in a damp tea towel to keep them soft.
Divide the squash blossom filling between the tortillas, placing it on one half of each. Top the filling with pieces of cheese, then fold the tortilla in half.

In a clean frying pan, heat a little oil over medium-high heat. Fry the quesadillas for 1–2 minutes per side until they are warmed through and the cheese begins to soften. Don't cook them so long the tortilla becomes crisp, they should stay tender.
Serve immediately with salsa verde and a squeeze of fresh lime.

notes: Squash blossoms are seasonal and peak in summer. If you can't find them, use thin zucchini slices or tender greens like spinach or kale.
Make ahead: prepare the filling up to 4 hours in advance and reheat gently before assembling the quesadillas.

title: Stinky Tofu
summary: Crispy fried stinky tofu with pickled cabbage and chilli sauce, pungent, QQ inside.

items.raw: 300 g stinky tofu (chou doufu), cut into 4 cm cubes
100 g pickled mustard greens, chopped (or pickled radish)

steps.text: Toss the stinky tofu cubes gently with cornflour and salt until coated.
Heat about 2 cm of neutral oil in a shallow pan or wok to 180°C. Test with a wooden chopstick, it should bubble gently around it.
Working in two batches, carefully slide the tofu into the hot oil. Fry for 4–5 minutes, turning once, until the outside is golden and crispy and the edges are bubbling. Drain on paper towels.
While the tofu fries, stir together the chilli sauce, soy sauce, sugar and 1 tbsp water in a small bowl.
Serve the hot tofu with pickled mustard greens on the side, the chilli sauce for dipping, and spring onion scattered over. Eat while it's still crackling.

notes: Stinky tofu (chou doufu) is the star here, its pungent, funky smell is what makes it special. Find it in the refrigerated section of Asian grocers, often near the fresh tofu.
The tofu needs to be truly crispy outside to contrast with the QQ creamy interior. Don't skip the cornflour coating or lower the oil temperature.
Pickled mustard greens (xue cai) cut through the richness beautifully, swap for pickled daikon if you prefer something milder.

title: Ayam Goreng Berempah
summary: Spiced fried chicken with deep, layered sambal paste.

items.raw: 3 red chillies, roughly chopped (adjust for your heat)
8 chicken thighs, bone-in and skin-on (about 1 kg)

steps.text: Make the sambal paste: Combine the shallots, garlic, chillies, candlenuts, tamarind paste and salt in a food processor. Pulse until you have a coarse, chunky paste, not smooth. Heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a pan over medium heat, add the paste and fry, stirring often, for about 5 minutes until it darkens and smells fragrant. Let it cool slightly.

Pat the chicken thighs dry with paper towel. Rub them all over with the cooled sambal paste, turmeric and coriander, working it into the skin and under it where you can. Ideally sit the chicken in a bowl for 30 minutes to an hour, but even 10 minutes helps.
Heat about 300 ml neutral oil in a large, heavy-based pan or wok over medium-high heat. Test the heat with a small piece of shallot, it should sizzle immediately.

Working in batches so you don't overcrowd the pan, carefully place the chicken skin-side down into the hot oil. Fry for 6–7 minutes until the skin is deep golden and crisps up, shaking the pan occasionally so it colours evenly.

Flip each piece and fry the other side for another 6–7 minutes until golden. The chicken should be cooked through, cut into the thickest thigh near the bone and check there's no pink; if unsure, the inside should reach 75°C.
Transfer the cooked chicken to a plate lined with paper towel to drain. Taste one piece and season with a pinch more salt if needed. Serve hot.

notes: Make the sambal paste in advance (up to 2 days ahead) and store in an airtight container in the fridge. Bring it to room temperature before rubbing it on the chicken.
For less heat, use 1 or 2 chillies instead of 3. For more punch, add a bird's eye chilli or two.
Leftovers keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days and are just as good cold the next day.
Food safety:

title: Snoek with Lemon and Garlic
summary: Whole snoek grilled on coals in foil, buttery and flaking.

items.raw: 1 whole snoek, about 600 g, gutted and scaled
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Get your braai hot, you want the coals glowing and ready.
Tear off a large piece of foil and lay the snoek in the middle. Season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Stuff the cavity with half the garlic slices and half the lemon slices. Top with a knob of butter.

Scatter the remaining garlic and lemon over the top, then dot with the last of the butter. Wrap the foil loosely around the fish, sealing it well so the steam stays inside, and bake until the fish is opaque and flakes easily with a fork.
Place the parcel on the hot coals and cook for about 10 to 12 minutes, until the flesh is opaque and flaking away from the bones.
Carefully unwrap the foil, watch the steam, and check that the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Slide the fish onto a plate. Spoon the buttery juices from the foil over the top.

title: Gazpacho Andaluz
summary: Silky chilled tomato soup with sherry vinegar and olive oil, a Seville classic.

image.credit: Photo: Juan Emilio Prades Bel / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

steps.text: Place the tomatoes, capsicum, cucumber and garlic in a large bowl. Pour over the olive oil and sherry vinegar, and add a pinch of salt. Let sit for 10 minutes to release the juices.

In batches, blend the vegetables and oil until completely smooth, this is a sieve-smooth gazpacho, not a chunky one. Pass the blended mixture through a fine sieve into a clean bowl, pressing gently to extract all the liquid. Discard the pulp.
Stir in the ice water to cool and lighten the soup. Taste and adjust the salt and vinegar to your liking.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until well chilled. Serve ice cold in small glasses or shallow bowls.

notes: Make this a day ahead if you like, it keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Lucía sometimes stirs in a splash of water to loosen it on the day if it's thickened overnight.
Serve with small glasses of ice water on the side, or pour into shallow bowls if you're feeling elegant.

title: Base Genep
summary: The foundational Balinese spice paste of chillies, garlic, ginger, turmeric and shallots.

items.raw: 3 cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and chopped
2 cm piece fresh turmeric, peeled and chopped (or 1 tsp ground turmeric)
1 cm piece galangal, peeled and chopped

steps.text: Combine the chillies, garlic, ginger, turmeric, shallots and galangal in a mortar.

Pound with the pestle until you have a smooth, fragrant paste, about 10 to 15 minutes. Work slowly and steadily, crushing and grinding until all the spices are fully broken down and release their oils.
Stir through the lime juice and salt. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
Use immediately in your Balinese dishes, or store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days.

notes: Base genep keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days, or freeze in ice-cube trays for up to 3 months.
If you don't have fresh turmeric, use 1 tsp ground turmeric instead.
A mortar and pestle gives the best flavour and texture, but you can use a food processor if needed, pulse until smooth, then stir through the lime and salt by hand.

title: Nozawana Zuke
summary: Quick-pickled turnip greens with chilli and vinegar, bright and tangy.

items.raw: 200 g nozawana (turnip greens), washed and drained
1 red chilli, finely sliced (seeds optional for less heat)

steps.text: Cut the nozawana into 5 cm lengths, discarding any tough stems. Pat dry.
Place the nozawana in a bowl and toss with the salt. Let sit for 2 minutes until the greens begin to soften and release liquid.
In a small bowl, whisk together the rice vinegar, caster sugar and soy sauce until the sugar dissolves.
Pack the nozawana loosely into a clean jar, scattering the chilli through the layers as you go.
Pour the vinegar mixture over the greens, pressing down gently so they are submerged. Cover and refrigerate.
The pickle is ready to eat after 30 minutes, and will keep for up to 2 weeks in the fridge.

notes: This keeps in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. The flavour deepens and mellows as it sits.
Serve alongside rice, grilled fish, or simply as a palate cleanser with any meal.

title: Khao Pad Gai
summary: Chicken fried rice with shallots and fermented shrimp paste, ready in 20 minutes.

items.raw: 200 g cooked jasmine rice, cooled (day-old rice works best)
2 spring onions, cut into 3 cm lengths

steps.text: Heat the wok over high heat until it's smoking hot. Add 1 tbsp oil, then the chicken. Cook, stirring constantly, until it's cooked through and golden at the edges, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining oil to the wok. Add the shallots and cook, stirring, until soft and just starting to colour, about 2 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the shrimp paste and stir it through the oil until it breaks down completely, about 1 minute.
Add the rice, breaking up any clumps, and toss constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until heated through. The rice should separate and coat lightly with oil.
Return the chicken to the wok. Add the fish sauce and white pepper, and toss everything together for 1 minute.
Add the spring onions, toss once, then transfer to a plate. Top with fresh coriander if you like, and serve with a lime wedge.

notes: Use day-old or cooled cooked rice, freshly cooked rice will clump and steam instead of fry.
Shrimp paste is pungent raw but mellows when cooked with oil and the other ingredients. Start with 1 tbsp and adjust to taste.
Double this easily if you're cooking for two, but it's designed for one burner and one wok.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Scallops with Apple and Corn
summary: Fresh scallops with sweet corn, apple and brown butter.

items.raw: 8 large scallops (about 400 g), without roe (use the day of purchase)
items.note: about 400 g; use the day of purchase

items.raw: 1 apple, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

items.raw: 200 g corn kernels, fresh or frozen

steps.text: Pat the scallops dry with paper towel and season lightly with salt and pepper.

Heat the neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Working in batches if needed, place the scallops flat in the pan. Cook for 1 minute without moving until the base is golden, then flip and cook for a further 1 minute. Transfer to a warm plate.
Reduce the heat to medium. In the same pan, melt 1 tbsp of the butter, then add the garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds.
Add the apple matchsticks and corn kernels, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 minutes until the apple is just tender.
Pour in the stock and simmer for 2 minutes, then stir in the remaining butter until melted. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Return the scallops to the pan, gently turn them to coat, and cook for 1 minute to warm through. Divide between two plates, scatter with parsley, and serve immediately.

notes: Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Wattleseed Damper
summary: Camp-oven baked bread with wattleseed, earthy and nutty, from local growers.

steps.text: Preheat your camp oven with coals underneath and on top, or preheat a conventional oven to 200°C.
In a large bowl, mix together the flour, baking powder, wattleseed and salt.
Add the cubed butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs.
Add the warm water gradually, stirring with a knife until the dough just comes together. Don't overwork it, damper should be rough and rustic.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and gently shape it into a round loaf about 20 cm across. Make a shallow cross on the top with a knife.
Place the damper on a piece of baking paper or directly on a lightly oiled cast-iron trivet in your camp oven (or on a baking tray for conventional oven).
Bake for 40–45 minutes until the top is golden and it sounds hollow when tapped on the base. In a camp oven, rotate the coals if needed to ensure even cooking.
Cool on a wire rack for a few minutes, then tear into pieces and serve warm with butter.

notes: Best eaten fresh and warm. Keeps for a day wrapped in a tea towel; refresh in a warm oven.
If you don't have access to wattleseed from local growers, online suppliers often stock it, but ground cumin mixed with a little cocoa makes a reasonable substitute.

title: Pāua Fritters
summary: Golden-fried abalone fritters, crispy outside and tender within.

steps.text: Pound each pāua gently but firmly with a meat mallet on both sides until soft and just starting to flatten. Don't overdo it or you'll tear them. Pat dry with paper towels.
Whisk together the flour, baking powder, salt and pepper in a large bowl. In another bowl, whisk the egg with the milk until combined.
Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and stir gently until just combined, the batter should be a little lumpy, not smooth.
Heat about 2 cm of neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Test with a drop of batter; it should sizzle and float.
Dip each pāua into the batter, coating both sides, then carefully place into the hot oil. Fry in batches of 2 or 3 so you don't crowd the pan, about 2 minutes each side until golden and crispy.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot with a squeeze of fresh lemon.

notes: If you can't find fresh pāua, tinned pāua from a specialist kai moana supplier works well, just drain and pound before battering.
Keep finished fritters warm in a low oven (120°C) while you fry the rest.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Ghormeh Sabzi
summary: Persian herb stew with kidney beans, black-eyed peas and beef kidney in aromatic broth.

items.raw: 300 g beef kidney, trimmed and cut into 1 cm cubes
items.prep: trimmed and cut into 1 cm cubes

items.raw: 400 g tin kidney beans, drained and rinsed
250 g tin black-eyed peas, drained and rinsed
3 dried limes (loomi), pierced with a knife
30 g fresh fenugreek leaves (kasuri methi), or extra parsley

steps.text: Pat the kidney dry and season with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a heavy-based pot over medium-high heat and brown the kidney in batches, 2–3 minutes a side. Set aside.
In the same pot, soften the onion over medium heat until golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Return the kidney to the pot. Add the kidney beans and black-eyed peas, stirring to combine. Pour in the stock and add the dried limes.
Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 45 minutes, until the kidney is tender.
Stir in most of the parsley, fenugreek and coriander, reserving a small handful for garnish. Taste and adjust salt and pepper. Simmer, uncovered, for another 10 minutes.
Serve hot in wide bowls, scattered with the reserved fresh herbs. Eat with steamed white rice, pushing some to the edges of the pot for tahdig if you have the nerve.

notes: Make the stew up to 2 days ahead; the flavours deepen overnight. Reheat gently before serving.
Don't skip browning the kidney, it anchors the stew. If you can't find beef kidney, use lamb kidney (200 g) or omit it and add 100 g more beans instead.
Dried limes are essential to the flavour; they're sold in Middle Eastern grocers and most good supermarkets.

Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done. If using dried kidney beans, soak them, then boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering, to destroy a natural toxin.

title: Choy Sum with Garlic and Oil
summary: Tender choy sum with bruised garlic and good oil, finished with high heat for wok hei.

items.raw: 600 g choy sum, cut into 8 cm lengths
60 ml good olive oil (or peanut oil)

steps.text: Get everything ready, the greens washed and cut, garlic bruised and sitting on the bench. High heat and speed matter here.
Heat your wok on high until it just begins to smoke lightly, about 2 minutes. Add the oil and swirl to coat the wok surface.
Add the bruised garlic and stir constantly for 20 seconds until fragrant. You want the oil infused but the garlic not burnt.

Immediately add all the choy sum. Toss and stir briskly, keeping the heat high, for 2 to 3 minutes until the stems are tender and the leaves have some char at the edges. The greens should still be bright.
Season with salt to taste. Serve immediately while the oil is still hot and the choy sum is at its best.

notes: Use oil you actually like the taste of, the simplicity means quality matters. Peanut oil or a fruity olive oil both work.
Don't prep the choy sum too early; it wilts quickly. Cut and dress it just before cooking.
If your stove doesn't run hot enough to get good wok hei, finish the pan under a very hot grill for 30 seconds instead.

title: Shorshe Ilish
summary: Hilsa fish in pungent mustard paste, the most Bengali of celebrations

items.raw: 800 g hilsa fillets (ilish), skin on, or 600 g fresh pomfret or mackerel fillets
items.prep: skin on, or 600 g fresh pomfret or mackerel fillets

items.raw: 4 tbsp mustard seeds, black and yellow mixed

steps.text: Soak the mustard seeds in a little water for 10 minutes, then grind to a coarse paste with the green chillies, turmeric and salt. The paste should be lumpy and pungent, not smooth.
Heat the mustard oil in a wide, shallow pan over medium-high heat until it just smokes, about 2 minutes. This is essential, the burnt edge of the oil gives shorshe ilish its character.
Gently lay the fish fillets skin-side up in the hot oil. Cook for 2–3 minutes without moving them, until the flesh begins to turn opaque at the edges.
Spread the mustard paste over the fish, then add 150 ml water around (not over) it. The sauce should be loose and gravy-like.

Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, uncovered and barely disturbing the fish, for 15–18 minutes, until the flesh is cooked through and flakes easily when tested at its thickest point. The sauce should reduce and thicken slightly.
Taste and adjust salt. Stir in the jaggery if using, a hint of sweetness balances the mustard's heat. Serve hot, with rice to soak up the sauce.

notes: Shorshe ilish is traditionally made during spring when hilsa is in season (March–May). If hilsa is unavailable, use fresh pomfret or mackerel, both have the oily texture this dish demands.
Prepare the mustard paste fresh; it loses its pungency if made too far ahead. The dish can be made a few hours in advance and gently reheated.

title: Cabbage Thoran
summary: Shredded cabbage stir-fried with grated coconut, mustard seeds and curry leaves.

items.raw: ½ head cabbage (about 500 g), finely shredded
200 g fresh grated coconut (or 150 g desiccated coconut, rehydrated in 80 ml warm water for 10 minutes)
items.note: or 150 g desiccated coconut, rehydrated in 80 ml warm water for 10 minutes

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or kadai over medium-high heat.
Once shimmering, add the mustard seeds. As soon as they pop and crackle, add the halved red chilli and curry leaves. Fry for 30 seconds, stirring, until fragrant.
Add the shredded cabbage and salt. Stir well to coat in the oil and spices.
Cook, stirring often, for 5–6 minutes. The cabbage should soften and turn glossy but stay bright; if water beads on the pan, keep stirring until it evaporates.
Add the grated coconut and toss to combine. Cook for 1–2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the coconut is warm and the cabbage is tender but still has a slight bite.
Taste and adjust salt if needed. Serve hot as a side to rice and curry.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the cabbage and coconut the morning before, store them separately in the fridge, and cook just before serving.
Swap: if fresh coconut is hard to find, use desiccated coconut rehydrated in warm water as given above.
Use waxy cabbage if possible; savoy can release more water and make the dish wetter.

title: Hijiki No Nimono
summary: Hijiki seaweed simmered with carrots, burdock and abura-age, a traditional bento side.

items.raw: 80 g burdock (gobo), cut into thin matchsticks
2 abura-age (fried tofu pockets), cut into thin strips

steps.text: Soak the dried hijiki in 200 ml room-temperature water for 5 minutes until soft and pliable. Drain well and squeeze gently to remove excess water.
Heat the oil in a wide shallow pan over medium heat. Add the carrot and burdock and cook, stirring, until they soften slightly, about 3 minutes.
Add the drained hijiki and the abura-age strips to the pan. Stir to combine.

Pour in the chicken stock, soy sauce, mirin and sugar. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cook, uncovered, stirring occasionally, until almost all the liquid has been absorbed and the vegetables are very tender, about 15 minutes.
Remove from the heat and let cool. Serve at room temperature, or pack into bento boxes.

notes: This keeps well in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 5 days, making it perfect for bento prep.
If you can't find burdock, use parsnip cut into thin matchsticks; it cooks a little faster but has a similar sweetness.
Hijiki expands as it soaks, so don't skip that step, the texture will be much better.

title: Chopped Salad with Feta and Oregano
summary: Tomato, cucumber, red onion and feta tossed with oregano and lemon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Chop the tomatoes, cucumber and red onion into roughly the same size pieces. Put them in a big bowl.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice and oregano. Toss everything together and season with salt and pepper.
Let it sit for 2 minutes, until the salt has drawn out a little juice and the vegetables are glossy, so the flavours come together.
Scatter the feta on top and toss through gently. Serve straight away.

title: Hobak Bokkeum
summary: Stir-fried zucchini with perilla leaf and sesame, bright, delicate banchan.

items.raw: 600 g zucchini, halved lengthwise and sliced into half-moons about 3 mm thick
items.prep: halved lengthwise and sliced into half-moons about 3 mm thick

items.raw: 8–10 perilla leaves (kkaenip), torn or cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: torn or cut into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Heat the sesame oil in a large wok or wide frying pan over medium-high heat.

Add the zucchini and salt. Stir-fry, tossing gently and frequently, until the zucchini is tender but still holds its shape and the edges are lightly caramelised, about 6–8 minutes. The zucchini will release a little moisture; let it cook off.
Remove from the heat and allow to cool for a minute. Add the perilla leaves and toss gently to combine.
Transfer to a serving bowl, scatter with the sesame seeds and black pepper, and serve at room temperature or slightly warm.

notes: Hobak bokkeum is best served at room temperature as part of a banchan spread, but it's also good warm.
Make it ahead and reheat gently, or prepare up to the stir-frying step and add the perilla leaves just before serving.

title: Causa Limeña
summary: Layered potato terrine with ají amarillo, chicken and avocado, Lima's most elegant potato dish.

items.raw: 1 kg waxy potatoes, peeled and chopped

steps.text: Boil the potatoes in salted water until just tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well.
Mash the hot potatoes with the ají amarillo paste, oil and lime juice. Season with salt and pepper. Let cool to room temperature.
In a bowl, combine the shredded chicken with mayonnaise, spring onions, chilli and lime juice. Season with salt and pepper.
Line a 1 litre loaf tin with plastic wrap. Spread half the potato mixture evenly on the bottom, smoothing it level.
Spread the chicken salad evenly over the potato layer. Top with the remaining potato mixture, smoothing it level.
Refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until completely set and chilled.
Invert the terrine onto a serving plate and gently peel away the plastic wrap.
Arrange the avocado and egg slices on top, scatter with olives, and garnish with fresh coriander. Slice at the table and serve.

notes: Make up to 24 hours ahead: unmould, wrap gently in plastic and refrigerate. Add avocado and toppings just before serving.
For the cooked chicken, use a store-bought rotisserie chicken or leftover roast chicken.
Ají amarillo paste is available from Latin American grocers or online; it's worth seeking out for its distinct fruity heat, but yellow chilli paste works in a pinch.

title: Smashed Avocado on Sourdough with Za'atar
summary: Thick-cut sourdough topped with smashed avocado, crispy za'atar and lemon juice.

steps.text: Toast the sourdough until golden and crispy, about 3 minutes.
While the bread toasts, scoop the avocado into a small bowl and mash roughly with a fork, leaving it chunky. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper.
Divide the smashed avocado between the two warm toasts and spread gently.
Sprinkle 1 tsp za'atar over each slice.
Squeeze lemon juice over the top and serve straight away.

notes: Use a ripe but not over-soft avocado for the best texture.
Make it a full breakfast by adding a squeeze of hot sauce or fresh chilli if you want more heat.

title: Pico de Gallo
summary: Fresh tomato, white onion, coriander and lime salsa, the real deal, made in five minutes.

items.raw: 1 small handful fresh coriander, finely chopped

steps.text: Dice the tomatoes into small, even pieces, about the size of a pea. If they release a lot of juice, drain them slightly.
Dice the white onion into small pieces the same size as the tomato.
Chop the fresh coriander roughly, then go over it once more with the knife so it's fine.
Combine the tomato, onion and coriander in a bowl.
Squeeze the lime juice over, add a pinch of salt, and stir gently until the tomato is glossy and lightly coated in juice. Taste and adjust salt and lime.
Serve right away, or cover and keep in the fridge for up to an hour.

notes: Make it no more than an hour ahead; after that it gets watery.
If your tomatoes are mealy, add a tiny pinch of sugar to wake them up.

title: Bún Riêu
summary: Crab and tomato noodle soup with crab paste, tangy and rich.

items.raw: 200 g fresh crab meat (or 150 g tinned crab)
3 tbsp crab paste (cua cốt, or more crab meat)
items.note: cua cốt, or more crab meat

items.raw: 2 tbsp fish sauce, plus extra to taste
300 g rice vermicelli, soaked in room-temperature water until pliable (about 10 minutes)
items.prep: soaked in room-temperature water until pliable

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add garlic and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add tomato paste and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook, stirring occasionally, until they begin to break down, about 5 minutes.

Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Add the crab meat (if using fresh or tinned), caster sugar, and 2 tbsp fish sauce. Simmer gently for 20 minutes to let the flavours meld and the tomato dissolve into the broth.
In the last 5 minutes of simmering, stir in the crab paste gradually, letting it warm through without boiling. Taste and adjust with extra fish sauce and salt as needed.
Bring a separate pot of water to a boil. Add the soaked rice vermicelli and cook for 2–3 minutes, then drain well.
Divide the noodles between two bowls. Ladle the hot broth and crab over the top. Scatter spring onion, fresh coriander, and fried shallots over each bowl. Serve at once.

notes: Make the broth ahead and reheat gently; it keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Cook the noodles fresh just before serving.
No fresh crab? Use a good tinned crab in brine (drain well), or substitute more crab paste with a little extra stock to thin it.
The fried shallots are worth finding at any Vietnamese or Asian grocer, they're the difference between good and the stall version.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Ayam Goreng Yogyakarta
summary: Golden fried chicken with sweet soy and garlic, a Yogyakarta workshop lunch favourite.

items.raw: 1 kg chicken pieces (thigh and drumstick), skin on

steps.text: Mix the crushed garlic, sweet soy sauce, oil and salt in a bowl to make the marinade. Add the chicken pieces and turn to coat well. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight if you have the time.
Remove the chicken from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to bring it closer to room temperature.
Heat 5 cm of neutral oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pan or wok to 160–170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, the oil is ready when a cube of bread browns in about 45 seconds.

Working in batches to avoid crowding the pan, carefully slide the chicken pieces into the hot oil, skin side down. Fry for 12–15 minutes, turning halfway through, until the skin is deep golden brown and the thickest part of the thigh reaches 75°C inside.
Transfer the cooked chicken to a paper-lined plate to drain. Serve hot with the pan juices spooned over.

notes: Marinate the chicken overnight for best flavour, it's worth the patience.
Use bone-in, skin-on chicken; it stays juicier and develops that crackling skin Yogyakarta style.
Serve at room temperature with steamed rice and sambal if you like heat.
Food safety:

title: Fatteh Hummus
summary: Crispy pita chips over creamy chickpea purée with yoghurt alternative, olive oil and pine nuts.

items.raw: 400 g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed
2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling
200 g unsweetened soy yoghurt (or other plant-based yoghurt)

steps.text: Preheat the oven to 180°C. Cut the pita breads into triangles, lightly brush or toss with a little olive oil, and scatter on a baking tray. Bake for 8–10 minutes, stirring halfway, until golden and crispy. Set aside.

While the pita crisps, make the hummus. Combine the chickpeas, tahini, lemon juice, garlic and 2 tbsp olive oil in a food processor. Blend until completely smooth, adding 2–3 tbsp water as needed to reach a creamy consistency. Taste and season with salt.
Spread the hummus onto a shallow bowl or plate, creating a well in the centre with the back of a spoon.
Dollop the soy yoghurt into the well and drizzle generously with extra virgin olive oil.
Top with the warm pita crisps, toasted pine nuts, and sumac and parsley if using. Serve immediately.

notes: Make the hummus up to a day ahead; store it covered in the fridge and bring to room temperature before serving.
Toast your own pine nuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes if you have time, it makes a real difference.
This is just as good made with tinned chickpeas as it would be with soaked dried ones.

title: Snapper and Sambal Oelek Pasta
summary: Pan-seared snapper with sambal oelek, garlic and parsley tossed through pasta.

items.raw: 2 snapper fillets (about 150 g each), skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the pasta until al dente, about 10 minutes. Drain, reserving 150 ml of pasta water.
While the pasta cooks, pat the snapper fillets dry and season with salt and pepper on both sides. Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat.
Place the snapper skin-side down in the hot pan and cook for 4 minutes until the skin is crispy. Flip and cook for another 2 minutes until just cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pan, add the sliced garlic and cook over medium heat for 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the sambal oelek and cook for another 30 seconds.
Add the cooked pasta to the pan with 100 ml of the reserved pasta water. Toss gently for 1–2 minutes, adding a little more pasta water if needed to coat the pasta lightly.
Break the snapper into large flakes and fold through the pasta gently. Squeeze over the lemon juice, scatter with parsley and serve immediately.

notes: Snapper is the go-to, firm, sweet, cooks quickly. Sub any fresh white fish fillet.
Make it vegetarian: swap the fish for 250 g firm tofu, cut into thick slices, pan-seared until golden.
Food safety:

title: Okra Soup
summary: Slippery okra stew with stockfish and shrimp, served with fufu.

items.raw: 500 g okra, topped and sliced into 1 cm rounds
items.prep: topped and sliced into 1 cm rounds

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the palm oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and ginger, stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, breaking it down into the oil.
Add the shredded stockfish and stir to coat. Cook for 3 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the sliced okra and stir well, don't worry if it looks very slimy at first. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the prawns and ground crayfish if using. Simmer for another 8–10 minutes until the prawns are pink and cooked through.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. The soup should be thick and slippery. Serve hot over fufu.

notes: Stockfish must be soaked in cold water for at least 4 hours (or overnight) before use, then flaked or shredded. Ask for it at West African or Asian grocers.
Make this soup in a big batch on Sunday and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat gently and add a splash of water if it's thickened too much.
The okra will release plenty of slime, that's what makes the soup silky and satisfying. Stir it well as it cooks.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Tonga Pumpkin & Coconut
summary: Roasted pumpkin simmered in coconut milk with onions and garlic.

items.raw: 1 kg jap pumpkin, cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, roast the pumpkin chunks until golden brown on all sides, about 10 minutes total. Set aside.
In the same pot, soften the onions over medium heat, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the pumpkin to the pot. Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock, then season with salt and pepper.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer until the pumpkin is completely soft and starting to break down, about 20 minutes. Stir occasionally and taste, adding more salt if needed.
Serve warm with fresh coriander if you like. Feeds the whole family on a weeknight.

notes: Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Molokhia
summary: Egyptian leafy green stew with garlic and coriander, served over rice.

items.raw: 400 g fresh molokhia leaves, roughly chopped (or 200 g dried molokhia, crushed)

steps.text: Bring the vegetable stock to a boil in a large pot, until it bubbles steadily.
Add the chopped molokhia leaves and stir to combine. Simmer for 5 minutes until the leaves start to break down.
While the molokhia simmers, heat a tablespoon of oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the chopped garlic and fry gently, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Crush the fried garlic with the salt using the back of a spoon or a mortar and pestle until it forms a paste.
Stir the garlic paste and ground coriander into the molokhia. Simmer for a further 3 to 5 minutes until the stew is thick and cohesive.
Serve the molokhia over a bed of steamed rice, with lemon wedges on the side for squeezing.

notes: Fresh molokhia is best and usually the cheapest; dried molokhia works too, use half the weight and crush it into a powder before adding. Frozen molokhia is also fine.
If you can't find molokhia, spinach is the closest substitute, though it's leafier and less slimy. Don't overcook spinach or it falls apart.
The stew thickens as it cools; add a splash more stock when reheating if needed.

title: Fava
summary: Silken yellow split pea purée from the Greek islands, dressed with olive oil and lemon.

items.raw: 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, to serve

steps.text: Rinse the yellow split peas under cold water, then tip into a large pot with the water and quartered brown onion. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for about 50 minutes, stirring often, until the peas have broken down completely into a thick purée.
When the peas are very soft and falling apart, remove from the heat and discard the onion pieces. Season generously with salt.
Whisk in the olive oil, a little at a time, beating to incorporate air and make the purée smooth and pale. This will take 3–4 minutes of steady whisking.
Stir in the lemon juice, then taste and adjust the seasoning, you want salt, brightness and richness in balance.
Divide among four bowls and top each with a handful of raw red onion slices and a crack of black pepper. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Fava keeps well for 3 days in the fridge, covered. Reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen it back to a purée consistency.
This is also lovely cold, straight from the fridge, with toasted bread and a scatter of caper berries or olives.

title: Tarhana Çorbası
summary: Tangy fermented grain and yoghurt soup, warming and sour, Anatolian comfort food.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Melt the butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring often, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the ground cumin and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the stock and bring to a simmer. Whisk the tarhana paste with a small cup of warm water until smooth, then slowly pour it into the simmering stock, whisking constantly so no lumps form.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the soup has thickened slightly and the flavours have melded. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with fresh mint if you like. Serve hot.

notes: If you can't find ready-made tarhana paste, you can order it online. Turkish delis often stock it.
Tarhana keeps for months in an airtight jar, so it's worth having on hand.
A dollop of yoghurt stirred in at the end is traditional, use about 1 tbsp per bowl.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Nihari
summary: Slow-cooked beef or lamb in a rich, dark spiced gravy, traditionally a breakfast dish.

items.raw: ½ tsp black cardamom pod, crushed
1 tbsp plain flour (or cornflour mixed with a little water)
items.note: or cornflour mixed with a little water

steps.text: Sear the meat: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. In batches, sear the beef until browned on all sides, about 2 minutes each side. Set aside.

Toast the spices: In the same pot, reduce heat to medium. Add cumin seeds, coriander seeds and crushed cardamom. Toast for 1 minute until fragrant, then add the dried red chillies and toast for another 30 seconds.

Build the base: Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until deeply caramelised and golden, about 15 minutes. Add the minced garlic, grated ginger and asafoetida, and cook for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Add the flour: Sprinkle the plain flour over the onion mixture and stir well to coat. Cook for 1 minute, then add the garam masala and stir to combine.

Simmer the meat: Return the beef to the pot and add the crushed tomatoes and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover and simmer for at least 2–3 hours, stirring occasionally. The meat should be very tender and the gravy dark and rich. If the gravy is too thin, uncover for the last 30 minutes to reduce.
Season and serve: Taste and add salt as needed. Serve hot in bowls with fresh coriander, sliced fresh ginger and a squeeze of lemon juice. Nihari is best with warm naan or roti for dipping.

notes: Nihari is best made a day ahead: cool completely, refrigerate overnight, and reheat gently before serving. The flavour deepens and the fat layer keeps the meat moist.
For a thicker gravy, mix cornflour with a little water and stir in during the last 15 minutes of cooking.
If you prefer lamb, use lamb shoulder instead of beef and reduce cooking time to 90 minutes.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Pad Cha Het
summary: Stir-fried wild mushrooms with fresh chilies and garlic, a simple northern Thai favourite.

items.raw: 500 g mixed mushrooms (cremini, oyster, shiitake), torn into bite-sized pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat until shimmering.
Add the mushrooms and cook, stirring occasionally, for 4–5 minutes until they begin to soften and release their liquid.
Add the garlic and chillies, stirring constantly for about 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the soy sauce and palm sugar, tossing everything together until the mushrooms are coated and tender, about 2 minutes more.
Taste and adjust the seasoning if needed.
Transfer to a serving plate, top with fresh Thai basil, and serve with a lime wedge on the side.

notes: If you can't find Thai basil, regular basil works well too.
For a deeper savoury note, replace soy sauce with tamari or add a teaspoon of coconut aminos.
Use whatever fresh or dried mushrooms you have; this dish works beautifully with any combination.

title: Chikni Dal
summary: Smooth, silky split pea dal with fried garlic and green chilli, served with roti.
