steps.text: Rinse the lentils under cold water until the water runs clear. Put them in a large pot with the halved onion, turmeric, salt and water. Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer.

Cook, stirring occasionally, for 35–40 minutes, until the lentils have completely broken down and the mixture is smooth and thick. If it's too thick, add a splash of water. Remove and discard the onion.

While the dal is cooking, heat the oil in a small frying pan over medium heat. Add the garlic slices and cook, stirring, for 2–3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Stir in the green chilli and cook for another 30 seconds.
Pour the hot garlic and chilli oil over the dal and stir through. Taste and add more salt if needed. Serve hot with roti, garnished with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: the dal keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if needed.
The garlic and chilli tempering can be made while the dal cooks and kept warm, or made fresh just before serving.

title: Pol Sambol
summary: Fresh coconut, lime, chilli and dried fish, a Sri Lankan sambol to eat with rice and curry.

items.raw: 1 fresh coconut, or 400 g freshly grated coconut
1 small red onion, very finely chopped

steps.text: If using a whole coconut, pierce the eyes and drain the liquid. Crack open the shell and peel away the brown skin with a vegetable peeler. Grate the white flesh on a fine grater or microplane until you have about 400 g of fine, fluffy coconut.
Put the grated coconut into a bowl and add the lime juice, chopped chillies, pounded dried fish, and red onion.
Mix gently but thoroughly until every grain of coconut is coated and the flavours are even.
Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt. The sambol should be bright, sharp, and hot, not timid.
Serve immediately alongside hot rice and curry.

notes: Make it up to 2 hours ahead and keep covered at room temperature; the coconut will soften slightly and the flavours will deepen.
If you can't find fresh coconut, use a block of frozen grated coconut, thawed, or good-quality desiccated coconut rehydrated in a little warm water and squeezed dry.
Ikan bilis (dried anchovies) are sold in Asian grocers; if you can't find them, use a small tin of anchovy fillets in oil, drained and mashed.

title: Pierogi Ruskie
summary: Potato and cheese dumplings with caramelized onions and sour cream.

items.raw: 500 g waxy potato, peeled and chopped into 2 cm pieces
items.prep: peeled and chopped into 2 cm pieces

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Make the dough: mix flour and salt in a bowl. In another bowl, whisk the egg, then stir in the sour cream. Pour the wet mixture into the flour and mix until you have a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the filling: boil the potato pieces in salted water until very tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well and mash roughly, you want some small lumps. Fry the chopped onion in 2 tbsp butter over medium heat until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Stir the onion and butter into the potato, then fold in the cheese. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Let cool.

Make the caramelized onions for serving: slice the 2 onions thinly. Melt 3 tbsp butter in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the onions, stirring often, until they're golden and soft, about 15 minutes. Set aside.

Roll the pierogi: flour your work surface lightly. Roll the dough out to about 2 mm thick. Using a 7 cm round cutter or a glass, cut out circles. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling on each circle, fold in half, then press the edges to seal, fold the corner of the half-moon up and over itself to make a small curved seal (this is the traditional shape). Oil your hands if the dough sticks.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Working in batches, drop the pierogi in. They'll sink at first, then float to the surface when they're nearly done, about 2 minutes. Boil for another 30 seconds after they float, then lift out with a slotted spoon.
Serve the pierogi warm with the caramelized onions spooned over the top and a dollop of sour cream. Scatter with fresh dill if you like.

notes: Make the filling and dough ahead: the filling keeps for 2 days in the fridge, and the dough keeps for up to 4 hours. You can freeze uncooked pierogi on a tray, then boil them straight from frozen (add 1 extra minute to the boiling time).
A potato ricer or food mill makes a smoother filling if you don't like lumps, though a rustic texture is traditional too.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Arancini di Ragù
summary: Golden-fried risotto balls stuffed with meat ragù, peas and mozzarella.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste
150 g fresh mozzarella, cut into 12 small cubes

steps.text: Make the ragù: heat oil in a heavy-based pot, add diced onion and cook gently until soft, about 5 minutes. Add beef and pork mince, stirring to break it up, until browned, about 8 minutes. Pour in wine and let it bubble away for 2 minutes. Add crushed tomatoes, season with salt and pepper, then lower heat and simmer gently, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes (longer is better). The ragù should be thick and the flavours rich. Let cool completely.

Make the risotto: bring stock to a gentle simmer in a separate pot and keep it there. In a heavy-based pan, melt butter over medium heat, add diced onion and cook until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add rice and stir constantly for 1 minute until the grains are coated and lightly toasted. Pour in wine and stir until absorbed.

Add stock one ladleful at a time, stirring often, letting each addition absorb before adding the next. After about 18 minutes, the rice should be creamy and just tender. Stir in parmesan and season with salt and pepper. Spread the risotto on a large tray to cool to room temperature, about 20 minutes.

Once risotto is cool, mix in 200 g (about half) of the ragù and all the thawed peas. Wet your hands and shape the mixture into 12 balls, each about the size of a golf ball. Make an indent in the centre of each ball with your thumb, press in a cube of mozzarella and a generous pinch of the remaining ragù, then seal the opening and reshape into a smooth ball. This takes patience but it's what keeps the filling hidden inside.

Set up three shallow bowls: one with beaten eggs, one with panko breadcrumbs, and one empty. Roll each arancino ball in egg, then roll in breadcrumbs until well coated. Place on a tray and chill for at least 30 minutes (or up to 12 hours) so the coating sets firmly.

Heat oil in a deep, heavy-based pot or deep-fryer to 170°C. If you don't have a thermometer, test with a wooden spoon handle: it should sizzle gently at the edge of the oil. Fry arancini in batches of 3–4, turning occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until golden brown all over. Don't crowd the pan. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve warm, while the mozzarella inside is still soft and the outside is crispy. Arancini are best eaten fresh but are still good at room temperature.

notes: Make the ragù on Sunday to let the flavours deepen overnight. You'll have leftovers, which freeze well.
If you don't have fresh mozzarella, use fior di latte or even a cube of cold butter instead.
Arancini can be coated and refrigerated for up to 12 hours before frying. This actually helps them hold their shape better.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Curry Rice with Sambals
summary: Fragrant turmeric rice with Cape Malay curry and fresh homemade sambals.

items.raw: 500 g beef mince (or lamb shoulder), cubed

steps.text: Make the sambals first: combine tomatoes, red onion, red chilli and coriander in a small bowl. Add lime juice and salt. In another bowl, combine cucumber, green chilli, mint, lime juice and salt. Set both aside.

For the curry rice, heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook, stirring, until softened and golden, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and ginger, stirring constantly for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add turmeric and stir for 30 seconds, then add rice, stirring to coat each grain in the oil and spices, about 2 minutes.
Pour in stock and add bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover and simmer for 15–18 minutes until the rice is tender and liquid is absorbed. Taste and adjust salt.

If making the suggested curry: heat oil in a separate pot over medium-high heat. Brown the meat in batches, set aside. In the same pot, cook onions until soft, about 5 minutes. Add curry powder and tomato paste, stirring for 1 minute. Return meat to pot, add stock and potatoes. Simmer, covered, for 20–25 minutes until potatoes are tender and sauce is thick. Season to taste.
Fluff the rice with a fork and remove bay leaves. Transfer to a serving dish, top with curry if using, and serve with both sambals on the side.

notes: The curry can be made a day ahead and reheated gently. The sambals are best made an hour or two before serving so the flavours meld.
Use leftover roast chicken or vegetables instead of making the curry, a generous spoonful stirred through the rice works just as well.
The rice can also be cooked in a rice cooker: fry the onion, garlic and ginger in a pot, add turmeric and rice to coat, then transfer to the rice cooker with the stock and bay leaves.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.

title: Tarte à la praline
summary: Pink praline tart, a Lyon specialty that's simpler than it looks.

steps.text: Make the pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the caster sugar and salt. Beat the egg yolk with the cold water and mix into the flour until just combined. Form a disc, wrap in cling film and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.

Preheat the oven to 200°C. Roll out the pastry between two sheets of baking paper to about 3 mm thick. Press into a 24 cm tart tin, trim the edges and prick the base. Blind bake with baking paper and beans for 12 minutes, then remove the paper and beans and bake for another 5 minutes until just set. Set aside to cool slightly.
Roughly crush about three-quarters of the pink pralines with the back of a spoon, you want some texture, not a smooth paste. Stir the softened butter through the crushed pralines.
Whisk the cream, milk, egg yolks and vanilla together until smooth. Fold in the praline mixture, then pour into the cooled pastry shell. Scatter the remaining whole pralines over the top.

Bake at 180°C for about 10 minutes, until the filling is just set but still trembling slightly in the centre. The tart will continue to set as it cools. Chill for at least 4 hours, or overnight, before serving.

notes: Make this a day ahead: the pralines soften beautifully overnight and the flavours deepen.
Pink pralines are a Lyon specialty and worth hunting down in good delis or online. They're crunchy, delicately flavoured hazelnut pralines and not like anything else.
If your oven runs hot, tent the tart loosely with foil if it's browning too quickly.
Food safety: The eggs are cooked until just set. For pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system, cook them until firm all the way through.

title: Kokt torsk med gräslök och smör
summary: Poached cod with chives and brown butter, a simple West Coast Swedish dinner.

image.credit: Photo: José Antonio Otegui Auzmendi / Pexels

items.raw: 4 white-fish fillets, about 150 g each (cod or similar)

steps.text: Pour the stock or water into a wide, shallow pan and add the bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, until the surface is barely trembling with tiny bubbles and not boiling.
Pat the fish fillets dry with paper towel and season lightly with salt on both sides.

Slide the fish into the simmering stock. The liquid should barely cover them. Poach gently, the surface should barely tremble, for about 8 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Carefully lift the fish onto warm plates using a slotted spatula, leaving the poaching liquid behind.
Melt the butter in a small pan over medium heat, swirling occasionally, until it turns a light golden brown and smells nutty, about 3 minutes. Watch it carefully so it doesn't burn.

Drizzle the brown butter, which should smell nutty and be golden brown, over each fillet, which should be opaque and flake easily. Scatter the chives over the top, and finish with a grind of black pepper. Serve at once.

notes: The whole point is freshness and gentleness. Don't rush the poaching, low heat keeps the fish tender. If your fillets are very thick, give them an extra minute.
Brown butter can be made ahead and kept warm; reheat gently before serving.
Food safety:

title: Marmitako
summary: Basque fisherman's stew with tuna, potatoes and peppers.

items.raw: 600 g fresh tuna, cut into chunks
500 g floury potato, cut into large dice
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic and paprika, stir well, and cook for 1 minute.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat in the oil. Pour in the stock and bring to a boil. Cook for 15 minutes until the potatoes are nearly tender.
Add the red and green capsicum and simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the tuna chunks and stir gently. Simmer for 8–10 minutes, until the tuna is just cooked through and the potatoes are tender. Don't overcook the tuna.
Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Serve hot in bowls.

notes: Use good-quality fresh tuna; frozen won't give you the same result.
Don't stir too much once the tuna is in, you want to keep the chunks intact.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Spring onion Pancakes
summary: Laminated flatbread layered with oil and spring onions, flaky and crispy outside.

items.raw: 3 tbsp neutral oil, plus extra for brushing
4 spring onions, white and light green parts, finely chopped
items.prep: white and light green parts, finely chopped

items.raw: 1 tsp coarse sea salt, for finishing

steps.text: Mix the boiling water into the flour and salt with a wooden spoon or chopsticks until shaggy. Let cool for 5 minutes, then knead by hand until smooth and soft, about 8 minutes. The dough will be slightly sticky, this is right. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a ball, brush all over with a little oil, and rest for 10 minutes covered.

On an oiled work surface, roll one ball into a thin rectangle about 30 cm × 20 cm. Brush generously with oil, scatter a quarter of the chopped spring onion evenly over the surface, then tightly roll up from one long edge into a log. Coil the log into a spiral, tucking the end underneath. Press gently to flatten slightly into a disc about 1 cm thick. Repeat with the remaining dough balls, spring onion and oil. Let rest for 5 minutes.
Roll each disc into a round about 20 cm across, being gentle so the layers stay distinct. If the dough springs back, let it rest for a minute and try again.

Heat 1½ tbsp oil in a large non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Once shimmering, place one pancake in and cook for 2–3 minutes until the underside is golden and crispy. Flip and cook the other side for 1–2 minutes until speckled and cooked through.
Transfer to a plate and immediately sprinkle with a pinch of coarse sea salt. Repeat with the remaining pancakes, adding a little more oil to the pan as needed. Serve warm, torn into pieces.

notes: The dough keeps well: store finished pancakes in an airtight container for 2 days, then reheat briefly in a dry frying pan. You can also freeze uncooked rested discs for up to a month, then cook straight from frozen (add 2 minutes to the cooking time).
Hydration is key here, 75% feels sticky at first, but it's what gives you those delicate, shattering layers. Don't add extra flour.

title: Frittata di Cipolla e Peperoncino
summary: Caramelised onions and fresh chilli eggs, best at room temperature with bread and a story.

items.raw: 2 fresh red chillies, deseeded and finely sliced

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a 25 cm non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Add the onions and a pinch of salt, and stir often until they're golden and soft, about 15 minutes. You want them sweet, not brown and crispy.
Scatter the chilli through the onions and cook for another 2 minutes, then taste and adjust the salt and pepper.
While the onions are cooking, crack the eggs into a bowl, whisk them together well, and set aside.
Turn the heat to medium-low. Pour the eggs over the onions, stir gently to distribute them, then leave it alone. Cook until the edges are set and the top is still a little soft, about 10 minutes.
Slide the frittata onto a plate and let it cool to room temperature. Scatter with parsley if you like, cut into wedges, and serve with good bread.

notes: Keep in the fridge for up to 3 days and serve cold, or reheat gently in a 180°C oven.
No chilli in the house? Use a pinch of dried oregano instead, or just the onions. The frittata doesn't need much.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Beef and Guinness Pie
summary: Rich beef and Guinness stew with a golden pastry crust.

items.raw: 1.2 kg beef chuck, cut into 3 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste
320 g puff pastry, thawed if frozen

steps.text: Heat oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium-high heat. Season beef with salt and pepper, then brown in batches, about 3 minutes each side. Transfer to a plate.
Add onions and carrots to the pot, cook, stirring, until the onions start to soften, about 5 minutes. Add garlic, cook 1 minute, then dust in flour and stir well.

Pour in Guinness and beef stock, scraping any browned bits from the bottom. Return beef and add bay leaves and thyme. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on low heat for 2 hours, until the beef is tender. Stir occasionally. Remove bay leaves and thyme sprigs.
Preheat oven to 200°C. Transfer the beef filling to a large pie dish, about 2 litres capacity. Let it cool slightly.

Roll out pastry to about 3 mm thick and roughly 5 cm larger than your pie dish. Brush the rim of the dish with beaten egg. Lay pastry over the filling, press down on the rim to seal, then trim excess. Cut a few slits in the top for steam to escape.
Brush the pastry with beaten egg. Bake for 25–30 minutes, until golden brown.

notes: Make the filling the day before and refrigerate; assemble and bake just before serving.
Works just as well in the slow cooker: combine all filling ingredients, cook on low for 6–8 hours, then proceed from step 4.
Food safety:

title: Rice and Peas
summary: Creamy coconut rice studded with red kidney beans and thyme, the everyday side that turns a plate into a meal.

items.raw: 400 g tin kidney beans, drained and rinsed
1 sprig fresh thyme (or 1 tsp dried thyme)

steps.text: Pour the coconut milk into a large measuring jug and add water to make 600 ml total. Stir well to combine.
Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened and fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 1 minute more.
Add the rice, stirring to coat in the oil, about 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk mixture and stock, then add the kidney beans, thyme, salt and pepper. Stir well and bring to a boil until the liquid is bubbling steadily.
Once boiling, reduce the heat to low, cover with a tight-fitting lid, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Do not lift the lid during cooking.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 2 minutes. Fluff with a fork, discard the thyme sprig if using fresh, and scatter with spring onion if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: cook it the day before, cool quickly, and refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Reheat gently in the pot with a splash of water.
This is Jamaican rice and peas, which uses kidney beans, not the peas you might find elsewhere in the Caribbean.

title: Waakye
summary: Millet and beans with rice, Ghana's beloved street breakfast made at home.

items.raw: 200 g dried brown beans (or tinned kidney beans)
1 litre water (or more, for tinned beans)

steps.text: If using dried beans, soak them in cold water for at least 2 hours or overnight. Drain and rinse. (Skip this if using tinned beans.)

In a large pot, bring water to the boil. Add the beans, bay leaves, ginger and onion. Simmer for 40 minutes if using dried beans, or 15 minutes if using tinned beans, until the beans are soft but not falling apart.
Add the millet to the pot. Stir well and cook for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the rice, stir, and bring back to a simmer. Cook, covered, for 20 to 25 minutes until the rice is cooked through and most of the liquid is absorbed. The mixture should be moist but not soupy.
Taste and add salt as needed. Remove the bay leaves.
Serve hot with your choice of toppings: grated hard-boiled egg, fried plantain, avocado, hot shito sauce, or a rich stew.

notes: If you can't find millet, substitute with 150 g of pearl barley or extra rice, though the texture won't be quite the same.
Make it the night before and reheat gently with a splash of water, the flavour deepens overnight.
The best toppings are fried plantain, avocado slices, grated hard-boiled egg, and a spoonful of hot shito (pepper) sauce on the side.

title: Smoked Mackerel with Horseradish Cream
summary: Smoked mackerel with sharp horseradish cream and buttered new potatoes.

items.raw: 2 tbsp fresh horseradish, finely grated (or 3 tbsp prepared horseradish)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the potatoes in a large pot of cold salted water and bring to the boil. Cook for 12 to 15 minutes until just tender when pierced with a knife, then drain well.
While the potatoes cook, make the horseradish cream: whip the cold cream to soft peaks, then gently fold in the horseradish, lemon juice, sugar and a pinch of salt and pepper.
Return the warm potatoes to the pot, add the butter and toss until coated and glossy. Season to taste.

Warm the smoked mackerel fillets gently by placing them skin-side up on a plate and letting them sit near (not on) a warm part of the stove for 2 to 3 minutes, or arrange them on a baking tray and warm through in a 160°C oven for 5 minutes.
Divide the potatoes among four plates, place a mackerel fillet alongside each portion, and top with a generous spoonful of horseradish cream. Scatter with fresh parsley if you like and serve at once.

notes: The horseradish cream can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept in the fridge.
Use the best smoked mackerel you can get, local fishmonger quality makes all the difference.

title: Lancashire Hotpot
summary: Layered lamb, potatoes and onions, baked low and slow until the potatoes crisp on top.

items.raw: 800 g lamb shoulder, diced into 3 cm pieces
700 g waxy potato, thinly sliced (about 3 mm)
2 tbsp butter, plus extra for dotting
1 tsp fresh thyme leaves (or ½ tsp dried thyme)

steps.text: Heat oven to 160°C. Layer half the potatoes in the bottom of a deep baking dish or casserole (about 2 litre capacity), then half the onions.
Add all the lamb pieces, then layer the remaining onions and remaining potatoes on top, seasoning each layer with salt, pepper and thyme as you go.
Warm the chicken stock and pour it over everything, it should come about three-quarters of the way up the dish. Dot the top with small pieces of butter.
Cover tightly with foil and bake for 2 hours at 160°C, until the lamb is completely tender.
Increase oven to 200°C, remove the foil, and bake uncovered for a further 15 minutes until the potato tops are golden and crispy.
Rest for 5 minutes before serving. The gravy should come from the lamb and stock, you don't need to make it separately.

notes: Make it the day before and refrigerate, it actually improves. Just add 10 minutes to the baking time if cooking from cold.
Lamb neck fillet works just as well as shoulder and gives you more flavour for the gravy.
Don't skip the second blast at high heat, that's what gets the potatoes crispy.
Food safety:

title: Shakshuka Tunisienne
summary: Eggs poached in fiery harissa tomato sauce with caraway and preserved lemon.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large shallow pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Stir in the harissa and cook for another minute.

Pour in the crushed tomatoes and bring to a simmer. Add the preserved lemon and caraway seeds. Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and the flavours have melded. Season with salt and pepper.
If using it, drizzle the extra harissa over the surface of the sauce.

Make 8 small wells in the sauce by pushing it gently to the sides. Crack an egg into each well. Cover the pan and cook over medium-low heat for 6–8 minutes, until the egg whites are set but the yolks are still soft.
Scatter fresh coriander over the top and serve straight from the pan.

notes: Serve with torn bread to soak up the sauce.
Make the sauce ahead and reheat gently before poaching the eggs.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Japanese Curry Rice
summary: Tender chicken, potatoes and carrots in sweet-savory roux over steamed rice

items.raw: 800 g chicken thighs, skin-on and bone-in, cut into large pieces
items.prep: skin-on and bone-in, cut into large pieces

items.raw: 2 medium brown onions, cut into thick chunks
3 medium waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into thick chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thick chunks

items.raw: 2 large carrots, peeled and cut into thick chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into thick chunks

items.raw: 100 g Japanese curry roux block (Vermont or S&B brand)

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot or deep frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the chicken pieces, skin-side down, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the skin is golden. Flip and cook for another 2 to 3 minutes on the other side. Remove and set aside.
Add the onion, potato and carrot to the pot. Stir and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the vegetables are lightly browned.
Return the chicken to the pot and add the water, bringing to a simmer. Cover and cook for 15 to 20 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the chicken is cooked through.

Break the curry roux into chunks and stir into the pot until dissolved. Simmer, uncovered, for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce thickens slightly. Taste and add salt if needed. Serve over steamed rice.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Salatit al-Khudar
summary: Simple Palestinian chopped salad of tomatoes, cucumber, parsley and lemon.

items.raw: 1 bunch fresh parsley, finely chopped (about 1 cup loosely packed)

steps.text: Dice the tomatoes into small, even pieces about the size of a pea, working over a bowl to catch the juice.
Dice the cucumber to the same size as the tomato.
Finely chop the parsley, removing the coarse stems and using mostly the leaves.
Combine the tomato, cucumber and parsley in a bowl.
Pour the lemon juice and olive oil over the vegetables and toss gently but thoroughly so everything is well coated.
Taste and add salt until it's right, not too much, just enough to bring out the flavour of the vegetables.
Serve straight away with warm bread to eat it with.

notes: Make this salad just before eating, if it sits too long, the vegetables release water and it becomes watery.
The dice should be fine and even. This isn't just cutting vegetables small; it's about texture, so every piece sits together in the bowl.

title: Tortellini in Brodo
summary: Hand-folded tortellini in clear broth, a Sunday project with a pork and cheese filling.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 l good chicken stock (or beef stock)

steps.text: Make the pasta: mound flour on a bench, crack eggs into centre, add a pinch of salt. Work with a fork until shaggy, then knead by hand for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.

Make the filling: fry pork mince in a pan over medium heat, breaking it up, until it loses its colour, about 5 minutes. Cool completely, then mix with ham, parmesan, breadcrumbs, egg yolk, nutmeg, salt and pepper. Taste and adjust.

Roll the pasta: divide dough into 4 pieces. Working with one at a time (keep others covered), roll very thin on a lightly floured surface, thin enough to read through. Using a 5 cm cutter or glass, cut circles.

Fill and fold: place ½ tsp filling slightly off-centre on each circle. Fold in half to make a half-moon, press edges firmly. Bring the two points of the half-moon together to seal into a ring. Place on a tray lined with baking paper, well spaced. Repeat until done.
Chill the tortellini on the tray, uncovered, for at least 30 minutes (or up to 4 hours before cooking).

Bring stock to a steady simmer in a large pot. Carefully drop in tortellini, a few at a time so the broth stays moving. They'll sink, then float to the surface; simmer for 2–3 minutes after they float.
Serve in bowls with hot broth, grated parmesan, a crack of black pepper, and parsley if you like.

notes: Make the filling and dough a day ahead; chill separately. Roll and fold the morning of, then chill on the tray.
Freeze uncooked tortellini on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag. Cook from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the simmer time.
The filling should taste bold, it seasons the broth. Don't be shy with salt, pepper, and nutmeg.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

title: Thieboudienne
summary: Senegal's national dish: fish and rice slow-cooked with caramelized vegetables and tomato.

items.raw: 1 kg whole white fish (barramundi or snapper), scaled and gutted
1 medium sweet potato, cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Pat the fish dry and season inside and out with salt and pepper. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes until deeply golden and caramelized.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the crushed tomatoes and let them simmer for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mixture darkens and thickens slightly.

Pour in the fish stock and bring to a simmer. Gently lay the whole fish into the liquid, then arrange the carrot, sweet potato, pumpkin and celery around it. Simmer gently for 15 minutes until the fish is just cooked through.
Carefully remove the fish and all vegetables to a plate. Cover loosely to keep warm.
Add the rice to the cooking liquid, stirring once, and bring back to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for about 20–25 minutes until the rice is tender and has absorbed most of the liquid.

Return the vegetables to the pot to warm through, then taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve the rice on a platter with the fish and vegetables arranged on top, scattered with fresh parsley if you like.

notes: Thieboudienne can be made a day ahead: cook the fish and vegetables up to step 5, cool and refrigerate, then finish the rice and reheat gently before serving.
If you can't find a whole fish, use thick fish steaks (about 200g each) and add them after the rice has cooked for 15 minutes, so they don't break up.
The caramelized onion base is everything, don't rush it. The darker and deeper the onions, the better the dish.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Pastitsada
summary: Rabbit or chicken stewed in tomato and red wine until very tender, served over pasta, a Cretan Sunday dish.

items.raw: 1 whole rabbit (about 1.2 kg), or 1.2 kg chicken thigh, cut into pieces
items.prep: or 1.2 kg chicken thigh, cut into pieces

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Season the rabbit or chicken pieces with salt and pepper. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the meat in batches, about 4 minutes each side, until golden. Set aside.
Add the diced onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the crushed garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Return the meat to the pot. Pour in the red wine and scrape up any brown bits from the bottom. Let it bubble for 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes, oregano and bay leaves.

Bring to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cover partially and cook, stirring occasionally, until the meat is very tender and falls easily from the bone, about 2 hours. The sauce should be rich and concentrated.
Taste and adjust salt and pepper as needed. Remove bay leaves.
Cook the pasta in salted boiling water until al dente, about 10 minutes (or as the packet says). Drain well.
Divide the pasta among bowls and top with the rabbit or chicken and its sauce.

notes: This keeps well in the fridge for 3 days, or freeze for a month. The flavour deepens as it sits.
Yiayia's notebook says rabbit is traditional, but chicken thigh works beautifully and is easier to find.

title: Pancit Lomi
summary: Creamy egg noodle soup with chicken liver and greens, a Kapampangan birthday staple.

items.raw: 200 g chicken liver, cleaned and cut into bite-sized pieces
items.prep: cleaned and cut into bite-sized pieces

items.raw: 2 tbsp cornflour, mixed with 3 tbsp water

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Fry the liver, stirring gently, until just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
In the same pot, sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Add the chicken breast and cook, stirring, until no longer pink, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the chicken stock and bring to a boil. Add the fresh egg noodles and cook until tender, about 5 minutes. Add the bok choy and spring onion.
Slowly pour the cornflour slurry into the simmering broth, stirring constantly until the soup thickens and turns creamy, about 2 minutes.
Return the cooked liver to the pot. Slowly drizzle in the beaten eggs while stirring gently to create egg ribbons, about 1 minute.
Season with salt and white pepper to taste. Serve hot.

notes: The chicken liver must not be overcooked or it becomes tough. Add it back to the pot at the very end.
Fresh egg noodles cook much faster than dried; if using dried noodles, add them earlier and cook for 8–10 minutes.
The cornflour slurry must be stirred in slowly to avoid lumps.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Gyutan
summary: Grilled sliced beef tongue with salt and lemon, izakaya-style.

items.raw: 300 g beef tongue, thinly sliced (about 3 mm)

steps.text: Bring the beef tongue to room temperature, about 10 minutes, while you heat a frying pan over high heat until it's very hot.
Add the oil to the pan. Once smoking, add the beef tongue slices in a single layer. Don't stir; let them sit for 1 to 2 minutes until lightly charred underneath.
Flip and cook for another 1 to 2 minutes on the second side. The meat should be just cooked through, still tender.
Transfer to a plate. Season generously with salt while the meat is still hot.
Serve with lemon wedges. Squeeze over each bite.

notes: Beef tongue keeps well raw for 2 days in the fridge, wrapped. Ask your butcher to slice it thin on the deli slicer, or freeze for an hour and slice yourself with a sharp knife.
Cooked tongue is best eaten fresh, but any leftovers are good cold the next day.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Canh Chua Cá
summary: Sour soup with white fish, pineapple and okra, bright and tangy with herbs.

items.raw: 500 g white fish fillet (barramundi or snapper), cut into large chunks
200 g fresh pineapple, cut into chunks

steps.text: Bring the stock to a gentle simmer in a large pot. Stir in the tamarind paste, fish sauce and sugar until the paste dissolves and everything is combined.
Add the pineapple and okra, and simmer for 5 minutes until the okra is just tender.
Gently slide the fish pieces into the broth. Simmer for 3–4 minutes until the fish is cooked through and opaque.
Add the tomato wedges and chilli, if using, and warm through for 1 minute.
Divide the soup among bowls and scatter with dill, coriander and mint before serving.

notes: If you can't find fresh tamarind paste, use 1½ tbsp tamarind concentrate or 2 tbsp lime juice for a lighter sour note.
The herbs are not optional, they're what makes it sing. Vietnamese mint (laksa leaf) is traditional, but use whatever fresh herbs you have.
Food safety:

title: Fafda-Jalebi
summary: Fried gram flour noodles and crispy vegetables with sweet jalebi and garlic chutney.

items.raw: 2 tbsp water (or more to reach piping consistency)
items.note: or more to reach piping consistency

items.raw: 2 tbsp neutral oil, plus 1 litre for deep frying

steps.text: Make the jalebi syrup first: In a heavy-bottomed saucepan, combine the caster sugar and 300 ml water. Bring to a boil, stirring until the sugar dissolves completely. Add the lemon juice and crushed cardamom pods. If using saffron, crumble it into the syrup. Simmer for 10 minutes until the syrup thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon. Set aside to cool completely.

Make the jalebi batter: In a bowl, whisk together the plain flour and bicarbonate of soda. Add the yoghurt and water, stirring until you have a smooth, lump-free batter with a consistency like double cream, thin enough to flow through a piping bag, but not watery. If using saffron, crumble it into the batter. Stir in the 2 tbsp of neutral oil. Set aside for 15 minutes to rest.
Make the garlic chutney: Blend all the ingredients together in a food processor or with a mortar and pestle until you reach a smooth paste. Transfer to a small bowl and set aside.

Make the fafda batter: In a large bowl, whisk together the gram flour, yoghurt, salt, turmeric and cumin. Add the chopped green chilli. Gradually add the 200 ml water, stirring until you have a thick, smooth batter, it should be slightly thicker than the jalebi batter, dropping slowly from a spoon. Gently fold in the carrot, peas and red onion. Let the batter rest for 10 minutes.

Heat the 1 litre of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed, deep saucepan or wok to 170°C. You can check the temperature with a thermometer; if you don't have one, a small piece of batter should sizzle gently and brown in about 60 seconds.

Fry the jalebi: Transfer the jalebi batter to a piping bag fitted with a thin nozzle (about 5 mm). Carefully squeeze the batter into the hot oil in spiral shapes, starting from the centre and spiralling outward, making each jalebi about 5 cm across. Fry 3–4 at a time so they don't touch. Fry for about 90 seconds until deep golden and crisp, then turn gently and fry the other side for another 30–45 seconds. Remove with a slotted spoon and immediately place in the cool jalebi syrup. Repeat until all the batter is used. Set the jalebi aside in the syrup.

Fry the fafda: Once the oil returns to 170°C, carefully lower a fafda mould (or use a kitchen spoon or ladle) into the oil if you have one. Alternatively, use your hands or two spoons to shape the batter into loose, irregular nests about 10 cm across, don't make them perfectly compact; fafda should be airy and crispy. Fry 2–3 at a time for 3–4 minutes, turning halfway, until golden and crispy all over. The edges should be lacy and crackly. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
Serve the fafda warm with a jalebi on the side, a spoonful of garlic chutney, and a small bowl of the syrup for dipping.

notes: Make the jalebi syrup and batter the day before if you like, this takes the stress out of frying day. Keep both in airtight containers at room temperature.
The garlic chutney keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Fafda is best eaten warm and fresh, but jalebi will keep in the syrup for up to 2 days.

title: Boerewors with Pap
summary: Homemade spiced sausage grilled over open flame, served with creamy maize porridge.

items.raw: 120 ml full-cream milk (optional, for creamy pap)

steps.text: Toast the coriander seeds, cumin seeds, peppercorns and cloves in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind to a coarse powder.
Place the pork mince, pork belly, ground spices, garlic, salt, ginger and turmeric in a bowl. Mix gently but thoroughly, then add the ice water and mix again. Keep everything cold while you work.

Soak the sausage casings in warm water for 15 minutes. Fit a casing onto a sausage maker, leaving a 5 cm tail. Fill slowly and evenly, twisting into 10 cm lengths. Prick any air pockets with a needle. Refrigerate until ready to grill.

For the pap: bring water or stock to the boil in a large pot. Slowly whisk in the maize meal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Reduce heat to low and stir often for 10–12 minutes until thick and creamy.
Stir in salt and butter. If you like it creamier, add the milk at the end and stir until smooth. Keep warm on the stove.
Heat your braai or barbecue to medium-high. Grill the boerewors for 12–15 minutes, turning regularly, until cooked through (internal temperature 75°C) and golden brown with a few charred spots.
Rest the wors for 2 minutes, then serve over the hot pap with lemon wedges and hot sauce on the side.

notes: Make the wors up to 2 days ahead and store in the fridge. They freeze beautifully too.
If you don't have natural casings, make pattie wors instead: shape the mixture into thick patties and braai or pan-fry them.
Pap reheats well, if it thickens too much overnight, loosen it with a splash of water or milk on the stove.
Food safety:

title: Eggplant with Garlic and Doubanjiang
summary: Soft eggplant in a savory-spicy doubanjiang sauce, a quiet Sichuan classic that needs no meat.

items.raw: 600 g eggplant, cut into 4 cm pieces
2 spring onions, white and green parts separated, sliced
items.prep: white and green parts separated, sliced

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of neutral oil in a large wok or wide pan over high heat until shimmering. Working in two batches, fry the eggplant pieces, turning occasionally, until golden and softened, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the pan. Lower the heat to medium and add the minced garlic, stirring for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the doubanjiang, breaking it up with the back of your spatula, and cook for 1 minute until the paste darkens slightly and releases its aroma.

Return all the eggplant to the pan. Add the soy sauce, sugar, white pepper, and water, stirring gently to coat the eggplant evenly. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has reduced and clings to the pieces.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the white parts of the spring onions and the sesame oil. Scatter the green parts over the top and serve immediately with rice.

notes: Don't skip the frying step. The eggplant needs to brown to develop texture and flavour; boiling or steaming leaves it waterlogged.
Leftovers keep for two days in the fridge and taste even better the next day. Reheat gently with a splash of water.

title: Idli
summary: Steamed rice and lentil cakes, soft and fluffy, made from ready-made batter.

items.raw: Salt, to taste (if the batter isn't already salted)
items.note: if the batter isn't already salted

steps.text: Bring water to a boil in a large pot with an idli stand or steamer rack inside, until it is bubbling steadily and steam is rising. The water should come just below the rack.
While the water heats, check your batter. It should fall off a spoon in a thick stream, if it's too stiff, thin it with a little water. Taste and add salt if needed.
Oil the idli moulds well (the little metal cups that come with the stand). This matters: the idli pops out cleanly when they're properly greased.
Gently pour batter into each mould until three-quarters full. Don't overfill or they'll puff out of shape.
Carefully place the mould onto the steamer rack. Steam, covered, until a skewer poked into an idli comes out clean, about 8 minutes.
Let rest for 30 seconds, then slide a knife around each idli and turn the mould over onto a plate. They should fall out easily. Serve warm with sambar, chutney or warm oil.

notes: Make idli within a day or two of preparing your batter, the fresher it is, the fluffier the idli.
If your batter has separated, give it a gentle stir before using. A good batter ferments evenly and keeps in the fridge for up to five days.
No idli mould? Use a muffin tin or small bowls lined with cling wrap, they won't pop out as cleanly, but they'll steam just fine.

title: Chicken Kyiv
summary: Tender chicken breast filled with dill butter, fried until golden and crisp.

items.raw: 4 boneless chicken breast fillets, about 200 g each
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Mix the softened butter with minced garlic, fresh dill, salt and a pinch of black pepper. Divide into 4 portions and shape each into a small block. Freeze for at least 15 minutes until firm.

Place each chicken breast between two sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or rolling pin, pound gently but firmly until the breast is about 5 mm thick. Work from the centre outwards, being careful not to tear the meat.

Lay one flattened chicken breast on a clean surface. Place a butter portion in the centre. Fold the long sides over the butter, then fold in the short sides to seal, creating a neat parcel. The seam should be on the bottom.

Place the flour on one plate, beaten eggs in a shallow bowl, and breadcrumbs on another plate. Coat each chicken parcel lightly in flour, shaking off excess. Dip in beaten egg to coat completely, then roll in breadcrumbs until fully covered. Place on a plate, seam-side down.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based frying pan over medium-high heat until a breadcrumb sizzles immediately when dropped in (about 160°C).

Carefully place the chicken parcels seam-side up into the hot oil. Fry for 5 to 6 minutes until the breadcrumb coating is deep golden brown, then gently turn and fry the other side for another 4 to 5 minutes until crisp and the internal temperature reaches 75°C.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels. Let rest for 2 minutes before serving. The butter inside will be hot, warn your family to cut carefully so they don't get splashed.

notes: You can prepare the breaded chicken parcels up to 4 hours ahead and refrigerate them before frying. This helps them stay together and cook evenly.
If the oil is too hot, the coating will brown too quickly before the chicken cooks through. If it's not hot enough, the chicken will absorb oil and become greasy rather than crisp.
Serve with boiled potatoes and a simple salad of beetroot and dill, if you like.
Food safety:

title: Croquetas de Jamón
summary: Crispy Spanish ham croquettes with a creamy centre, fried until golden.

steps.text: Melt the butter in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Stir in the flour to make a paste, cooking for 2 minutes, stirring constantly.
Gradually whisk in the warm milk, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Continue cooking for 5 minutes until the sauce is thick and smooth.
Stir in the chicken stock and the diced ham. Season with salt and white pepper, tasting as you go. Cook for another 2 minutes until the ham is heated through.
Pour the mixture onto a baking tray lined with baking paper and spread it out to about 1.5 cm thick. Cover with more baking paper and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, or until firm enough to shape.
Using two spoons or your hands, shape the mixture into cylinders about 6 cm long and 2 cm wide. You should have about 16 croquetas.
Set up three bowls: one with the beaten eggs, one with the breadcrumbs, and one empty for finished croquetas. Dip each croqueta into the egg, then into the breadcrumbs, coating well. Place on a tray.

Heat the oil to 170°C in a deep pan or deep-fryer (a cube of bread should turn golden in about 60 seconds). Working in batches, fry the croquetas for 2–3 minutes, turning once, until golden and crispy all over.
Transfer to paper towels to drain. Serve hot with a squeeze of lemon or a spoonful of aioli.

notes: Make the béchamel mixture and chill it the day before for easier shaping.
For a ham-forward flavour, use ham stock instead of chicken stock if you have it.
Freeze uncooked croquetas on a tray for up to 3 months; fry straight from frozen, adding 1–2 minutes to the cooking time.

title: Beef and Black Bean Stir-Fry
summary: Thin-sliced beef tossed fast with fermented black beans and garlic in the wok.

items.raw: 500 g beef sirloin, thinly sliced across the grain
3 tbsp douchi (fermented black beans), rinsed and roughly chopped

steps.text: Slice the beef thinly against the grain and set aside. Rinse the black beans, drain well, and chop roughly. Slice the garlic and chilli.
Heat the wok over high heat until smoking, about 2 minutes. Add 1 tbsp oil, swirl to coat.
Working quickly, add half the beef and let it sit for 30 seconds without stirring, this helps it catch colour. Toss for 30 seconds, then transfer to a plate. Repeat with the remaining oil and beef.
Return the wok to high heat. Add the garlic and chilli, toss for 10 seconds until fragrant. Add the black beans, toss for another 10 seconds.
Return all the beef to the wok with the oyster sauce and sesame oil. Toss everything together for 30 seconds, until coated and heated through.
Serve immediately over steamed rice, scattered with spring onion.

notes: Slice the beef when it's partially frozen (about 30 minutes in the freezer) for cleaner, thinner cuts.
This is best served immediately. The beef toughens if it sits in the wok too long, aim for 2 minutes total cooking time from wok to plate.
If you can't find fermented black beans (douchi), use 2 tbsp more oyster sauce and a pinch of extra salt, though it won't be quite the same dish.
Food safety: Steaks and roasting cuts of beef or lamb can be served pink: about 60°C in the centre is medium-rare, 70°C is well done.

title: Black Bean and Charred Corn Salad with Coriander Lime
summary: Smoky charred corn, earthy black beans, tomato and red onion with bright coriander and lime.

items.raw: 400 g tin black beans, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pan over high heat. Add corn kernels and cook, stirring occasionally, until charred and golden, about 6–8 minutes. Season with salt and pepper, then transfer to a bowl.
While the corn cooks, combine black beans, tomato and red onion in a large bowl.
Add the charred corn to the tomato and bean mix. Toss through lime juice and zest, then fold in most of the fresh coriander.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Scatter the remaining coriander on top and serve at room temperature or chilled.

notes: Make it ahead: prepare the beans, tomato and onion up to a day before. Char the corn fresh and toss together just before eating for the best char flavour.
Works great as a side to grilled tofu or with warm tortillas on the side.

title: Rendang Ayam
summary: Chicken braised in fragrant coconut and spice paste until tender and deeply flavoured.

items.raw: 800 g chicken thigh, bone-in skin-on, cut into pieces

steps.text: Blend the shallots, garlic, ginger, galangal and dried chillies with 100 ml water until smooth. This is your rendang paste.
Heat the oil in a large, heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the paste and caraway seeds. Fry, stirring often, until fragrant and the oil begins to separate from the paste, about 8 minutes.
Add the chicken pieces and stir to coat well in the paste. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until the chicken is sealed.
Pour in the coconut milk and stir. Add the turmeric, lime leaves and a pinch of salt. Bring to a gentle simmer until the sauce is bubbling lightly and fragrant.
Reduce heat to low. Simmer uncovered for 60 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes or so. The sauce will gradually reduce and thicken, and the oil will begin to separate again, this is what you want.
Keep simmering until the sauce is thick, glossy and coats the chicken, and the chicken is very tender. Taste and adjust the salt. Serve with rice.

notes: Make it a day ahead: flavour deepens overnight. Reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if needed.
For deeper colour and flavour, fry the paste longer in step 2, dark brown is better than light.
Serve with steamed white rice or fragrant jasmine rice to soak up the sauce.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Nyama Choma
summary: Grilled meat with lime and salt, charred and tender, the Kenyan way.

items.raw: 800 g beef chuck steak (or beef ribs), cut into 5 cm chunks

steps.text: Heat your grill or barbecue to hot. If using charcoal, wait until the coals are white and glowing; if gas, get it smoking.
Pat the beef dry with paper towel until the surface is no longer wet. This helps it char, not steam.
Rub the meat lightly with oil, then season generously with salt on both sides.
Lay the meat on the grill in a single layer. Don't move it for the first 4 minutes, you want a good char.
Flip and cook the other side for another 4 minutes. The meat should have a dark crust but still be pink inside (about 55°C on a meat thermometer).
Transfer to a warm plate. Squeeze lime over the hot meat, it'll sizzle and the juice will run into all the crevices.
Let it rest for 2 minutes, then serve with extra lime wedges and salt on the side for dipping.

notes: Beef ribs (short ribs or beef back ribs) cook beautifully the same way, just allow an extra 2–3 minutes per side.
No grill? A heavy cast-iron pan on the stove over high heat works. You won't get the same char, but the flavour will be there.
Best eaten straight off the heat with your flatmates and cold beers.
Food safety:

title: Suquet de Peix
summary: Catalan fisherman's stew of white fish and shellfish in a slow-cooked tomato and onion broth.

items.raw: 4 waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes

items.raw: 600 g firm white fish fillet (barramundi, snapper or bream), cut into chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or cazuela over a low-medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, for 15 to 20 minutes until very soft and golden. This is the sofregit, don't rush it. The onions should be almost jammy. Add the garlic and cook for another 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the crushed tomatoes and paprika. Cook gently for 5 minutes, letting the tomato meld with the sofregit base.
Add the potatoes and fish stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 12 to 15 minutes until the potatoes are almost tender.

Add the white fish chunks and mussels. Simmer gently for 4 minutes, then add the prawns. Cook for another 3 to 4 minutes until the fish is just opaque and cooked through, the mussels have opened, and the prawns are pink.
Discard any mussels that haven't opened. Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with fresh parsley. Serve with crusty bread to soak up the broth.

notes: Use the freshest white fish and seafood you can find, suquet is a stew that lets them shine.
The sofregit is the soul of this dish. Those 20 minutes of slow cooking transform the onions into something deep and essential.
Serve with aioli or toum on the side if you like, a dollop in each bowl is very Catalan.
Food safety:

title: Enchiladas Verdes
summary: Corn tortillas filled with chicken and cheese, smothered in green salsa and sour cream, then baked until golden.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180°C. Pour half the salsa verde into the bottom of a 20×30 cm baking dish.
In a bowl, mix the shredded chicken with 100 g of the tasty cheese and a pinch of salt.
Warm the tortillas briefly (so they don't crack when rolling): hold each one over a gas flame for a few seconds, or wrap them in a clean tea towel and microwave for 30 seconds.
Fill each tortilla with a generous spoonful of the chicken mixture and roll tightly. Lay seam-side down in the baking dish.
In a small bowl, stir the remaining salsa verde with the sour cream until smooth. Pour this mixture over the enchiladas, spreading it evenly.
Scatter the remaining cheese on top and bake for 20–25 minutes, until bubbling at the edges and the cheese is golden.
Let rest for 2 minutes. Top with spring onions and coriander if you like, then serve.

notes: Use a rotisserie chicken from Coles if you don't have cooked chicken on hand, shred the meat, skip the skin.
Salsa verde comes in jars in most supermarkets (Coles has it). If you can't find it, blend canned green tomatoes (tomatillos) with a jalapeño, coriander, and lime juice.
Make ahead: assemble the dish, cover with foil, and refrigerate up to 24 hours. Bake for an extra 5 minutes if cooking from cold.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Doro Wat
summary: Spiced chicken stew with hard-boiled eggs and niter kibbeh for Ethiopian Sunday feasts.

items.raw: 1.2 kg chicken thighs, bone-in, skin on, cut into large pieces
items.prep: bone-in, skin on, cut into large pieces

steps.text: Heat the niter kibbeh in a large pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onions and cook, stirring often, until they are very soft and golden, about 15 minutes. Do not let them brown too quickly.
Add the garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the berbere, fenugreek, chilli flakes and cardamom. Stir constantly for 2 minutes to toast the spices in the fat. The spices should smell warm and rich.
Add the chicken pieces and stir well so they are coated in the spice mixture. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is lightly coloured on the outside.
Pour in the water and stir. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and cook gently for 45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is cooked through and very tender.
Add the hard-boiled eggs, nestling them into the stew. Simmer uncovered for a further 15 minutes so the flavours meld. The sauce should be thick and rich. Taste and add salt as needed.
Serve hot with injera, spooning the stew onto the spongy bread so people can tear it and scoop the chicken, eggs and sauce together.

notes: Make niter kibbeh at home: melt 200g butter over low heat, add 1 tsp fenugreek seeds, ½ tsp cardamom pods, 2 cloves, 1 bay leaf and a pinch of ground turmeric. Let it infuse for 10 minutes, then strain through muslin into a jar and refrigerate.
Doro wat keeps well: store in the fridge for up to 3 days and reheat gently with a splash of water if needed.
For a thinner sauce, add more water and simmer a few minutes longer. Selam likes her stew thick enough to sit on the injera without running.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Tom Yum Pla
summary: Hot and sour fish soup with lemongrass, galangal and Thai herbs.

items.raw: 600 g firm white fish fillets, cut into 4 cm chunks (barramundi or snapper)
3 stalks lemongrass, white part only, cut into 3 cm pieces, bruised
items.prep: white part only, cut into 3 cm pieces, bruised

steps.text: Bring the stock to a simmer in a large pot. Add the lemongrass, galangal and whole chillies, and let it infuse for 5 minutes until fragrant.
Add the fish sauce, lime juice and palm sugar, and stir until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust the balance of heat, sour and salty to your liking.
Gently add the fish chunks and cherry tomatoes, and poach for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring very gently once halfway through, until the fish is cooked through and opaque.
Ladle into bowls and scatter fresh Thai basil and coriander over the top. Leave the lemongrass, galangal and chillies in the soup; people can push them aside as they eat.

notes: Make the stock infusion up to an hour ahead; the flavours only get better. Add the fish just before serving.
If you can't find fresh Thai basil, use regular basil, but add it at the last second so it doesn't wilt into the broth.
Barramundi is perfect here because it's sweet and holds its shape, but snapper, bream or any firm white fish works.
Food safety:

title: Zeytinyağlı Patlıcan Dolması
summary: Eggplant halves stuffed with rice, pine nuts and herbs, served cold with olive oil.

items.raw: 1 tsp Aleppo pepper, plus extra to serve
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 125 ml olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Working in batches, fry the eggplant halves skin-side down until golden and softened, about 6 minutes. Transfer to a plate and let cool. Using a small spoon, scoop out the flesh from the centre of each half, leaving a 1 cm border, and roughly chop the scooped flesh.

In the same pan, heat the remaining 125 ml olive oil over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until softened and lightly golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the chopped eggplant flesh to the pan and cook, stirring, for 3 minutes. Stir in the rice, pine nuts, currants, mint, parsley, cumin and Aleppo pepper. Cook, stirring, for 2 minutes until everything is combined and the rice is lightly toasted.
Season the rice mixture with salt and black pepper to taste. Divide evenly among the eggplant halves, pressing gently to fill. Arrange the stuffed eggplant in a baking dish, skin-side down.
Pour the water around (not over) the eggplant. Cover loosely with foil and bake at 180°C for 35 to 40 minutes, until the eggplant is very tender and the rice is cooked through.

Remove from the oven and let cool to room temperature. Transfer to a serving platter, drizzle with any pan juices, and serve at room temperature or chilled, scattered with extra Aleppo pepper and fresh mint if you like.

notes: Make these a day ahead and refrigerate, they taste better when the flavours have settled. Bring to room temperature before serving.
If you can't find Aleppo pepper, use a mix of smoked paprika and a pinch of chilli flakes.

title: Paksiw na Bangus
summary: Milkfish braised in vinegar and ginger with banana leaves until silky and tender.

items.raw: 1 whole milkfish (about 800 g), gutted and scaled

steps.text: Soften the banana leaves by holding them briefly over a flame or dipping them in hot water, then line a large heavy-based pot or casserole dish with them.
Lay the milkfish on the banana leaves and scatter the ginger, garlic, onion and chillies around it.
Pour the vinegar and water over the fish, season with salt, and fold the banana leaves loosely over the top to partially cover.
Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to low. Cover with a lid and braise for 35–45 minutes, until the fish is very tender and the flesh flakes away from the bones easily.
Carefully transfer the fish to a serving dish, spooning the braising liquid and soft ginger and onion over the top.
Serve hot with steamed rice and the pan juices on the side.

notes: Milkfish can be bony: eat slowly and you'll find most of the small bones soften in the vinegar. If you can't find it, use any firm white fish about the same size, barramundi or snapper work well.
Make ahead: braise to completion, cool in the liquid, and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat gently over low heat, covered.

title: Spaghetti with Fresh Sardines and Breadcrumbs
summary: Spaghetti with fresh sardines, garlic, breadcrumbs and parsley, simple, salty, deeply satisfying.

items.raw: 300 g fresh sardines, cleaned and gutted
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the spaghetti and cook until al dente, about 9 minutes.

While the pasta cooks, heat 30 ml of olive oil in a wide, shallow pan over medium heat. Add the breadcrumbs and toast, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Transfer to a small bowl.
In the same pan, heat the remaining 30 ml of olive oil over low heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, until soft and pale golden, about 2 minutes. Don't let it brown.
Add the whole fresh sardines to the pan with the garlic. Cook, turning gently once or twice, for about 3 minutes until just cooked through.
Drain the pasta, reserving about 200 ml of the cooking water. Add the pasta to the pan with the sardines.
Toss gently, adding enough of the reserved pasta water to create a light sauce that coats the spaghetti. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Transfer to a serving bowl. Scatter the toasted breadcrumbs over the top and finish with the fresh parsley. Drizzle with a little extra olive oil if you like.

notes: Very fresh sardines are essential here. If you can't find them, use fresh anchovies (alici) instead.
The pasta water is crucial, it helps emulsify the oil and coat the spaghetti properly.

title: Ika ni Lolo
summary: Fijian fish baked in coconut cream with onions and lime.

items.raw: 800 g firm white fish fillets, skin on
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C, then arrange the fish fillets, skin side down, in a baking dish large enough to hold them in a single layer. Season with salt and pepper.

Scatter the sliced brown onion over the fish. Pour the coconut cream and water around the fish, then squeeze the juice from the lime halves over the top. Season again lightly with salt and pepper. Cook until the fish is opaque and flakes easily and the onion is soft.
Bake, uncovered, for 25–30 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Scatter the chopped spring onion over the top and serve hot with the coconut broth spooned over. Serve with steamed rice and pickled onions on the side.

notes: Food safety:

title: Tori Soboro Don
summary: Chicken mince with scrambled egg over warm rice, cooked in one pan.

items.raw: 1 carrot, finely diced (or other leftover veg)

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large frying pan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the diced onion and carrot, and cook, stirring, until softened, about 3 minutes.
Add the garlic and ginger, stir for 30 seconds until fragrant, then crumble in the chicken mince. Cook, breaking it up with a spoon, until no longer pink, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the soy sauce, sugar, and mirin. Simmer for 1 minute to combine.

Push the chicken mixture to the sides of the pan, creating a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the well and scramble gently, stirring to break up the yolks. Once the egg starts to set, gently fold it into the chicken until cooked through, about 2–3 minutes.
Divide the warm rice among four bowls. Top each with the chicken and egg mixture, scatter with spring onion if using, and sprinkle with aonori if you've got it.

notes: Swap the carrot for peas, corn, or any cooked veg you have left over.
If you've got leftover cooked chicken, use 400 g and add it after the garlic and ginger, just heat through before the soy mixture.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Lawar
summary: Balinese ceremonial salad of finely minced cooked chicken with grated coconut, spice paste and rice flour.

items.raw: 400 g cooked chicken, finely minced or shredded
200 g fresh grated coconut (or desiccated coconut, rehydrated in warm water)
items.note: or desiccated coconut, rehydrated in warm water

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine the minced cooked chicken with the grated coconut.
Add the base genep and mix until the spice paste is evenly distributed through the chicken and coconut.
Sprinkle the rice flour over the mixture and fold it in gently to bind everything together without compacting it.
Add the spring onions and lime juice, then taste and season with salt.
Serve at room temperature, traditionally on a bed of banana leaf.

notes: This recipe uses cooked chicken for safe home cooking. Traditional lawar is made with raw poultry only when the cook has direct knowledge of the animal's health and handling.
Make base genep fresh if you can: blend together 4 shallots, 3 garlic cloves, 1 tbsp ginger, 1 tsp galangal, 1 tsp ground turmeric, 2–3 red chillies and 1 tbsp coconut oil.
Lawar is best served the same day it's made, on banana leaf if you have it.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.

title: Braised Brisket with Onions
summary: Low-and-slow braised brisket with soft onions and rich broth, the Shabbat classic.

items.raw: 4 large brown onions, sliced into thick rings

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the brisket dry with paper towels and season generously on both sides with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches if needed, brown the brisket on all sides until deep golden, about 3 minutes per side. Set the meat aside.
Add the sliced onions to the pot and cook, stirring, until they start to soften and caramelize, about 5 minutes. They don't need to be fully cooked, they'll finish in the oven.
Pour in the beef stock, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Return the brisket to the pot, nestling it into the onions. Add the bay leaves.
Cover the pot with a lid and transfer to the oven. Braise for about 3 hours, until the brisket is fork-tender and the meat shreds easily.
Remove from the oven and let the brisket rest in the braising liquid for 10 minutes. Slice against the grain and serve with the soft onions and braising liquid spooned over the top.

notes: Make this a day ahead, it reheats beautifully and tastes even better the next day.
Serve with egg noodles, boiled potatoes, or just good bread for soaking up the gravy.
Food safety:

title: Okra Stew
summary: Slow-simmered okra, tomatoes, and corn with andouille sausage, a weeknight Low Country staple.

items.raw: 400 g andouille sausage, sliced into 1 cm rounds
600 g okra, trimmed and cut into 2 cm pieces
items.prep: trimmed and cut into 2 cm pieces

items.raw: 200 g corn kernels (fresh, frozen, or tinned)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat your cast iron over medium-high heat. Brown the andouille slices, 3–4 minutes per side, until they've got a nice colour. Transfer to a plate.
Add the oil to the same pan. Sauté the onion until it's soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the okra and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 8 minutes. Don't fuss with it too much, you want it to brown slightly.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and their juice, then add the corn and chicken stock. Bring to a simmer until the stew is bubbling gently and starting to thicken.
Return the sausage to the pan. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, for 15–20 minutes, stirring gently now and then, until the okra is tender and the flavours have married.
Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve warm.

notes: Serve with rice, cornbread, or just a spoon and good company.
Tastes even better the next day, the flavours deepen as it sits.

title: Pelau
summary: One-pot rice, meat and pigeon peas with caramelised onions and fresh herbs, classic Trini comfort food.

items.raw: 500 g chicken thigh, cut into bite-sized pieces
2 green chillies, chopped (or 1 if you want less heat)
items.note: or 1 if you want less heat

items.raw: 1 cup pigeon peas (tinned or dried and cooked)
Salt and black pepper, to taste
1 lime, cut into wedges, to serve

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Sprinkle the caster sugar evenly across the base and let it sit without stirring for 2 to 3 minutes. Once it starts to brown at the edges, stir constantly until it's a deep golden brown, almost black, this is the burnt sugar that gives pelau its dark gravy, about 5 to 6 minutes total. It'll smell slightly burnt; that's right.

Working quickly, add the chicken pieces to the burnt sugar, stirring constantly to coat them. They'll sizzle and stick a little, that's fine. Cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes until the chicken is sealed on the outside.
Add the sliced onions and stir well, scraping up any stuck bits from the bottom of the pot. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes until the onions soften and start to caramelise.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and green chillies, and cook for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the ground cumin and ground coriander, stir, and cook for another minute.
Add the tomato paste and stir through, coating everything for about 1 minute. Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock, stirring to loosen any stuck bits. Add the thyme sprigs.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low. Cover and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside) and the liquid is starting to reduce.

Stir in the rice and pigeon peas, mixing well so the rice is submerged. Season with salt and black pepper to taste. Cover and simmer over low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is tender and has absorbed most of the liquid. If it looks dry but the rice isn't quite cooked, add a little more stock or water.
Remove from heat, let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff with a fork, sprinkle with fresh coriander, and serve with lime wedges on the side.

notes: Rohan likes his pelau hot; remove the green chillies before serving if your household prefers it milder.
Leftover pelau keeps in the fridge for 3 days and reheats beautifully on the stove with a splash of water.
You can swap the chicken for beef chuck or lamb shoulder for a different flavour, both work beautifully and need the full cooking time.
Food safety:

title: Minestra di Cicoria
summary: Bitter greens and beans in a simple garlic broth, a Calabrian nonna's kitchen staple.

items.raw: 400 g tin cannellini beans, drained and rinsed
500 g chicory (or dandelion greens), roughly chopped
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and cook, stirring gently, until golden and fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add the chopped greens and stir to coat in the oil. Cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they start to wilt.

Pour in the vegetable stock and bring to a simmer. Add the drained beans and stir gently. Simmer uncovered for 15–20 minutes, until the greens are completely tender and the broth has taken on their flavour.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. Serve hot with thick slices of crusty bread.

notes: Use any bitter greens on sale: dandelion, radicchio, or turnip tops all work beautifully.
The recipe doubles easily and tastes even better the next day as the flavours settle.

title: Aloo Posto
summary: Potatoes with poppy seed paste and nigella in mustard oil, a humble Bengali classic.

items.raw: 600 g waxy potato, cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a large pan over medium-high heat until it smokes lightly and settles, this takes about 1 minute. This is important; the oil must announce itself.
Add the nigella seeds and let them crackle for a few seconds until fragrant.
Add the potatoes and stir to coat in oil. Cook for 3–4 minutes until they begin to colour at the edges.
Sprinkle in the turmeric and stir well.
Add the green chilli and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8–10 minutes until the potatoes are three-quarters cooked and lightly golden.
Mix the poppy seed paste with 2 tbsp water to loosen it slightly. Add to the pan and stir to coat the potatoes evenly. If it seems dry, add another tablespoon of water.
Cook, stirring gently now and then, for 5–7 minutes until the potatoes are tender and the paste is no longer raw. The dish should be almost dry, with the potatoes well coated in the dark paste.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve warm, scattered with fresh coriander if you wish.

notes: This is best eaten hot or warm with rice. It keeps, covered, in the fridge for 2 days.
If you can only find white poppy seeds (which are less common), grind them to a paste with a little water; the result will be paler but still good.

title: Etli Lentil Stew
summary: Brown lentils simmered slowly with lamb and tomato, the kind of home stew that fills the taxi with nostalgia.

items.raw: 300 g lamb shoulder, cut into 2 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the lamb on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Set aside.
Add the diced onion to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Return the lamb to the pot and stir in the cumin. Cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tinned tomatoes, breaking them up with the back of a spoon, then pour in the stock and add the lentils. Stir well and bring to a simmer until the liquid is bubbling gently.
Reduce the heat to low, cover partially, and simmer for 50 minutes, stirring occasionally. The lentils should be very soft and starting to break down, and the lamb should be tender.
Season with salt and pepper to taste. If the stew is too thin, simmer uncovered for a few more minutes until it is thick and the lentils are soft. Serve hot.

notes: This stew reheats beautifully and tastes even better the next day. Keep in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Serve with crusty bread for soaking up the broth, or with plain white rice.
Food safety: Braised beef and lamb cook well past 75°C on the way to tender, so they are safe once soft.

title: Chicken and Sausage Gumbo
summary: Dark roux-based gumbo with andouille sausage, chicken and the holy trinity simmered until rich.

items.raw: 400 g andouille sausage, sliced into rounds
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Melt butter in a large heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add flour and stir constantly, scraping the bottom, until the roux turns deep chocolate brown, about 25–30 minutes. Don't rush it, burnt roux tastes bitter, so keep the heat medium and stay patient.
Add the diced onion, celery and capsicum to the roux. Stir and cook until the vegetables begin to soften, about 5 minutes, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom.
Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the andouille sausage and cook, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it releases its oil and the edges colour.
Add the chicken thighs and turn to coat in the roux. Cook for 2–3 minutes, then pour in the chicken stock. Add the bay leaves and thyme.
Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce heat to low. Simmer, partially covered, for 1 hour, stirring occasionally. The chicken should be very tender and the broth rich and dark.
