Remove from heat. Pull the chicken thighs from the pot, let cool slightly, shred the meat from the bones and return it to the pot. Discard the bay leaves.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper.
Serve over cooked white rice in wide bowls with a spoon and fork for the broth and meat.

notes: Make ahead: Gumbo tastes even better the next day. Cool completely, refrigerate for up to 3 days, and reheat gently on the stove.
The roux is the foundation, keep the heat medium and stir constantly. A dark roux (not burnt) gives the gumbo its signature flavour and colour.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Bandeja Paisa
summary: The legendary Medellín feast: beans, rice, meat, egg, arepa and chicharrón all on one plate.

items.raw: 400 g tin red kidney beans, drained and rinsed
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: For the beans: heat 1 tbsp oil in a pot over medium heat. Add the onion and garlic, and cook until soft, about 5 minutes. Add the drained beans and 200 ml water, bring to a simmer, and cook gently for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beans are creamy but still whole. Season with salt.

For the rice: heat 1 tbsp oil in a separate pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes until translucent at the edges. Pour in the stock, bring to a boil, then cover and reduce heat to low. Cook for 15–18 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed. Season with salt.

For the meat: heat 1 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the garlic and cumin, cook for 1 minute. Add the beef mince, breaking it up with a spoon, and cook until browned through, about 8–10 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Fry the eggs: in a separate pan, heat 2 tbsp oil over medium heat. Fry the eggs to your liking (typically over-easy or sunny-side up), about 4–5 minutes.
Warm the chicharrón and arepas gently while you finish the other components.

To serve: arrange each component on a large plate: a portion of beans on one side, rice on another, the seasoned mince, the fried egg, a piece of chicharrón, and a warm arepa. Garnish with fresh coriander if you like. Serve hot.

notes: Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Ají de Gallina
summary: Shredded chicken in a creamy ají amarillo and walnut sauce, served over boiled potatoes.

items.raw: 1 whole chicken, about 1.5 kg, or 800 g cooked chicken
items.prep: about 1.5 kg, or 800 g cooked chicken

items.raw: 2 ají amarillo peppers (or 2 tbsp ají amarillo paste)

steps.text: If using a whole chicken: bring a large pot of salted water to a boil with the halved onion and crushed garlic. Add the chicken and simmer until cooked through, about 35 minutes. Remove, let cool, then shred the meat, discarding skin and bones. If using cooked chicken, shred it; set aside. Reserve 200 ml of the cooking liquid, cooled, as your stock.
Make the ají paste: if using fresh ají amarillo peppers, remove the seeds and blend with 50 ml water until smooth. Sieve to remove the skin. (If using paste, use as is.)
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes until fragrant. Let cool, then grind finely in a food processor or mortar.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and ají paste, stirring constantly, for 2 minutes.
Add the shredded chicken and stir to coat. Pour in the chicken stock and evaporated milk, stirring well.
Stir in the ground walnuts and breadcrumbs. Simmer gently for 10 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce thickens and coats the back of a spoon. Season with salt.
Serve the ají de gallina over warm boiled potatoes, topped with a halved hard-boiled egg and an olive. Garnish with fresh coriander if you like.

notes: Make ahead: cook the chicken and prepare the ají paste the day before. Reheat gently before serving.
Use leftover roast or poached chicken to save time on a weeknight.
Fresh ají amarillo peppers are best, but bottled paste (found in Latin American shops) works perfectly well.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Grøntsager fra haven i smør og dild
summary: Summer vegetables braised in butter with fresh dill.

items.raw: 400 g carrots, cut into batons about 5 cm long
items.prep: cut into batons about 5 cm long

items.raw: 300 g kohlrabi, peeled and cut into batons about 5 cm long
items.prep: peeled and cut into batons about 5 cm long

items.raw: 250 g green beans, trimmed and halved
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Melt the butter in a large, wide pot or deep frying pan over medium heat.
Add the carrots and kohlrabi. Stir to coat in the butter, then pour in the water. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook for 12 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Add the green beans, stir well, and continue cooking for another 10 to 12 minutes, until all the vegetables are tender but still hold their shape and most of the liquid has reduced. The vegetables should be lightly glazed in buttery sauce.
Remove from the heat. Stir in the fresh dill, and the mustard if using. Taste and season with salt and pepper.
Serve warm, spooning the buttery cooking liquid over the vegetables.

notes: If kohlrabi is hard to find, use turnip or celeriac instead, cut the same way.
Lovely served alongside simply roasted chicken or with smørrebrød.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for two days.

title: Gulai Ubi Kayu
summary: Soft cassava in a rich, spiced coconut curry, comfort food made to stretch.

items.raw: 900 g cassava, peeled and cut into 5 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 5 cm chunks

items.raw: 3 dried chillies, or fewer for less heat

steps.text: Soak the dried chillies in hot water for 5 minutes until soft, then drain.
Grind the soaked chillies, shallot, garlic, ginger, turmeric and cumin seeds to a paste using a mortar and pestle or spice grinder, adding a little water if needed.
Heat the oil in a large pot or wok over medium heat. Fry the paste for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until fragrant and darkened slightly.
Add the cassava chunks and stir to coat with the paste, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and water. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to medium-low until the sauce is just bubbling at the edges.

Cook, uncovered, for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the cassava is completely tender and the sauce has thickened slightly. The cassava should break apart easily when tested with a fork.
Add the fish sauce and taste. Adjust salt and heat to your preference, remembering the chillies will have released their full flavour by now.
Simmer for another minute, until the sauce is thick and glossy and the cassava is tender, then serve hot with steamed rice.

notes: This gulai keeps well in the fridge for up to 3 days and tastes even better the next day as the spices settle.
Freeze it in portions, it thaws and reheats beautifully.
Use 2 dried chillies for mild heat, 4 for proper burn; it depends on the family eating it that night.

title: Pastilla aux Amandes
summary: Crispy phyllo pastry filled with spiced chicken, almonds and eggs, a festive Moroccan showstopper.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
Salt and black pepper, to taste
½ tsp ground cinnamon, for dusting

steps.text: Place the chicken breast, quartered onion, ginger, turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper in a large pot. Cover with water and bring to a simmer. Cook for 20 minutes until the chicken is cooked through. Remove the chicken, let it cool slightly, then shred the meat finely, discarding the skin. Chop the coriander and parsley and set aside.
Toast the almonds in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant. Add 2 tbsp oil, the cinnamon, sugar and salt. Cook, stirring, for 1 minute, then transfer to a plate to cool.
In a small non-stick frying pan, lightly beat the eggs with salt and pepper. Melt 30 g butter and scramble the eggs gently until soft and creamy, about 3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Preheat the oven to 180°C. In a bowl, gently toss the shredded chicken with the herbs.
Lay a sheet of filo on a clean work surface and brush lightly with melted butter. Layer a second sheet on top and brush again. This is your base, it will be half the pastilla.
Spread half the scrambled eggs in a rough rectangle on the lower half of the filo stack, leaving a 5 cm border. Top with half the chicken mixture, then half the almonds.
Fold the sides of the filo inward, then roll up tightly from the bottom, creating a tight cylinder. Place seam-side down on a baking tray and brush the top with melted butter.
Repeat steps 5 to 7 with the remaining filo, eggs, chicken and almonds to make a second pastilla.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastilla is deep golden brown and crisp.
Let rest for 2 minutes, then transfer to a serving plate. Dust generously with icing sugar and cinnamon at the table. Serve hot.

notes: Make ahead: assemble the pastilla up to 2 hours before baking and refrigerate, covered with cling film. Brush with melted butter just before baking.
The eggs must stay soft and creamy, don't cook them through. They'll cook gently in the oven.
Filo dries out quickly. Keep sheets under a damp tea towel until you use them.

Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Salsa de Pasilla Oaxaqueña
summary: Charred pasilla chilhuacle salsa ground on the molcajete, as it's made at Oaxacan market stalls.

items.raw: 6 dried pasilla chilhuacle chillies (chillies pasilla oaxaqueña)
1/2 tsp salt, plus more to taste

steps.text: Heat a heavy frying pan or comal over medium-low heat. Place the dried chillies in the pan and toast them, turning every 20 seconds, until fragrant and darkened but not blackened, about 4 to 5 minutes total. They should smell rich and earthy, almost like chocolate.
Remove the stems and most of the seeds from the cooled chillies, shaking out what comes loose. Leave a few seeds for heat.
In the same dry pan, toast the garlic cloves, turning occasionally, until lightly charred and soft, about 3 minutes.

Using a molcajete (lava rock mortar and pestle), grind the toasted chillies, garlic, and salt together in slow, circular motions. Work the pestle in a grinding motion until you reach a coarse paste, this takes patience, but the friction releases the true flavour. Stop when you reach your preferred texture; some like it smooth, some leave it rough.
Taste and add more salt if needed. If the salsa is too thick, stir in a few drops of water.

notes: This salsa keeps for up to a week in an airtight container in the fridge.
Don't rush the toasting, low heat brings out the deep, complex flavours that make this salsa special.

title: Frijoles Negros Refritos
summary: Slow-cooked black beans mashed smooth with garlic and oil for a creamy, intense side dish.

items.raw: 400 g tinned black beans, drained (or 200 g dried black beans, soaked overnight and cooked until tender)
items.note: or 200 g dried black beans, soaked overnight and cooked until tender

steps.text: Heat the oil in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and cook for 1 minute, stirring, until fragrant.
Add the drained beans to the pan, stirring to coat them in the oil and aromatics.

Mash the beans with the back of a wooden spoon or a potato masher as they warm, breaking down the cell walls gradually. This is the key, you're not trying to purée them all at once, but rather let the starch and pressure do the work over time.

Continue cooking and mashing over medium-low heat for about 8–10 minutes, adding splashes of water (or bean cooking liquid if you have it) as needed to reach a creamy, spreadable consistency. The beans should hold together but not be stiff.
Taste and season with salt and cumin if using. The beans are ready when they're smooth, glossy, and slightly darker in colour from the slow breakdown of their starches.

notes: Make ahead: cook dried beans the day before, or use quality tinned beans. Refried beans reheat beautifully on the stove with a splash of water.
The texture depends on mashing technique and cook time, not the fat. If they seem too thick after cooling, warm and stir in a little hot water.
Serve with warm tortillas, as part of breakfast, or alongside grilled vegetables.

title: Popiah
summary: Fresh spring rolls filled with turnip, shrimp and pork, Nyonya-style with sweet-savory dipping sauce.

items.raw: 200 g Chinese turnip (jicama), cut into thin matchsticks
Spring onion, cut into 2 cm pieces

steps.text: Blanch the turnip matchsticks in boiling salted water for 1 minute, then drain well and squeeze dry with a clean cloth. Set aside.
Heat the oil in a wok or large pan over high heat. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the pork mince and fry, breaking it up as it cooks, for 2 minutes until cooked through.
Stir in the chopped prawn and cook for 1 minute until just cooked and still tender.
Add the blanched turnip, oyster sauce, soy sauce and salt. Toss everything together for 1 minute, then remove from heat and let cool to room temperature.
While the filling cools, make the sauce: stir together the hoisin, sweet chilli sauce, lime juice, sesame oil and minced garlic. Set aside.
Lay one popiah skin flat on a clean surface. Spread a thin line of the filling across the middle, don't overfill. Top with a small handful of fresh coriander and a few pieces of spring onion.
Fold the two sides of the skin over the filling, then roll tightly from the bottom up, tucking in the sides as you go. Place seam-side down on a plate.
Repeat with the remaining skins and filling.
Arrange the popiah on a serving plate, sprinkle with crispy fried shallots, and serve with the sauce on the side for dipping.

notes: The filling can be made up to 4 hours ahead and kept in the fridge. Assemble the popiah just before serving so the skin stays soft.
Popiah are best eaten fresh, but you can wrap them tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for up to 2 hours. Don't freeze, the skin will crack when thawed.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Fischfrikadellen
summary: Pan-fried fish patties with potato and onion, Hamburg style, served with mustard.

steps.text: Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Cut the potato into chunks and cook until just tender, about 12 minutes. Drain and let cool slightly.
Meanwhile, check the fish for any fine bones and discard. Finely chop the onion.
Grate the cooled potato into a large bowl. Finely chop or pulse the fish in a food processor until roughly textured but not a paste, then add to the potato.
Add the onion, egg, breadcrumbs, mustard, salt and white pepper. Mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it.
Shape the mixture into 8 patties about 7 cm across and 1.5 cm thick. Rest for 5 minutes if time allows.

Heat a thin layer of oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. When hot, fry the patties in two batches, about 3–4 minutes each side, until golden and cooked through. Don't move them around; let them develop a good crust.
Serve warm with a dollop of Dijon mustard on the side or a squeeze of lemon.

notes: Make ahead: shape and refrigerate the patties up to 4 hours before frying.
Serve with a simple green salad or steamed beets, Hamburg style.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Flour Tortillas
summary: Soft, buttery handmade flour tortillas, warm off the griddle.

items.raw: 60 g lard, cut into small pieces

steps.text: Mix flour and salt in a large bowl. Add lard and rub it through the flour with your fingertips until it resembles breadcrumbs, about 3 minutes.
Add warm water a little at a time, mixing gently with one hand until a shaggy dough comes together. Don't overwork it.
Knead lightly on a bench for 2 to 3 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover with a damp cloth and rest for 15 minutes.
Divide dough into 8 equal pieces. Roll each into a smooth ball, then flatten with your palm to a disk about 4 cm thick.
Heat a griddle or heavy-based frying pan over medium-high heat until a drop of water sizzles immediately.
Working with one disk, use a rolling pin to roll it out to about 20 cm across and 3 mm thick. Dust with flour if it sticks.
Place the tortilla on the hot griddle. It should puff and brown lightly in spots in about 45 seconds. Flip and cook the other side for another 45 seconds until soft and spotted.
Transfer to a clean cloth to keep warm. Repeat with remaining dough. Serve warm, stacked and wrapped in the cloth.

notes: Make these up to 4 hours ahead and reheat wrapped in foil in a 180°C oven for 10 minutes.
The dough will keep in the fridge, covered, for up to 2 days. Bring to room temperature before rolling.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).

title: Fish Fragrant Pork Shreds
summary: Thinly sliced pork stir-fried with pickled chilies and bamboo shoots in fish-fragrant sauce.

items.raw: 400 g pork loin (or pork fillet), thinly sliced into shreds
150 g tinned bamboo shoots, drained and sliced
2 spring onion whites, finely chopped (save greens for garnish)

steps.text: Toss the pork shreds with soy sauce and cornflour in a bowl. Set aside for 10 minutes to coat evenly.

Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in a wok over high heat until smoking. Add the pork in a single layer and let it sit for 30 seconds to sear before stirring. Cook until just cooked through, about 2–3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.
Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil to the wok. Add the pickled chillies, doubanjiang, garlic, ginger and spring onion whites. Stir and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Return the pork to the wok with the bamboo shoots. Stir to combine.
Pour in the rice vinegar, caster sugar and chicken stock. Stir to coat everything evenly. Cook for 1–2 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly and coats the pork.
Drizzle with sesame oil and toss through. Garnish with spring onion greens and serve immediately with steamed white rice.

notes: Slice the pork thinly while it's cold, pop it in the freezer for 30 minutes first if it's hard to cut.
Pickled chilies are the soul of this dish. Look for them in a tin in the Asian aisle, not the fresh chilli section.
This reheats beautifully; store leftovers in the fridge and warm gently in a wok or pan with a splash of water.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Nasi Kuning
summary: Turmeric and coconut rice cooked slowly to absorb all the flavours.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the turmeric, cumin seeds, cloves, and cinnamon stick. Toast, stirring gently, for 2–3 minutes until the spices smell rich and the seeds start to pop.
Pour in the coconut milk and chicken stock, then add the lemongrass stalks. Stir well and bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is steaming and lightly bubbling and the kitchen smells fragrant.
Add the rinsed rice and salt. Stir once to combine, then reduce the heat to low. Cover with a tight-fitting lid.
Cook without lifting the lid for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is tender and all the liquid has been absorbed.
Remove from the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, discard the lemongrass stalks and cinnamon stick, then scatter spring onions over the top if you like.

notes: Make it ahead: cook the rice the morning before and reheat gently with a splash of water in a covered pot. The flavours deepen overnight.
Serve alongside rendang, grilled chicken, or slow-cooked beef, whatever you have time for.

title: Bánh Mì Chay
summary: Vietnamese vegetarian sandwich with crispy baguette, seasoned tofu, pickled vegetables and mayo.

items.raw: 400 g firm tofu, pressed for 20 minutes

steps.text: Make the pickled vegetables: combine carrot and daikon in a bowl. Heat rice vinegar, caster sugar and salt until warm and the sugar dissolves. Pour over the vegetables and set aside for at least 30 minutes.
Press the tofu between clean kitchen towels with a weight (a plate or two cans) for 20 minutes to remove excess moisture.

Cut the pressed tofu into 8 slices, about 1 cm thick. Combine soy sauce, sesame oil, minced garlic, caster sugar and black pepper in a shallow bowl. Turn the tofu slices gently to coat, then let sit for 10 minutes.

Heat 2 tbsp neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Working in two batches, fry the tofu slices until golden and crisp on both sides, about 3 minutes per side. Set aside on a paper towel.
Lightly toast the baguette halves in the same pan, cut-side down, until golden and warm, about 2 minutes.

Spread mayo on each baguette half. Layer the crispy tofu, pickled vegetables, fresh coriander, sliced green chillies and cucumber (if using). Press together gently, cut in half, and serve immediately.
If storing leftovers, keep the pickled vegetables and tofu separately from the assembled sandwiches and refrigerate for up to 1 day. The baguette is best eaten fresh.

notes: The pickled vegetables keep for up to 5 days in the fridge, so you can make them ahead.
Press the tofu well, this is what makes it absorb flavour and fry up crisp. If you skip this step, you will have a sad bánh mì.
Leftover fried tofu keeps in an airtight container for 2 days and can be reheated gently in a low oven.

title: Sukju Namul
summary: Mung bean sprout salad with toasted sesame and ginger, a Korean temple staple.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Add the bean sprouts and cook for 4 minutes, they should be tender but still have a slight bite. Drain well and spread on a clean kitchen towel to cool completely.
Toast the sesame seeds in a small dry pan over medium heat, stirring often, for 2 minutes until fragrant. Transfer to a mortar and pestle and crush lightly, leaving some seeds whole.
In a large bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, sesame oil and ginger. Add the cooled sprouts and toss gently to coat. Taste and adjust salt if needed.
Sprinkle the toasted sesame over the top just before serving.

notes: Sukju namul keeps in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. Add the sesame seeds just before serving so they stay crisp.
For a warmer dish, you can enjoy it at room temperature straight after dressing, or gently warm it in a pan with the sesame oil before serving.

title: Bánh Hỏi Nướng
summary: Charred grilled thin noodle cakes topped with prawns and crispy pork belly, dipped in tangy fish sauce vinegar.

items.raw: 250 g raw prawns, peeled and cleaned
150 g pork belly, thinly sliced (5 mm)

steps.text: Pour chicken stock into a saucepan and bring to a simmer. Add rice vermicelli and cook until just tender, about 3 minutes, stirring occasionally. The noodles will be soft and may break slightly, this is right. Drain in a fine sieve and spread on a tray to cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes.
While the noodles cool, make the dipping sauce: stir fish sauce, lime juice and sugar together in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Set aside.

Divide the cooled noodles into 8 equal portions. Take one portion and press it gently on an oiled piece of baking paper, forming a flat rectangle about 15 cm × 10 cm and roughly 1 cm thick. Do not press too hard or the cake will become dense. Repeat with the remaining noodle portions.
Heat a large grill pan or outdoor grill to medium-high heat until very hot and a drop of water sizzles on contact. Brush the grill grates lightly with oil.

Carefully transfer one noodle cake to the hot grill (start with the baking paper if using, then slide it away). Grill until the underside is golden and charred in patches, about 3–4 minutes. Flip carefully and grill the other side until golden and crispy, another 2–3 minutes. Transfer to a warm plate. Repeat with the remaining noodle cakes.

On the same grill or a separate pan at medium-high heat, grill the pork belly slices for 2–3 minutes per side until the fat has rendered and the edges are crisp and caramelised. The pork should be cooked through with no pink remaining. Transfer to a warm plate.
Grill the prawns over medium-high heat for 1–2 minutes per side until they are opaque throughout and have a light char. Transfer to a warm plate.

Arrange one noodle cake on each serving plate. Tear or arrange the grilled pork belly and prawns over the top. Garnish with fresh coriander if using and serve immediately with lime wedges and the fish sauce dipping sauce on the side.

notes: The noodle cakes can be formed up to 2 hours ahead; stack them between sheets of baking paper and refrigerate. Grill straight from the fridge, adding 1–2 minutes per side.
If your grill pan is small, grill the components in batches and keep them warm on a plate in a low oven (120°C) while you finish cooking.
The pork belly will spit as the fat renders, keep the heat steady and watch closely after the 2-minute mark to avoid burning.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Tahchin
summary: Jewelled rice cake with chicken and yoghurt, flipped to show the golden crust.

items.raw: 1 tsp saffron threads, steeped in 60 ml warm water
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add rice and cook until just tender, about 12 minutes. Drain well.
While rice cooks, whisk together yoghurt, egg yolks, and half the saffron water (about 30 ml). Season generously with salt and pepper.
In a bowl, gently fold the drained rice, shredded chicken, pistachios, cranberries and raisins into the yoghurt mixture until everything is evenly coated.
Heat oil in a 25 cm non-stick or cast iron pan over medium-high heat until shimmering. Spread the rice mixture evenly in the pan, gently pressing it down with the back of a spoon to help form a cake.
Reduce heat to medium. Cook, undisturbed, until the bottom is deeply golden and crispy, 25–30 minutes. Listen for gentle crackling sounds; that's the tahdig forming.
Pour the remaining warm saffron water over the top. Place a large plate over the pan, then flip quickly and confidently. The tahchin should slide onto the plate, crust-side up.
Let rest 5 minutes. Garnish with a few extra pistachios and dried fruit if you like. Serve warm.

notes: The crust is everything. Don't rush it, you want deep gold, not pale. If it's not crackling by minute 25, turn heat up slightly.
Use day-old cooked chicken if you have it; rotisserie works perfectly. The yoghurt binds everything and keeps the rice from drying out.
Make ahead: prepare the rice and yoghurt mixture up to 4 hours in advance. Cook in the pan just before serving.

title: Appam with Stew
summary: Soft, fermented rice pancakes with mild coconut chicken stew, a weekend breakfast.

items.raw: 500 g chicken breast, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.text: To make appam, soak the rice in water for 30 minutes, then drain well. Grind with the coconut to a smooth, thick batter (it should hold together but be pourable). Stir in the sugar, salt and yeast. Cover and leave to ferment at room temperature for 8 hours or overnight until the batter rises and becomes foamy.
For the stew, heat the coconut oil in a pan over medium heat. Fry the onion, stirring, until it's soft and lightly golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger and curry leaves, and stir until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add the turmeric and stir through.
Add the chicken pieces and cook, stirring occasionally, for 4–5 minutes until they're pale on the outside.
Pour in the coconut milk and water, add the green chilli, and bring to a simmer. Cook gently, uncovered, for 12–15 minutes until the chicken is cooked through. Season with salt.
About 20 minutes before serving, heat your appam pan (or a shallow non-stick pan with a lid) over medium-high heat. Lightly oil the pan.
Stir the fermented batter gently. Pour about 80 ml into the centre of the appam pan and tilt it in a circular motion to spread the batter thin and even. Cover with the lid.
Cook for 2–3 minutes until the edges are set and crispy and the base is golden, then slide onto a plate. Repeat with the remaining batter.
Serve the appam warm with the chicken stew alongside for dipping.

notes: The batter must ferment 8 hours or overnight, start the day before.
If you don't have an appam pan, use a shallow non-stick frying pan with a lid; the pancakes will be less lacy but still delicious.
The stew can be made up to 2 days ahead and warmed through before serving.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Txuleta de Buey
summary: Massive grilled beef chop, salt and pepper only. The meat speaks for itself.

items.raw: 800 g beef rib eye steak, bone in, 4 cm thick
Black pepper, freshly ground, to taste

steps.text: Take the txuleta out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it comes to room temperature.
Get your grill smoking hot, charcoal if you can, or a cast-iron griddle over high heat if you can't.
Pat the meat dry. Season both sides generously with salt when it hits the grill, which should be smoking hot so the meat sizzles on contact.
Grill for 5–6 minutes on the first side without moving it. You want a dark crust.
Flip once. Grill for another 4–5 minutes for medium-rare (around 52°C inside). A thick chop like this needs time; don't rush it.
Rest on a warm plate for 3–4 minutes. Crack pepper over the top and serve.

notes: Use the best beef you can find, this dish lives or dies by the meat. Ask your butcher for a thick-cut rib eye on the bone, minimum 4 cm.
A txuleta is not about technique. It's about respecting good meat and not mucking it about.
Food safety:

title: Jerk Chicken
summary: Jamaican chicken marinated in spiced jerk seasoning, then charred until sticky and smoking.

items.raw: 2 Scotch bonnet chillies, roughly chopped (seeds removed for less heat, optional)
3 cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and roughly chopped
1.2 kg chicken pieces (thigh and drumstick), skin on

steps.text: Blend the spring onions, Scotch bonnets, garlic, ginger, thyme, allspice, black pepper, salt, olive oil, soy sauce and lime juice in a food processor until you have a thick, textured paste. Taste it, it should make you sit up straight.

Rub the jerk paste all over the chicken, working it into the skin and under any flaps you can lift. Put the chicken in a bowl, cover, and refrigerate overnight (or at least 6 hours, though overnight is better).
Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it comes to room temperature.
Heat a large cast-iron or heavy-based pan over medium-high heat until it's very hot, or preheat your grill to high. Lightly oil the pan or grill grates.
Working in batches if needed so you don't crowd the pan, place the chicken skin-side down. Don't move it for 6–8 minutes until the skin is charred and sticky. You want some blackened edges.

Turn the chicken and cook for another 8–10 minutes on the other side until cooked through (the thickest part of the thigh should reach 75°C inside, or the juices run clear when pierced with a knife). If the outside is colouring too fast, lower the heat slightly.
Rest the chicken for 5 minutes, then serve hot with rice and peas, or with a simple salad and lime wedges.

notes: The marinade also works on pork shoulder, beef or cauliflower. Cook times will vary.
If you don't have time to marinate overnight, 4 hours is the minimum, but the flavour won't be as deep.
Food safety:

title: Khichdi
summary: Buttery rice and lentil comfort dish with seasonal vegetables and tempered asafoetida.

items.raw: 100 g split yellow moong dal (mung beans)
150 g mixed vegetables (peas, diced potato or zucchini)

steps.text: Rinse the rice and moong dal together under cold water until the water runs clear.
Heat the ghee in a large saucepan over a medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and dried red chilli, and let them crackle for about 30 seconds.
Add the asafoetida and stir for a few seconds until fragrant, then add the rinsed rice and dal, stirring to coat in the ghee for about 2 minutes.
Add the turmeric and salt, stir, then add the water and bring to a boil until the water is bubbling steadily.
Add the diced carrot and other vegetables, stir well, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid and cook for about 12–15 minutes, until the rice and dal are tender and the water is absorbed.
Stir through gently with a fork to fluff, taste and adjust the salt if needed. Serve hot.

notes: Serve with Greek yoghurt, a squeeze of lemon, and sliced fresh chilli on the side.
Make ahead: Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water, or in the microwave covered with a damp paper towel.

title: Ispanakli Borek
summary: Layered yufka pie with spinach, feta and pine nuts, baked until crispy.

items.raw: 500 g frozen spinach, thawed and squeezed dry
40 ml neutral oil, plus extra for the pan
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Toast the pine nuts in a dry frying pan over medium heat, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Heat 20 ml of the oil in the same pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more. Tip in the spinach and stir to combine. Cook for 2 minutes, then remove from the heat. Stir in the feta and toasted pine nuts. Season with salt and pepper, then let cool slightly.
Preheat the oven to 200°C. Brush a 22 cm × 32 cm baking tray with a little oil.

Lay one yufka sheet on the tray. Brush lightly with oil (you'll use about 1 tsp per sheet). Repeat with two more sheets, brushing each lightly. Spread half the spinach filling evenly over the third sheet.
Layer three more yufka sheets on top, brushing each lightly with oil as you go. Spread the remaining spinach filling over the top sheet.
Top with the final yufka sheet, brush lightly with oil, and press gently to seal. Score into 12 squares with a sharp knife, cutting three-quarters of the way through the layers.
Bake for 25–30 minutes, until the top is golden and crispy. Let rest for 5 minutes, then cut along the scored lines and serve hot or warm.

notes: Make ahead: Prepare the filling a day ahead and refrigerate. Assemble and bake just before serving for crispy yufka.
Swap: If you can't find yufka, use filo pastry, but yufka's thicker and won't tear as easily.

title: Ojja
summary: Spicy merguez sausage with peppers, tomatoes and runny eggs.

items.raw: 2 merguez sausages, cut into thick rounds
1 red capsicum, cut into thick strips

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, shallow pan over medium-high heat. Add the merguez rounds and cook until browned on both sides, about 4 minutes, then set aside on a plate.
In the same pan, add the capsicum and onion. Cook, stirring, until softened and just starting to caramelize, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the harissa and tomato paste, cooking for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and return the merguez to the pan. Stir to combine, then simmer for 3–4 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly.
Make two small wells in the sauce and crack an egg into each. Cover the pan and cook until the whites are set but the yolks are still runny, about 3 minutes.
Season with salt to taste and serve straight from the pan.

notes: Use a good, spicy harissa here, it's not a garnish, it's the whole point.
Make sure the eggs go into a shallow pan so the yolks stay runny while the whites cook through.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Fa'alifu Talo
summary: Taro and coconut cream baked in banana leaves, creamy and comforting.

items.raw: 1 kg taro, peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks
items.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm chunks

steps.text: Preheat oven to 180°C. Prepare banana leaves by briefly wiping with a damp cloth and cutting into 30 cm squares, you'll need about 6 pieces.
In a bowl, combine taro chunks, sliced onion, salt and white pepper. Divide the mixture among the banana leaf squares, spooning about 150 ml coconut cream over each portion.
Fold the banana leaves over the filling to make neat parcels, tucking the edges underneath. Place seam-side down on a large baking tray.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until the taro is very tender when pierced with a fork and the coconut cream is bubbling gently at the edges.
Remove from oven and let rest for 5 minutes. Unwrap carefully, the steam inside is very hot, and serve straight from the banana leaf.

notes: Fa'ausi keeps in the fridge for 2 days and reheats gently in a covered dish at 160°C for 15 minutes.
You can prep the parcels several hours ahead and refrigerate them before baking, add 10 minutes to the cooking time.

title: Dakjim
summary: Braised chicken in soy and ginger, sticky and tender.

items.raw: 8 bone-in chicken thighs (about 1 kg), skin on
1 brown onion, cut into thick wedges
2 spring onions, cut into 4 cm lengths

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan or shallow braising pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches to avoid crowding, cook the chicken skin-side down until golden and the fat has rendered, about 5 minutes. Flip and cook for another 2 minutes, then remove to a plate.
Drain off all but 1 tbsp of fat from the pan. Add the onion and ginger, and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds.

Return the chicken to the pan, skin-side up. Pour in the soy sauce, sugar and mirin, then add just enough water to half-cover the chicken. Bring to a simmer, cover and braise for 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (75°C inside).

Remove the lid, increase the heat to medium and cook until the liquid reduces to a glossy glaze and coats the chicken, about 3–4 minutes. Stir in the spring onions and sesame oil, and cook for 1 minute more. Serve hot.
Serve with steamed rice to catch every drop of sauce.

notes: Make it ahead: cool and refrigerate for up to 2 days, then reheat gently on the stove with a splash of water if the glaze has set. The flavours deepen overnight.
No mirin? Use 1 tbsp more caster sugar instead, though you'll lose a bit of the subtle sweetness.
Serve with steamed rice or over kimchi and rice for something richer.
Food safety:

title: Chimichurri Verde
summary: Inés's herbaceous chimichurri with parsley, garlic and vinegar, done the proper Argentine way.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Finely chop the parsley, not in a food processor, by hand with a sharp knife. This matters.
Mince the garlic very fine; Inés says you should be able to see each piece.
In a bowl, combine the parsley, garlic, and red wine vinegar. Let it sit for 2 minutes so the vinegar softens the parsley.
Slowly pour in the olive oil while stirring until the sauce is glossy and just slightly emulsified, so it stays bright and fresh, not heavy.
Taste and season with salt and black pepper. If you like, add the oregano and chilli flakes, but Inés says this is between you and your conscience.
Let it rest for at least 10 minutes before serving so the flavours marry. Serve at room temperature with grilled meat, bread, or anything that needs the taste of home.

notes: Chimichurri lasts 3 days in an airtight jar in the fridge, though the parsley will darken slightly.
Make it fresh the day you need it if you can. Inés never makes it more than a few hours ahead.
Serve with grilled beef, chicken, or even crusty bread, it's not just for meat, though that's what Inés says it's for.

title: Simit
summary: Chewy sesame-crusted bread ring, Istanbul street-food gold.

image.credit: Photo: Ana Caroline  Mendes Mathias / Pexels

steps.text: In a large bowl, combine bread flour, salt, caster sugar and instant dried yeast. Make a well in the centre and add olive oil and warm water. Mix with your hand until a shaggy dough forms, about 3 minutes.

Knead on a lightly oiled bench for 10 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic. Shape into a ball, oil the bowl lightly, return the dough, cover with plastic wrap and let it rise at room temperature for 1 hour until doubled.
Turn the dough out onto a lightly oiled bench and divide into 8 equal pieces. Roll each piece into a rope about 30 cm long and 2 cm thick, keeping the thickness even.
Form each rope into a ring by wrapping one end around the other and pressing the seam firmly to seal. Place on a baking tray lined with baking paper, cover loosely, and let rise for 30 minutes.
While the rings rise, preheat the oven to 220°C. Pour sesame seeds into a shallow bowl. In another shallow bowl, stir molasses and water together until the molasses dissolves.

Working with one ring at a time, dip the top half into the molasses mixture, then immediately dip it into the sesame seeds, pressing gently so they stick. Place back on the tray seeded-side up. Repeat with remaining rings.
Bake at 220°C for 20–25 minutes until golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped on the base. The sesame should be lightly toasted and adhered firmly.
Transfer to a wire rack to cool for a few minutes. Simit are best eaten warm with Turkish tea or cheese.

notes: Make ahead: shape the rings, let them rise, then freeze for up to 3 weeks. Bake directly from frozen, adding 5 minutes to the bake time.
The molasses dip is key, it makes the sesame stick like glue. Don't skip it or use water alone.

title: Taro Dalo ni Lolo
summary: Taro root baked soft and creamy in coconut milk with onions

items.raw: 1 kg dalo (taro), peeled and cut into 4 cm pieces
items.prep: peeled and cut into 4 cm pieces

items.raw: 1 large brown onion, cut into wedges
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Preheat your oven to 180°C. Arrange the dalo pieces and onion wedges in a baking dish, spreading them out in a single layer.
Pour the coconut milk and water into a jug, add the salt and stir well to combine. Pour this mixture over the dalo and onions.
Cover the baking dish tightly with foil and place in the oven. Bake for 40 to 45 minutes, until the dalo is very soft and you can easily pierce a piece with a fork.
Remove from the oven and let rest for 5 minutes. Season with freshly ground black pepper to taste. Serve warm in shallow bowls with the creamy coconut sauce spooned over.

notes: If you can't find taro root, use potato or yam, either works well and cooks in about the same time.
This dish is even better the next day: cover and store in the fridge, then reheat gently in a 160°C oven for 15 minutes with a splash of water.

title: Tagine de Poisson aux Olives et Citron
summary: Sea bream or white fish braised with green olives, preserved lemon and gentle spices in a Moroccan tagine.

items.raw: 800 g white fish fillets (sea bream, snapper or barramundi)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in a large tagine or heavy-based pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring gently, until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic, ginger, turmeric and cinnamon. Stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the stock and bring to a gentle simmer until the liquid is bubbling lightly. Add the preserved lemon and olives, and season lightly with salt and pepper.
Nestle the fish fillets into the liquid, skin-side up if they have skin. Simmer gently for 12–15 minutes, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily when tested with a fork.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Scatter with fresh coriander if you like, and serve straight from the tagine with couscous or crusty bread.

notes: A tagine pot keeps the braise gentle and even, but a wide shallow pan works just as well.
This is equally good made a few hours ahead and gently reheated before serving.
Food safety:

title: Andouillette à la moutarde
summary: Chitterling sausage with a silky Dijon mustard and cream sauce.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed frying pan over medium-high heat. When it shimmers, add the andouillettes and fry for 3–4 minutes on each side until the skin is deep golden and crispy. They should smell wonderful. Transfer to a plate and keep warm.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium. Add the shallot and cook, stirring, until soft and just starting to colour, about 2 minutes.
Pour in the white wine and use a wooden spoon to scrape up the fond stuck to the bottom of the pan. Let it bubble and reduce by half, about 3 minutes.
Add the chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Let it reduce gently for about 5 minutes to concentrate the flavour.

Whisk the Dijon mustard into the cream in a small bowl until smooth. Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the mustard cream. Add the butter and stir until it melts. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Slide the andouillettes back into the sauce, turn to coat them, and warm through for 2 minutes over low heat. Do not boil, or the cream will split.
Serve immediately on warm plates with the sauce spooned over and around the sausages.

notes: Andouillettes are sold fresh at good butchers and some French delis. If you can't find them, they're not worth substituting, save this recipe for when you do.
The success of the dish depends on getting the sausage skin crispy in the pan. Don't crowd them, and don't fidget with them while they cook.
Serve with mustard-roasted potatoes or a simple green salad to cut through the richness.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety:

title: Egg Noodles and Caramelized Cabbage
summary: Tender egg noodles with soft, golden caramelized cabbage and crispy onions, ready in 30 minutes.

items.raw: 1 small head green cabbage (about 600 g), sliced into thin ribbons
2 brown onions, sliced into thin rings
Salt and black pepper, to taste
Fried shallots (or crispy fried onions), to serve (optional)

steps.text: Cook the egg noodles in salted boiling water until tender, about 8 minutes. Drain well and set aside.

While the noodles cook, melt the butter in a large heavy-bottomed pan over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and cook, stirring often, until they're soft and deeply golden, about 12 minutes. This is where the flavour happens, don't rush it.
Add the sliced cabbage to the pan with the caramelized onions. Stir to coat with butter. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the cabbage is very soft and golden at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Tip the cooked noodles into the pan with the cabbage and onions. Toss everything together until well combined. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Divide among bowls and top with crispy fried onions or fried shallots if you like the crunch, they're optional, but they add something special.

title: Dashimaki Tamago
summary: Savoury dashi-seasoned rolled egg omelette, a bento essential.

items.raw: 60 ml dashi (or 1 tsp instant dashi powder mixed with 60 ml water)
items.note: or 1 tsp instant dashi powder mixed with 60 ml water

steps.text: Whisk the eggs in a bowl until well combined, then stir in the dashi, mirin and salt until smooth. Strain through a fine sieve into another bowl to remove any chalky bits.

Heat a rectangular tamagoyaki pan (or a 20 cm non-stick frying pan) over medium heat. Lightly oil it, then pour in about a quarter of the egg mixture. Tilt the pan to spread it into a thin, even layer, and cook until the top is just set but still shiny, about 1 minute.
Using chopsticks or a spatula, fold the cooked egg layer in half from one end. Push the rolled egg to one side of the pan.
Oil the empty part of the pan. Pour in another quarter of the egg mixture, tilting it to spread under and around the existing roll. Cook until just set, about 1 minute.
Fold this new layer over the roll, creating a thicker log. Push it aside and repeat with the remaining egg mixture in two more layers, rolling and folding each time.
Transfer the rolled omelette to a cutting board and let it cool for 2 minutes. Slice into 8 pieces with a damp sharp knife and serve with a drizzle of soy sauce, or pack into bento.

notes: Make ahead: cook the dashimaki tamago the night before, wrap in cling film and refrigerate. It's fine cold or at room temperature.
No tamagoyaki pan? A regular non-stick frying pan works, but you'll get a circular roll instead of rectangular slices.
If you can't find instant dashi, use 60 ml water mixed with a tiny pinch of salt and bonito flakes instead.
Food safety: The eggs are cooked until just set. For pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system, cook them until firm all the way through.

title: Thai Green Curry with Prawns and Beans
summary: Creamy green curry with prawns and beans, ready in 20 minutes from frozen.

items.raw: Fresh Thai basil (or coriander), to serve (optional)

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp coconut milk in a large pan over medium-high heat. Stir in the curry paste and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Pour in the remaining coconut milk and stock, stirring to combine. Bring to a simmer until the curry is bubbling gently and fragrant.
Add the green beans and cook for 5 minutes until just tender.
Add the frozen prawns and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3–4 minutes until they're pink and cooked through.
Stir in the fish sauce, lime juice and sugar. Taste and adjust the seasoning, add more fish sauce or lime to taste.
Serve over steamed jasmine rice with fresh Thai basil or coriander if you have it.

notes: Swap the green beans for whatever green veg you have: broccolini, bok choy, snap peas or zucchini all work.
Use fresh prawns if you have them, they'll cook in about 2 minutes instead of 3–4.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Cơm Hến
summary: Rice with tiny clams and crispy fried shallots, a humble Huế comfort dish with serious flavour.

items.raw: 400 g littleneck clams (or hến if you can find them)
items.note: or hến if you can find them

items.raw: 2 cups white rice, cooked and cooled

steps.text: Heat 3 tbsp neutral oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the shallots and fry, stirring often, until deeply golden and crispy, about 8 minutes. Transfer to paper towel with a pinch of salt.

In a large pan over high heat, add 2 tbsp neutral oil and half the garlic. Cook for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the clams and cover. Cook, shaking the pan occasionally, until all clams open, about 8 minutes. Discard any that don't open.
Remove clams from their shells and set aside. Strain the cooking liquid through a fine sieve into a bowl.

In the same pan, add the remaining garlic and cook for 30 seconds. Add the cooked rice, fish sauce, salt, and black pepper. Stir-fry until the rice is hot and just starting to crisp at the bottom, about 3 minutes.
Add the clams back to the rice with 3 tbsp of their cooking liquid. Toss gently to combine.
Divide between two bowls. Top with crispy shallots, sliced red chilli, spring onion, and fresh coriander. Serve hot.

notes: Cook and cool the rice ahead, leftover rice works best. You want it cold and separate so it fries properly.
If clams are very sandy, soak them in salted water for 30 minutes before cooking to help them expel grit.
Fried shallots can be made several hours ahead and stored in an airtight container.

Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through. Throw away any mussels or clams whose shells stay closed after cooking. Cool any leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it within an hour; reheat it until steaming hot.

title: Sayur Asem
summary: Sour vegetable soup with tamarind, peanuts and galangal, cheap, filling, and tastes even better the next day.

items.raw: 200 g green beans, cut into 5 cm pieces
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add shallots, garlic and galangal, stirring until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Stir in tamarind paste and cook for 1 minute, then pour in stock and bring to a boil.
Add pumpkin and green beans. Simmer for 10 minutes until the pumpkin starts to soften.
Add corn kernels and peanuts. Simmer for another 8 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the peanuts have softened and flavoured the broth.
Tear in makrut lime leaves and season to taste with salt and pepper. If using chilli, add now.
Taste and adjust the sourness (add more tamarind if needed) or salt. Serve hot.

notes: Make a double batch, it tastes better the next day when the flavours have settled. Keeps in the fridge for 3 days.
Don't have makrut lime leaves? A squeeze of fresh lime juice works, but the leaves are worth hunting for.
Use whatever vegetables are cheap at the market: zucchini, cabbage, or even frozen mixed vegetables all work.

title: Pappardelle al Ragù di Maiale
summary: Wide ribbon pasta with slow-cooked wild boar ragù, rustic Tuscan comfort.

items.raw: 600 g pork shoulder, cut into rough chunks
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the pork on all sides, don't crowd the pan. Set aside, about 10 minutes total.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the carrot, celery and onion to the same pot and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 12 minutes. This is your soffritto; don't skip it.
Return the pork to the pot. Pour in the wine and let it bubble away, scraping up the brown bits, about 2 minutes. Add the tomatoes, stock and bay leaves. Stir.
Bring to a gentle simmer. Partially cover and cook for 3 hours, stirring occasionally. The ragù is done when the meat falls apart and the sauce is thick and dark. Season with salt and pepper.
Twenty minutes before serving, bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the pappardelle until al dente, about 3 minutes for fresh pasta. Reserve a cup of pasta water.
Drain the pappardelle and add directly to the ragù. Toss, adding pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce coats the ribbon. Serve with grated Parmesan.

notes: Make the ragù the day before and reheat gently. It improves overnight.
If you can't find pork shoulder, beef chuck works just as well.
Cook pork until it reaches at least 70°C in the thickest part (75°C for mince and sausages).
Food safety:

title: Dolma Garaz
summary: Grape leaves stuffed with spiced meat and rice, served with tomato and yoghurt.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Stir in the mince and cook, breaking it up with the spoon, until browned, about 6–8 minutes. Drain off any excess fat.
Stir the rice, cumin, coriander, cinnamon, cayenne, salt and pepper into the mince. Cook, stirring, for 2 minutes. Remove from heat and let cool slightly.

Lay a grape leaf shiny side down on a clean work surface. Place about 1 tbsp of filling near the base of the leaf. Fold the bottom edge over the filling, then fold in the sides and roll tightly away from you. Repeat with the remaining leaves and filling. You should have about 20 dolma.

Wipe out the pan and add the remaining 1 tbsp oil. Working in two batches, arrange the dolma seam side down in the pan and cook, without stirring, until lightly golden on the bottom, about 2 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate.

Return all the dolma to the pan, seam side down. Pour the tomatoes and stock over them. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then reduce to low. Cover and cook gently for 30 minutes, until the rice is tender and the sauce has thickened slightly.
Transfer the dolma to a serving plate and spoon the warm sauce over them. Serve with Greek yoghurt on the side.

notes: Make ahead: prepare the dolma up to the end of step 3, then cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours before cooking.
Swap the beef for lamb mince for a richer flavour, which some prefer.
Cook mince and sausages until they reach 75°C in the centre, with no pink left.
Food safety:

title: Seekh Kebab
summary: Charred minced meat kebabs with onions and spices, griddled until juicy.

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Put the mince in a bowl with the minced onion, garlic, ginger and green chilli. Add the cumin, coriander, garam masala and chilli powder. Crack in the egg, season with salt and pepper, and mix gently with your hands until just combined, don't overwork it or the kebabs will be tough.

Wet your hands with water and divide the mixture into 8 equal portions. Mould each portion around a metal skewer (or flat wooden skewer soaked in water), pressing gently to form a long, even kebab about 15 cm long.

Heat the oil in a large frying pan or griddle over medium-high heat until it's smoking. Working in batches if needed, lay the kebabs in the pan and cook without moving them for 2–3 minutes until darkly charred on the bottom.
Turn the kebabs and cook the other side for another 2–3 minutes until charred and cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
Serve hot with lime wedges and fresh coriander.

notes: Make ahead: form the kebabs up to 2 hours ahead and keep in the fridge covered.
Swap: lamb mince works beautifully here, use the same amount and follow the same method.
Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C.

title: Adobong Gata
summary: Creamy coconut chicken adobo, slow-cooked with vinegar and spices.

items.raw: 1.2 kg chicken thigh, bone-in, cut into 4 cm pieces

steps.text: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Working in two batches, brown the chicken pieces on all sides until golden, about 3 minutes per batch. Set aside.
In the same pot, add the crushed garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Pour in the vinegar and scrape up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Let it simmer for 2 minutes.
Return the chicken to the pot. Add the turmeric, peppercorns and bay leaves. Stir well to coat the chicken.

Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook over low heat, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is very tender and the sauce is creamy and reduced, about 35 to 40 minutes.
Taste and add more salt if needed. The adobo should be rich, slightly sweet, sour and savory all at once. Serve hot with steamed white rice.

notes: This adobo keeps well in the fridge for 3 days. The flavour deepens overnight.
For a less rich version, use light coconut milk instead of full-fat.
Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Farofa de Linguiça
summary: Toasted cassava flour with sausage and egg, crispy and golden.

items.raw: 200 g linguiça sausage (or Italian sausage), finely diced
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the diced linguiça until the fat renders and it's golden, about 5 minutes. Push to the side and add the diced onion, cooking until soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the minced garlic and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Push everything to the side of the pan. Crack the eggs into the empty space and scramble gently until just cooked through, then stir everything together, about 2 minutes.
Add the cassava flour in three stages, stirring well after each addition to avoid lumps. Let it toast between each addition, about 2 minutes per stage. It should be golden and smell nutty.
Stir through the spring onion and fresh coriander. Taste and season with salt and pepper. Serve warm, this is best eaten straight from the pan at a churrasco.

notes: Make it ahead: Toast the farofa in bulk and store it in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Warm it in a dry pan before serving.
Swap the sausage for bacon, chorizo, or diced leftover churrasco meat.
Serve with grilled meat, rice and beans, this is the trifecta of a proper churrasco plate.

Food safety: Cook mince and sausages until no pink remains and the centre reaches 75°C. Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Tarte Tatin aux pommes de Tasmanie
summary: Caramelised Tasmanian apple tart with butter, vanilla and puff pastry.

items.raw: 8 medium Tasmanian apples (about 1.2 kg), peeled, cored and halved

steps.text: Heat your oven to 200°C. Have a 25 cm ovenproof frying pan ready.

Sprinkle the caster sugar evenly over the base of the pan. Place over medium heat and watch as it begins to melt at the edges. Resist the urge to stir; instead, tilt the pan gently so the unmelted sugar slides into the liquid. When all the sugar has dissolved and turned a deep amber, about 8 minutes, remove from heat. It should smell like caramel, nutty and rich.
Working quickly, dot the 60 g butter over the caramel in small pieces. Stir in the vanilla extract.

Arrange the apple halves cut-side up in concentric circles, starting at the outside and working towards the centre. They will fit snugly and overlap slightly. The apples will release their juice and seem to fill the pan; this is normal.
Return the pan to medium heat and cook, without stirring, for 15 minutes. The apples will soften and the caramel will darken further. Tilt the pan occasionally to ensure even cooking.
Roll out the puff pastry to a circle slightly larger than the pan. Lay it over the apples, tucking the edges down inside the pan. If the handle is not ovenproof, wrap it in foil.
Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the pastry is golden and puffed. The edges will brown before the centre, this is fine.

Remove from the oven and let rest for 5 minutes. Place a serving plate over the pan, then quickly and confidently invert the tart onto the plate. If any apples stick, gently replace them. Serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: Tarte tatin is best served warm or at room temperature on the day it is made, though it can be gently reheated. Once cooked, do not refrigerate, the pastry will lose its crispness.
The apples can be prepared an hour ahead; keep them in a bowl of lemon water to prevent browning, then pat dry before arranging in the pan.
If your pan handle is not ovenproof, wrap it in foil before the tart goes into the oven.

title: Mì Vàng Xào Mềm
summary: Soft egg noodles stir-fried with chicken and aromatics, ready in 30 minutes.

items.raw: 2 spring onions, cut into 4 cm pieces
150 g choy sum, cut into 5 cm lengths

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Add the egg noodles and cook for 2 minutes until just softened but still a little firm, they'll cook a bit more in the pan. Drain well in a colander.
Heat 1 tbsp of the neutral oil in a large wok or frying pan over high heat. Add the chicken and cook, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes until cooked through. Transfer to a plate.

Add the remaining oil to the pan. Add the garlic and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the spring onions and choy sum, and stir-fry for 2 minutes until the choy sum is tender and bright.

Return the chicken to the pan. Add the cooked noodles, soy sauce, oyster sauce and sesame oil. Toss everything together, stirring gently but constantly, for 2 minutes until heated through and well mixed. Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and white pepper.
Divide between bowls and top with fried shallots if you like.

notes: Food safety: Cook chicken and other poultry until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.

title: Pasta con Broccoli, Aglio e Peperoncino
summary: Calabrian pasta with crispy broccoli, garlic and chilli

items.raw: 1 red chilli, thinly sliced (or 1 tsp chilli flakes)

steps.text: Heat a large frying pan over high heat without any oil. Add the broccoli and toss it around for 5–6 minutes, stirring often, until the florets are brown and crispy on the edges and tender inside. Tip onto a plate.
In the same frying pan, warm the olive oil over low-to-medium heat. Add the sliced garlic and chilli, stirring gently for 1–2 minutes until fragrant but not brown. The oil will flavour as it warms.
While the oil and garlic warm, bring a pot of salted water to a boil and cook the pasta until just al dente, about 10–12 minutes.
Drain the pasta, reserving a cup of the cooking water. Add the hot pasta to the frying pan with the garlic oil, tossing gently to coat. Add the crispy broccoli back in and toss again.
If it looks dry, splash in a splash of the pasta water to loosen it, you want it silky, not oily. Taste and add more salt and chilli if you like. Serve straightaway.

notes: This is best eaten fresh, the moment it comes off the stove, the broccoli stays crispest that way.
If you don't like chilli heat, leave it out or just use half a slice. It's your table.

title: Rasam
summary: Peppery tamarind and tomato soup, quick and warming, a Tamil dinner staple.

items.raw: 1 dried red chilli, broken in half

steps.text: Dry-roast the cumin seeds, black peppercorns and dried red chillies in a small pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until fragrant. Grind to a fine powder in a spice grinder or mortar and pestle.

Bring the stock to a boil in a large pot. Add the chopped tomatoes, tamarind paste, ground spices and turmeric. Simmer for 8–10 minutes until the tomatoes are soft and the flavours meld. Taste and adjust the salt.

While the rasam simmers, heat the oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the mustard seeds and let them crackle (about 30 seconds). Add the broken chilli and curry leaves, and fry for another minute until the curry leaves darken slightly.
Pour the tempering into the pot of rasam, stir through, and serve hot with rice, dosa or a simple bread. A sprig of fresh coriander on top is nice, if you have it.

notes: If you don't have tamarind paste, use ½ tsp tamarind concentrate or a squeeze of lemon juice, adjust to taste.
Rasam keeps well in the fridge for 2–3 days. Reheat gently on the stove; make the tempering fresh each time for maximum crackle.

title: Ojingeo Bokkeum
summary: Spicy stir-fried squid with gochugaru, garlic and sesame, a banchan that keeps all week.

items.raw: 500 g calamari, cleaned, cut into thin rings and 5 cm pieces
items.prep: cleaned, cut into thin rings and 5 cm pieces

items.raw: 1 spring onion, white and green parts separated, sliced
items.prep: white and green parts separated, sliced

steps.text: Blanch the calamari in boiling water for 1 minute, then drain and set aside, this stops it toughening when you stir-fry it.
Heat the sesame oil in a large pan or wok over medium-high heat. Add the garlic and fry, stirring, for about 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the gochugaru and stir for another 30 seconds to bloom the spice. Pour in the soy sauce and sugar.
Add the calamari and the white parts of the spring onion. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until everything is coated and heated through. Don't overcook or the squid will be rubbery.
Remove from heat. Fold through the green parts of the spring onion and sprinkle with sesame seeds.
Let it cool to room temperature, then transfer to a clean jar. It keeps covered in the fridge for 5 days.

notes: Make a double batch on Sunday: divide into two jars and it lasts the week. The flavour deepens after day two.
Serve cold or at room temperature with white rice and other banchan.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Apple and Cider Pork Braise
summary: Pork shoulder slow-cooked with cider, Tasmanian apples and thyme until it falls apart.

items.raw: 1.5 kg pork shoulder, skin and excess fat trimmed, cut into 5 cm chunks
items.prep: skin and excess fat trimmed, cut into 5 cm chunks

items.raw: Salt and black pepper, to taste
3 sprigs fresh thyme (or 1 tsp dried thyme)
4 medium Tasmanian apples, peeled, cored and quartered

steps.text: Heat the oven to 160°C. Pat the pork dry and season generously with salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Working in batches, brown the pork for 2–3 minutes on each side, then set aside on a plate. Don't crowd the pan, you're looking for a good golden colour, not steam.

In the same pot, cook the onions and garlic until the onions soften and just begin to colour, about 5 minutes. Pour in the cider, scraping up the browned bits at the bottom, and let it bubble for a minute.
Return the pork to the pot, add the stock, thyme and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, then cover and transfer to the oven for 2 hours, stirring occasionally.
Add the apples and stir through. Return to the oven, uncovered, for another 30 minutes, until the pork is very tender and the apples have softened into the sauce.
Taste and adjust the seasoning. If you like, stir through the honey for a little sweetness. Serve with crusty bread or mashed potato.

notes: Make this a day ahead and reheat gently; the flavours deepen overnight. Serve with mashed potato, crusty bread or steamed greens.
A dry Tasmanian apple cider works best, but you can use any dry cider. If you only have sweet cider on hand, reduce the honey.
Leftovers keep in the fridge for up to 4 days and freeze well for a month.
Food safety: Cook fresh pork to at least 70°C in the thickest part.

title: Blistered Shishito Peppers with Sesame and Fish Sauce
summary: Quick pan-charred peppers with a Southeast Asian dressing of fish sauce and toasted sesame.

steps.text: Heat the neutral oil in a large pan over high heat until it's shimmering. Working in batches if needed, add the shishito peppers and let them sit undisturbed for 1 to 2 minutes until the skin blisters and blackens in spots.
Toss the peppers and cook for another minute or two, shaking the pan occasionally, until they're soft and blistered all over. Transfer to a serving bowl.
While the peppers are still hot, whisk together the sesame oil, fish sauce, lime juice and caster sugar. Pour over the warm peppers and toss gently to coat.
Taste and add a pinch of salt if needed. Scatter the toasted sesame seeds over the top and serve warm or at room temperature.

notes: If you can't find shishitos, long green chillies work fine, just halve them lengthways so they cook through faster.
Make the dressing ahead of time if you like, but toss the peppers while they're still hot so they soak up the flavours.

title: Moi Moi
summary: Steamed bean pudding with hard-boiled eggs tucked inside, served warm with bread or rice

steps.text: Boil the 2 eggs for 8 minutes until just hard-boiled, then peel and set aside.

In a blender, combine the drained black-eyed peas, red onion, red chillies, garlic, raw egg, oil, ginger, salt and pepper. Blend until completely smooth, 2–3 minutes; the batter should be light and silky.
Lightly oil four small ramekins (about 200 ml each) or line four coffee cups with plastic wrap.
Divide one-third of the batter among the ramekins. Place a hard-boiled egg in the centre of each, then top with the remaining batter until each ramekin is three-quarters full.
Pour water into a large pot to a depth of 3 cm. Place a trivet or heat-proof saucer in the bottom. Bring to a boil until the water is bubbling steadily and steam is rising.

Carefully place the ramekins on the trivet. Cover the pot with a lid and steam over medium heat for 40 minutes, until the moi moi is set and springs back when lightly touched. Refill the water if it falls below the level of the trivet.
Remove from the pot and let rest for 5 minutes. Run a knife around the edge of each ramekin and turn out onto a plate (if using ramekins) or unwrap carefully. Serve warm with bread or rice.

notes: Make ahead: Prepare the batter up to 4 hours before steaming and keep chilled. Assemble and steam when ready.
Banana leaves: If you have fresh or frozen banana leaves, wrap each portion in a leaf before steaming for that authentic texture.
This uses raw or lightly cooked egg. Use fresh, clean, uncracked eggs (pasteurised if you can get them), keep it cold, and skip it for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or with low immunity.
Food safety: Raw and lightly cooked foods aren't recommended for pregnant women, young children, older people or anyone with a weakened immune system.

title: Spiced Potato Roti Filling
summary: Mashed potatoes with cumin and green chilli for stuffing roti, a weeknight Indo-Fijian favourite.

items.raw: 800 g floury potato, peeled and cut into chunks
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Drain well.
While the potato cooks, heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them crackle for 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add the diced onion and cook, stirring, until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the chopped green chillies and cook for another minute, until fragrant and the chillies have softened slightly.
Tip the hot potato into the pan and mash gently with the back of a wooden spoon, breaking it into floury pieces rather than a smooth paste. The potato should be chunky and still slightly warm.
Mix in the salt and pepper to taste. Set aside to cool slightly before using to fill roti.

notes: Make the filling up to 3 hours ahead and reheat gently before using. It's best warm but not piping hot when you wrap it.
Use waxy potato if floury is hard to find, it'll be a bit stickier but still work fine.

title: Grilled Octopus with Charred Lemon
summary: Tender grilled octopus with charred lemon, olive oil and oregano

items.raw: 1 kg whole octopus, fresh or thawed
1 tbsp fresh oregano, leaves (or 1 tsp dried oregano)
Salt and black pepper, to taste

steps.text: Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil. Add the octopus, onion and bay leaves. Simmer gently for 45–60 minutes, until the octopus is tender, a fork should pierce it easily. Drain and let cool slightly.
Cut the octopus in half lengthwise, then cut each half into 4 or 5 pieces. Pat dry with paper towel.
Heat your grill to high until very hot and smoking lightly. Brush the octopus pieces with a little olive oil and season with salt and pepper.
Grill the octopus for 3–4 minutes each side until charred and crispy on the outside. Transfer to a plate.
Place the lemon halves cut-side down on the grill and char for 2–3 minutes until dark and caramelised.
Arrange the octopus on a serving platter. Drizzle generously with olive oil, scatter with oregano, squeeze the charred lemon juice over everything and season with more salt and pepper. Serve warm.

notes: You can prep the octopus the day before: boil it, cool, cut it, and store it in the fridge. Grill it fresh on the day.
Charring the lemon is crucial, don't skip it. The bitterness and colour make the dish.
If you can't find whole fresh octopus, use frozen. Thaw it overnight in the fridge first.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Egg White Soup with Crab
summary: Silken egg white ribbons in delicate crab and chicken broth.

items.raw: 200 g crab meat, fresh or tinned, drained
2 tsp cornstarch, mixed with 3 tbsp water
2 spring onions, green parts only, finely sliced (optional)

steps.text: Bring the chicken stock to a gentle boil in a large saucepan over medium-high heat. Add the crab meat and simmer for 2 minutes, stirring gently, until the crab has warmed through.

In a small bowl, beat the egg whites lightly with a fork until just combined and slightly foamy. Pour the beaten egg white in a thin, steady stream into the simmering broth while stirring gently in one direction with a wooden spoon. The egg white will form delicate, silken ribbons as it cooks, about 1–2 minutes. Don't stir aggressively or the ribbons will break into small pieces.
Give the cornstarch slurry a quick stir and pour it slowly into the soup while stirring gently. The broth should thicken slightly and become translucent, about 1 minute.
Taste and season with salt and white pepper. Stir in the sesame oil.
Pour into serving bowls and scatter the spring onion greens on top, if using. Serve immediately while the soup is hot.

notes: Use sashimi-grade or very fresh crab meat if available; tinned crab in brine works too.
White pepper, not black, keeps the soup's refined appearance, no dark specks.
Don't let the broth boil hard when pouring the egg white, or it will scramble into lumps instead of forming ribbons.
Cook chicken until it reaches 75°C in the thickest part and the juices run clear.
Food safety: Cook fish until it is opaque and flakes easily (63°C in the thickest part), and prawns until pink and opaque all the way through.

title: Sweet Potato and Kale Sheet Pan with Tahini Drizzle
summary: Roasted sweet potato wedges and massaged kale with tahini, garlic and lemon dressing.

items.raw: 700 g sweet potato, cut into thick wedges

steps.text: Heat oven to 220°C. Toss the sweet potato wedges with 2 tbsp oil, salt and pepper. Spread on a large sheet pan and roast for 15 minutes until starting to soften and colour.
While the sweet potato cooks, whisk together tahini, minced garlic, lemon juice and 1 tbsp oil in a bowl with 3 tbsp water until smooth and pourable. Season with salt and pepper.

Toss the kale with a pinch of salt and massage with your hands for 1 minute until it softens slightly. Push the kale to the sides of the pan, then add it to the sweet potato. Toss everything together.
Roast for another 5 minutes until the kale is tender and the sweet potato is golden and crispy at the edges.
Divide between bowls and drizzle with the tahini dressing. Serve hot.

title: Gotamba
summary: Sweet crispy fried dough with banana and jaggery, a Sri Lankan street breakfast.

items.raw: 60 ml neutral oil, plus extra for frying

steps.text: Mix flour and salt in a bowl. Add 60 ml oil and rub between your fingers until the mixture is crumbly, about 2 minutes. Add warm water a little at a time, mixing with your hand until you have a soft, sticky dough. Knead gently for 1 minute and set aside to rest for 5 minutes.
Divide the dough into 2 portions. On a lightly oiled surface, stretch and flatten each portion into a thin rectangle, about 3 mm thick.

Scatter half the banana slices over each rectangle, then sprinkle with jaggery. Roll up tightly from one end, then coil the roll back on itself to make a tight spiral. Flatten slightly with the heel of your hand to about 1 cm thick.
Heat 2–3 cm neutral oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers, about 3 minutes. When a small piece of dough sizzles immediately, it's ready.
